CONFIDENTIAL. 


Correspondence respecting the Rights and Privileges of 


the Latin and Greek Churches in Turkey. 


(EASTERN QUESTION) 


PART VIII. 


No, 1. 
Mr. Elliot to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 19.) 


(Secret. ) 
My Lord, Vienna, November 14, 1855. 


YOUR Lordship is already acquainted with the language held by Count 
Buol to M. de Bourqueney, on the day of the departure of the latter for Paris, 
in which the disposition of the Austrian Government to adopt towards Russia a 
more decided line of policy than they haye hitherto pursued, was plainly 
indicated, 

During his stay at Paris, M. de Bour ueney was made thoroughly aware of 
the views and opinions of His Majesty the Emperor Napoleon and of Count 
Walewski; on his return here, therefore, a fortnight ago, he informed Count 
Buol that he was authorised, unofficially, to resume the conversation which had 
been commenced at the moment of his leaving Vienna, Count Buol expressed 
his willingness to do so, but said that, although these communications would be 
of an unofficial and strictly confidential nature, he considered it essential, and 
due to Her Majesty's Government, that I should be informed of everything that 
passed between them. 1 need not say how entirely M. de Bourqueney coincided 
in this view; but I must bear testimony to the complete and unreserved confi- 
dence with which he has regularly kept me acquainted with all that was passing, 
Count Buol likewise alluded to these conversations, but left it to Baron de 
Bourqueney to inform me of the details of them. 

It is unnecessary for me to detain your Lordship by going minutely into 
these details, or to describe the gradual development of Count Buol’s views, till 
they finally took the form of a proposal, that the Austrian Government should 
send to St. Petersburgh an ultimatum, on the rejection of which, or on its non- 
acceptation within a determined number of days, the immediate rupture of 
relations between the two countries should take place. 

As, under the Treaty of the 2nd of December, no step of this nature can be 
taken by Austria without having previously consulted the Governments of 
Great Britain and France, the labours of Count Buol and of M. de Bourqueney 
have been directed to the object of making the proposed ultimatum as acceptable 
to them as possible. 

A memorandum embodying this proposal has been drawn up, and will 
probably be signed by Count Buol, and “« paraphé” by Baron de Bourqueney

to-night or to-morrow morning, and will be forthwith transmitted to Paris, As

within a few hours after you receive this despatch: I will therefore confine 
myself to stating that it is proposed there should be concluded between Great 
Britain, Austria, and France, a ‘Treaty guarantecing the independence and 
integrity of the Turkish Empire, and establishing, as a casus bel, any attempt 
upon them by Russia, or any infraction of the other terms on whieh the peace is 
to be concluded, and which comprise — 

l. The abandonment by Russia of lier Protectorate over the Principalities, 
whose military position is to be secured by a change of the frontier of the Pruth, 
and according to which, in exchange for the territory now occupied by the alhed 
armies, Russia will be required to give up a considerable portion of Bessarabia, 

2. The freedom of the navigation of the Danube, which will be regulated 
by the rules established at the Congress of Vienna with respect to navigable 
rivers, 

3. The entire neutralisation of the Black Sea, where neither ships of war 
nor military establishments are to be permitted. | 

4. The maintenance of the privileges of the Christian subjects of the Porte, 

all due regard being puid to the sovereignty of the Sultan: and deliberations 
being held upon the means of accomplishing this object, Russia will be admitted 
to her share in them on her acceptation of these terms of peace, 
,. the Austrian Government are to be empowered to signify to the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh that if, within the prescribed idelay, the present proposal is 
accepted without change or alteration, the allied Governments are prepared 
immediately to sign preliminaries of peace, to be followed by a general 
armistice, and the negotiation of the permanent ‘Treaty, 

If, on the contrary, this unconditional acceptance should not be made, the 
complete and immediate rupture of ail relations between the two countries will 
take place, and means considered for compelling Russia to make peace. The 
cooperation of the whole of Europe would be invited to this end, and Prussia 
would be informed that upon her breaking offall relations with Russia she would 
be admitted to the deliberations to be held, 

Such are the main features of the proposal for which it is my duty to 
prepare your Lordship, and which is now so far matured that there is little 
prospect of any material change being made init. The strictest secrecy has been 
preserved with regard to it, and Count Buol attaches the greatest importance to 
its continuance, 

He intends, if the acquiescence of the Cabinets of London and Paris is given 
to the plan, that nota day shall be lost in the transmission of it to St. Petersburgh. 

A communication of it would also be made at the sume time to the Ring of 
Prussia, with an invitation to afford it his support. 

The policy of the Austrian Government has hitherto been so cautious, not 
to say pusillanimous, that the attitude now suddenly adopted is almost caleu- 
lated in the first instance to awaken distrust, and a suspicion that some secret 
motive must be at the bottom of so great a change; but I fully believe the cause 
of it may safely be attributed to the suceess of the allied armies: betore 
Sebastopol, 

Nobody can have had intimate communication with Count Buol without 
becoming convinced that his own wishes would long ago have led him to follow 
amore worthy line of policy, and that he was at times painfully conscious of the 
smallness of the part borne by Austria on a question in which she should have 
taken a leading position. 

He has had especially to contend against the influence of persons who had 
constant access ta the Emperor, who, while they would rather persuade His 
Majesty to identify himself with the cause of Russia than ally himself closer to 
England and France, never ceased urging upon him the hopelessness of the 
undertaking of the allies in the Crimea; and un opinion so confidently given by 
those who were considered on tuilitary matters the highest authorities of the 
Empire, not unnaturally had its weight with the Emperor. 

The influence of this party was entirely shaken by the news of the capture 
of Sebastopol, and on the arrival of Count Buol at eahs he found the Emperor 
animated hy the best dispositions towards the allies, und his own ascen ancy 
firmly established. 

He lost no time in availing himself of bis improved position, and two days 


a 


after his return to Vienna, he held to Baron de Bourqueney the language which 
gave the first intimation of the possible adoption of a new line of policy. M. de 
Bourqueney remained absent a month, but on his return found that there had 
been not only no relapse to past timidity, but that Count Buol’s views had 
become strengthened and matured in the interval, and that the Emperor had 
adopted unreservedly the policy of his Minister, and was cordial in his desire ta 
see it carried out,

EN arrétant le plan de conduite & suivre par Je Gouvernement Autrichien, de

de la paix sur des bases fixées en commun par les trois Cours alliées, M. le Comte

A cet effet, au moment de parapher avec moi le memorandum de ce jour,

toute l’authentieité désirable, je crois ne pouvoir mieux faire, M. le Comte, que 
de les consigner textuellement dans la présente dépéche, dont la substance a été 
communiquée par moi id M. le Comte de Buol. 

Aux termes du memorandum paraphe ce matin, le rejet par la Russie de 
ultimatum Autrichien entrainerait immeédiatement, et de plein droit, ‘les 
conséquences suivantes :— 


L. La rupture des relations diplomatiques entre les Cours de Vienne et de 
St. Pétersbourg ; 

2, La conclusion d’un accord entre les trois Puissances alliées sur les 
moyens de-contraindre la Russie & souserire aux conditions posées dans 
Pultimatum ; 

a. La coopération de ees mémes Puissances 4 [effet d’amener les autres 
Etats Européens & s‘associer 4 V'action commune contre la Russie, 


Reprenant successivement ces trois points, M. le Comte de Buol ena précieé 
le sens par les explications qui suivent. 

La rupture des relations diplomatiques devra étre immediate et complete: 
immédiate, puisqu'elle suivra ipso facto le rejet de l'ultimatum en tout ou en 
partie; compléte, en ce qu'elle entrainera la cessation absolue de toutes relations 
diplomatiques, et, par conséquent, le retrait en totalité des deux Missions 
respectives. Elle impliquera naturellement, de la part de l’Autriche, adoption 
des mesures nécessaires pour repousser la force par la force. Ce sera la guerre 
moins aggression. 

L’accord 4 intervenir sur les moyens de contrainte n’entrainera pas néces- 
sairement l'entrée actuelle de |’Autriche en campagne. auf les modifications 
que les évenements ultéricurs pourront apporter, sous ce rapport, aux ves de. 
lAutriche et méme de ses allies, M. le Comte de Buol établit l'inopportunité 
d'une déclaration de guerre de la part du Gouvernement Autrichien suivant 
Immeédiatement la rupture diplomatique avec la Russie, Atiaquée par l'Autriche, 
la Russie, dit en effet M. de Buol, se défendrait avec I'énergie du désespoir ; 
attirant l'ennemie chez elle, et évoquant contre lui les souvenirs de 1812, elle 
ranimerait le courage de ses populations, et imposerait peut-(tre aux Puissances 
alli¢es dimmenses sacrifices en hommes et en argent qui ne les rapprocheraient 
pas du but de leurs efforts, le rétablissement de la paix. Des questions 
presqu’insolubles seraient infailliblement souleyées par la guerre portée au sein 
méme de l'Europe; et ces questions, M. de Buol avoue franchement vouloir les 
écarter le plus longtemps qu il sera possible. 

Mais si l'entente d intervenir n'entraine pas, selon M. de Buol, dans lintérét 
méme de la cause commune, lentrée effective de l'Autriche cn campagne, elle 
implique foreément la combinaison des réles de chacune des trois Puissances 
dans l'action commune contre la Russie, ainsi que la correlation préétablie des 
opérations militaires respectives, 

En ce qui concerne |’ Autriche (et M. de Buol voit dans sa proposition un 
moyen de faire taire fous les soupgons, de détruire toutes les méfances dont la 
politique de son Gouvernement a été Vobjet depuis dix-huit mois) elle serait 
préte 4 déterminer par Traité les Sun ane de occupation prolongée des Princi.

Ainsi. dans l’Article des Prineipautés Danubiennes nous n’avons pas seule. 
ment frappé le protectorat exclusif, nous avons annulé tout droit particulier

tions également irréprochables: Vassentiment des Puissances garantes et le yoru

__ Nous avons pose le principe fondamental du développement du systéme

“contre toute agression étrangere” répondent 4 cette préoccupation, et le Comte 
Buol en les acceptant s'est parfaitement rendu compte d'une désignation indirecte

_ La rectification de frontiére est a vral dire pour la Russie la perte de la 
moitié de la Bessarabie. C'est l'annulation des Traiteés de Jassy et d'Andrinople: 
c'est la Porte vengée de revers de 1828 et 1829; c'est l’Angleterre, cest la

L'affranchissement du Danube continue 4 trouver sa garantie dans Vinstitu-

La neutralisation de la Mer Noire une fois admise par le Comte Buol comme 
base des préliminaires de la paix, ne comportait pas, dans 1’Article qui Ia concerne, 
des modifications de forme; toutefois, elle me semble mieux définie et plus 
solennellement proclamée dans la nouvelle rédaction. Sous la forme de quelques 
principes généraux, elle embrasse plus d’application et précise mieux la seule 
exception admise @ la régle de la cléture des Détroits, dans la présence des station-

L' Article relatif & l'ameélioration du sort des populations Chreétiennes sujettes 
de la Porte, a & peine été modifié; il stipule néanmoins d’une maniére plus 
explicite que les Conférences ouvertes & Constantinople devront avoir achevé

rencontrera naturellement vers le Souverain ct les alliés au lieu de s’égarer en

Le memorandum enfin contient l'engagement de lAutriche de signer avee

ment Glargi, puisqu'il ne fesait pour V'Autriche un cas de guerre que de Vaug- 
mentation du nombre des vaisseaux Russes au dela d'un chiffre déterminé, 

elles sont, M. le Comte, les considérations que mon devoir était de placer

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No, 1,356, Confidential.) 

My Lord, Foreign Office, November 24, 1855. 
ON the 19th instant the French Ambassador communicated to me a 

despatch from Count Walewski, together with some despatches from the French 

Minister at Vienna to Count Walewski, and 1 lose no time in informing your 


Excellency of the contents of those despatches, and stating the opinion of 
Her Majesty’s Government upon the important matters to which they relate. 

Count Walewski announces that Austria offers to send, on her own account, 
an ultimatum to St. Petersburgh, and to declare to Russia that if in fifteen days 
that ultimatum is not accepted, the Austrian Minister would be ordered to quit 
St. Petersburgh, and the diplomatic relations between the two Empires would be 
broken off. As soon as the rupture was effected, the Cabinet of Vienna would 
eoncert with those of London and Paris upon the means that could be best 
employed in order to attain the object of the alliance. Prussia would be invited 
to take part in this concert between the three Powers, but upon the absolute 
condition of having, like Austria, previously broken off her relations with 
Russia. 

Count Walewski states that the ultimatum of Austria is founded upon the 
scheme, revised and greatly extended, which formed the basis of the last negotia- 
tions at Vienna, and his Excellency is of opinion that it would be impossible, 
with respect to the first guarantee, to frame a larger or better basis, nor one that 
would more completely answer the object that En land and France have in view 
for the new organization of the three Danubian rincipalities. With regard to 
the second point, which concerns the establishment of a Russian frontier on the 
side of the Principalities, and which, instead of a small river, substitutes a cliain 
of mountains difficult of nceess, and which takes away from Russia all the mouths 
of the Danube, Count Walewski considers that it would be superfluous to point 
out the great importance of such an arrangement. 

The problem of the third guarantee being solved by the system to which 
Russia has hitherto offered the most determined resistance, Count Walewski 
does not hesitate to alfirm that the question for which the war was undertaken is 
thereby effectually settled. 

His Excellency further gives his entire approbation to the plan by which 
the delicate questions involved in the fourth guarantee are to be discussed and 
settled without the concurrence of Russia; and he states that that Power would 
thon have to adopt the decisions taken upon a subject which has served as the 
pretext, if it was not the real motive, of the present war, without her Plenipo- 
tentiarics having been even admitted to the discussion. 

Count Walewski then proceeds to remark, that in whatever point of view 
the ultimatum proposed by Austria is regarded, it is impossible not to admit 
that she makes a great advance towards the Western Powers, and in the same 
dewree recedes from Russia; and his Excellency states that, in the opinion of the 
Emperor of the French, the offer of the Cabinet of Vienna should at once be 
accepted, His Imperial Majesty also thinks that as, at present, there is no 
question of framing definitively a Treaty of Peace, and as the text of Count 
Huol's ultimatum does not attempt to define precisely the conditions upon which 
peace shall be concluded, it would he advisable not to attempt the introduction 
of amendments or modifications of which the necessity was not clearly demon- 
strated, but that, on the contrary, it would be expedient to adopt the ultimatum 
in its entirety, reserving for the definitive negotiation the mature discussion of 
details, and the additions upon which it might then be necessary to insist. 

Count Walewski remarks that in the event of the ultimatum being rejected 
by Russia, the attitude that Austria would then assume would be favourable 
alike to the policy and to the military position of the allies; for Russia, when 
once her relations with Vienna are broken off, will be compelled to guard her 
frontier from the Danube to Galicia, as upon the whole of that line she may at 
any moment expect to be attacked ; and it is not improbable that this constant 
menaee may determine the evacuation of the Crimea, in order that the Russian 
army might take its positions along the frontiers of Austria, in Bessarabia, 
Volhynia, and Podolia, ‘This attitude of Austria menacing various points of the 
Russian territory, to which Russia would be unable to put an end by entering 
into w conflict at the point which best suited her, would be more detrimental to 
Russia than an immediate declaration of war. In fact, the day that war was 
declared, Russia might choose her own ground, and nothing need prevent her 
from invading the Austrian territory; but Russia, if war is not declared, will 
cautiously abstain from invading the territory of Austria, 4s she well knows that 
she would then draw down upon herself Prussia and the whole of Germany, who 
are bound to come to the aid of Austria if she is attacked in her own dominions. 
or even in the Principalities. 


13 


_ Finally, Count Walewski expresses an earnest hope that the views con- 
tained in his despatch may meet with the concurrence of Her Majesty’s 
Government, and he strongly recommends the aduption of the Austrian 
ultimatum. 

M. de Bourqueney states that, in discussing the conduct which the Austrian 
Government would adopt in concert with the Cabinets of Paris and London for 
the re-establishment of peace upon bases agreed upon between the three allied 
Powers, Count Buol had expressed his determination to avoid the renewal of the 
misunderstandings which have hitherto at various times threatened to com- 
promise the relations of Austria with the Western Powers, while M. de 
Bourqueney on his part, throughout these discussions, established with seru- 
pulous care that the belligerent Powers refused to take the initiative in this 
matter, and that they would confine themselves to examining and accepting, if 
they were offered to them, the conditions of peace which they were irrevocably 
determined to obtain by force of arms. | 

Austria accordingly, M. de Bourqueney says, appropriates to herself the 
proposed conditions of peace, if France and England consent to recognise in 
them a basis of preliminaries. Austria will send them to St. Petersburgh as her 
own ultimatum, and will make the rupture of her relations depend on their 
aeceptance. At the same time that the ultimatum leaves Vienna for St, Peters- 
burgh, the King of Prussia will be invited by Austria to support if, 

_ I herewith inclose a copy of the conditions which form the Austrian 
ultimatum. M, de Bourqueney enters at considerable length upon an expla- 
nation of these conditions, and the consequences to which they would lead in 
the event of their being either accepted or rejected by Russia; but [do not 
think it necessary to place his statements on record, as they are accurately 
summed up in the despatch of Count Walewski to the French Ambassador, 

It is right, however, for me to state that Count Buol declared to M. de 
Bourqueney that the rupture of diplomatic relations would be immediate and 
complete: immediate, because it would ipso facto follow the rejection of the 
ultimatum in whole or in part; complete, because it would be the absolute 
cessation of all diplomatic relations and the withdrawal of the whole of the 
respective Missions. It will naturally imply on the part of Austria the adoption 
of measures for repelling force by force; it will be war without aggression. 

Austria would, moreover, be prepared to determine by a Treaty the 

conditions on which the Austrian troops should continue to occupy the 
Principalities ; and she would undertake the effective defence of the whole 
Danubian frontier of the Ottoman Empire to the sea, with the understanding, 
however, that such arrangements should in no way interfere with the Western 
Powers nor affect their complete liberty to select the field of their future 
operations. ; 
_ Count Buol lastly considers that the cooperation of the three allied Powers 
in order to bring the other States of Europe to join them, will be an effectual 
means of accelerating the reestablishment of peace, for Russia, if she still 
perseveres in her blind resistance, would then be placed to the ban of Europe. 

These proposals, in the framing of which Her Majesty's Government have 
had no part (although Mr. Elliot was duly informed by the Baron de-Bour- 
queney of what is passing), have been considered with the anxious care that 
their gravity and importance demanded. 

__ Her Majesty's Government have no wish to extend the war to objects 
different from those for which it was undertaken ; they deeply feel the reapon- 
sibility which would weigh upon them if they continued the war longer than 
might be necessary for obtaining a safe and honourable peace ; they admit, that 
it is their duty to entertain and frankly to express theie opinion upon any 
proposals, from whatsoever quarter they may come, by which such a peace ma 
be obtained ; but it is also their duty to reject all propositions for peace whie 
will not effect the objects for which the war was undertaken and England has 
made such yast sacrifices, and for the attainment of which the honour of the 
British nation is pledged. Her Majesty’s Government are moreover determined 
not again to enter upon negotiations for peace which do not afford a fair 
prospect of being carried to a successful issue, nor rashily to incur the danger of 
creating false hopes and of postponing indefinitely the restoration of peace, by u 
second failure of negotiation, 

With a full sense of these obligations Her Majesty's Government have 
E 


14 


considered the Austrian proposals, and I need hardly assure your Excellency 
that the earnest opinions of the Emperor in favour of these propositions, which 
were conveyed in the despatch of Count Walewski and were expressed to 
me by the French Ambassador, have had great weight with Her Majesty's 
Government, 

Her Majesty's Government concur with that of the Emperor in thinking 
that Austria has voluntarily made an important step towards the Western 
Powers, and they observe with satisfaction that the ultimatum consists of certain 
distinct and definite conditions which admit of no modifications, and which 
Russia is to be called upon to accept or to reject, and that consequently in the 
event of their being accepted, negotiations for peace would be resumed upon the 
admission of demands exceeding those which Russia has already refused, and her 
rejection of which led to the rupture of the former negotiations. 

Her Majesty's Government do not hesitate to recognise the value of the 
engagement taken by Austria to break off diplomatic relations with Russia if her 
ultimatum should be wholly or in part rejected by that Power; and for the 
reasons assigned hy Count Walewski, they are disposed to think that an 
‘mmediate declaration of war on the part of Austria as a consequence of that 
rupture would be impolitic, but that immediate preparations for war must be 
the necessary result of the position which Austria will then assume. ‘That 
position will restore to Austria the influence she is entitled to exercise it 
Germany, and it is hardly to be doubted that the German Powers, who must 
now be aware that they have little to fear, and still less to hope, from Russia, 
will then be prepared to: cooperate wgainst the common enemy of that peace 
which Europe anxiously desires. . 

Upon a careful review of these different considerations, Her Majesty s 
Government feel bound to give their assent to the ultimatum, provided that 
certain modifications are agreed to which appear necessary for giving full effect 
to the intentions of the Powers concerned, 

L will then, in the first place, inform your Excellency that although Her 
Majesty’s Government do not propose to make any material change in the 
wording of the Austrian ultimatum, which must be regarded as chiefly laying 
down general principles, yet they cannot hold themselves bound by that wording, 
and must reserve to themselves the right to propose such amendments a8 muy 
appear necessary to guard the great interests affected by the ultimatum. 

Austria proposes that the stipulations with reference to the Black Sea 
should be the subject of a separate ‘Treaty between Russia and the Porte, which 
Treaty should then be annexed to the General Treaty, and be considered to have 
equal force and value with it, But to this mode of settling the most important 
question at issue, and of establishing the guarantee upon which the safety of 
Turkey and the peace of Hurope must in future depend, Her Majesty's 
Government entertain an insuperable objection. 

We know by experience that such separate arrangements are held to 
concern only the Contracting Parties, and that their annexation to General 
Treaties is contended to be only a registration of the act and a record of the 
sanction given to it by other Powers, and that when war or private arrangement 
annuls that separate Act between the Contracting Parties, the Powers who 
rete the General ‘Treaty to which the Separate Treaty is annexed, are not 

led upon to interfere, and their right to do so has even been disputed, This 
doctrine has been held by Austria, Russia, and Prussia; and although it hus 
never been admitted by England, yet Her Majesty's Government cannot 
to a form to which such an interpretation has been given by some of the 
Powers who would be parties to the arrangement. 

Now, it is not difficult to imagine the various causes which hereafter might 
lead to the abrogation of a separate ‘Treaty between Russia and the Porte, and 
if Austria, England, and France were under no obligation, and lad no right, to 
interfere, and to maintain that ‘Treaty inviolate, Europe might again be exposed 
to a renewal of the dangers against which it is the object of the allies to guard, 
It is manifest, therefore, that no separate arrangement should take place between 
Russia and the Porte, and that all stipulations concerning the Black Sea should 
form an integral part of the General Treaty. 

A stipulation will be necessary for the reception of Consuls in the Russian 
ports of the Black Sea. 

Military arsenals must be understood to comprehend naval arsenals, 


15 


‘The Austrian Government very properly suggests that the belligerents should 
reserve to themselves the right of proposing any further conditions that they 
may think necessary; but Her Majesty's Government are of opinion that it 
would not be just as regards Austria, nor honourable towards Russia, if they 
abstained from indicating such conditions as at the present moment they are 
clearly of opinion must be proposed, though without engaging that it will not 
be their duty to insist upon others. 

The first is, that no military or naval establishments shall be restored or 
created in the Aland Islands. 

Secondly, The right to consider the state of the territories on the east of 
the Black Sea, 

In the consideration of these various matters, the gravity of which cannot 
be exaggerated, Her Majesty's Government, although they found themselves 
unable to agree to the recommendation of Count Walewski that the Austrian 
proposals should be adopted in their entirety, yet they trust that the moditica- 
tions which they have suggested for the sole purpose of rendering these 
proposals more clear and effective, will meet with the concurrence of the French 
Government, and be accepted by the Cabinet of Vienna, 

It only remains for me to state that Her Majesty's Government do entire 
justice to the motives which induce the Austrian Government to appropriate to 
itself the ultimatum, and on its own account to transmit it to St. Petersburgh ; 
but Her Majesty’s Government conceive that this course can hardly be adopted 
with correctness, and with reference to the real state of things. It is 
perfectly true that Her Majesty's Government had no part in framing the 
ultimatum, and that they had no wish that any communication on the part of 
England should be made to the Cabinet. of St. Petersburgh ; but the ultimatum 
has been submitted to them as well as to the French Government, and they have 
in general terms agreed to it. ‘The sanction of England and France has, 
therefore, been obtained by Austria, and it is in fact by their authority that 
Austria will transmit her ultimatum to St. Petersburgh. Any disguise upon 
this matter would, therefore, be useless and unbecoming. It may indeed be 
said that it docs not become the dignity of England and France to make 
proposals to Russia, but the dignity of England and France, and the position 
which they occupy, are not to be impaired by a frank avowal of the conditions 
on which they will consent to lay down their arms, and a manifestation of the 
good faith with which they will treat for the restoration of peace. 

As the Austrian Government propose to make the rupture of diplomatic 
relations with Russia depend upon the rejection of the ultimation in whole or in 
part by the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, Her Majesty's Government trust that 
there will be no difficulty in obtaining from the Austrian Government a positive 
declaration that they will receive no counter propositions from Russia, nor 
consent to any modification whatever of the terms to which England and France 
have given their adherence. Your Excellency is instructed to read and give a 
copy of this despatch to Count Walewski. 


Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received November 26.) 


(No, 1,522. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, November 22, 1855. 

COUNT WALEWSKI stated to me yesterday afternoon that he had 
received from M, de Persigny an account of his conversation with your 
Lordships, after the Cabinet had had under their consideration the propositions 
made to the French Government by Austria. M. de Persigny reports the 
decision of Her Majesty’s Government to be as follows :— 

Her Majesty's Government regret that the propositions should have been 
made at all; they see no safe issue to negotiations based upon them, and were it 
not for the stronz desire evinced by the Emperor that the propositions should be 
favourably considered by Her Majesty’s advisers, the Government would, in ‘all 
probability, have declined entertaming them. But taking into their considera- 
tion the decided wishes of the Emperor, and desirous of thus showing their 
ileference for His Majesty's opinions, they are willing to agree to ustria 
pursuing the course whieh she proposes; but they desire that the following 
conditions and observations should accompany their expression of adherence -— 

They demand that the stipulations concerning the neutralisation of the 
Black Sea shall {orm an integral part of the Treaty of Peace to he signed between 
the allies and Russia, and that they shall not be made the object of a separate 
Convention between the Porte and Russia, to be annexed to the General 
‘Treaty. 

‘They require that the words “ military arsenals,” should be made to comprise 
naval arsenals. 

They understand that the Sea of Azoff is included im the Treaty arrangements 
respecting the Black Sen. 

They consider that it would not be fair to leave Austria in doubt as to the 
intentions of the allies in regard to any further conditions they may ask, and that 
Austria should be told that an engagement may be demanded of Russia not to 
reconstruct fortifications on the Aland Islands, and that the general position of 
the territories east of the Black Sca may have to be considered according to the 
events of the war, 

Her Majesty's Government insist, farther, that Austria should, in sending 
the ultimatum to St, Petersburgh, represent that she has no authority from 
France or Enyland to make these proposals, though Her Majesty’s Government 
will not object to her stating that she has reason to believe that the terms, if 
accepted by Russia, will be agreed to by the allies. 

Her Mujesty’s Government declare, further, that they cannot enter into 
negotiations without the consent of the Porte, and they require that Austria 
should be informed that Sardinia will take part in those negotiations. 

M, de Persigny stated that he considered that these alterations were 
reasonable, and did not change the character of the proposals. I regret to add 
that his opinion is not partaken by Count Walewski, nor, as the sequel of this 
despatch will show, by the Emperor. 

After thus communicating to me the substance of M. de Persigny’s 
despatches, Count Walewski said that he did not know whether he was to 
consider them as containing the official answer of Her Majesty’s Government, 
but that he should proceed to reason upon the different points adverted to by 
your Lordship, as if it was an official communication, though he could only be 
considered as giving his own opinions, not having been able as yet to show 
M. de Persigny’s despatches to the Emperor. 

He must begin by saying that he did not consider that the proposed 
Austrian ultimatum required the explanations or additions asked, for by 


l7 


Her Majesty's Government, and he must take this opportunity of stating that it 
was not because France wanted peace that the Emperor and his Government 
desired that these terms should be accepted, but because they held that the 
terms were good and acceptable in themselves. Moreover, he could not under- 
stand what was meant by accepting these terms as a deference to the Emperor’s 
opinions, when their nature was changed by the alterations and additions which 
were demanded. 

Count Walewski then proceeded to examine your Lordship’s observations 
one by one. 

He agreed, he said, that the neutralisation of the Black Sea, should be one 
of the conditions inserted in the General Treaty of Peace, and he considered that 
Count Buol intended that the first and last paragraphs under the head of that 
oe of his ultimatum entitled ‘‘La Mer Noire,” should be included in the 
Jeneral ‘Treaty. It was only the stipulations for carrying into effect the prin- 
ciple of neutralisation, that were to form the subject of a Separate Convention 
between Russia and the Porte, 

Count Walewski agreed that the word “arsenal” should be defined as 
relating to maritime as well as to military armaments. 

His Excellency objected to the Sea of Azoff being considered as subject to 
such arrangements as might be made for the Black Sea. Moreover, he thought 
the stipulation superfluous, because the Sea of Azoff was not navigable for 
large ships; at the same time the condition would be most humiliating to 
Russia, for the Sea of Azoff was an inland sea, watering Russian territory only, 
a an attempt to impose conditions there would be met with an obstinate 
refusal, 

Count Walewski considered it quite unnecessary to apprize Austria of the 
nature of any other demands which the allies might have to make; and with 
respect to the particular conditions put forward by Her Majesty s Government, 
not to permit the reconstruction of fortifications on the Islands of Aland, and 
to reserve, for consideration, the future conditions of the countries to the east 
of the Black Sea, he observed, in regard to the first, that although he should 
be very glad if Russia could be brought to agree to such a condition, he should 
not be inclined to make it a sine qud non to the signature of peace. We had 
objected to the Polish question being brought forward ; he should place that of 
the Aland Islands in the same category, to be determined upon by events. 
With regard to the fate of the countries to the east of the Black Sea, Her 
Majesty's Government, he observed, had felt the difficulty of making any definite 
proposition, and the expressions made use of by your Lordship were too vague 
to render a discussion of them possible. 

It was already understood, his Excellency eontinued, that Austria was to 
absolve the allies from having taken the initiative in the proposed proceedings. 
He assented to the course which Her Majesty’s Government desired to follow 
in this part of the matter. 

He was also of opinion, with your Lordship, that the Porte must be 
consulted as to the terms of pence, but this need not interfere with the action of 
Austria at St. Petersburgh. 

Lastly, there could be no doubt that Sardinia would take part in any 
negotiations for peace within the limits already assigned to her. 

Having listened to Count Walewski's observations, | proceeded ta remark 
upon those which expressed a different opinion from that of Her Majesty's 
Government, 

With regard to the stipulations to effect the neutralisation of the Black 
Sea being made matter of separate negotiation between Russia and the Porte, I 
observed, that to consign the guarantees for the future safety of Turkey, to 
obtain which France and England had mainly gone to war, to an act in the

not a proceeding very honourable to the allies, I called Count Walewski's 
recollection also to the fate of more than one of the Separate Conventions which 
had been annexed to the Treaty of Vienna. The doctrine had been held by 
two of the Powers who would participate in the negotiations respecting Turkey, 
that such Conventions were only binding so long as the parties more imme- 
diately interested in them did not modify or annul them, but that their 
annexation to the General Treaty of iets id not givea right to Powers who 


18 


signed that ‘Treaty, but who had not signed the Separate Conventions, to interfere

With regard to the Sea of Azoff, | observed that we ought not to be deterred

‘To the objections raised by Count Walewski to apprizing Austria of the

that those conditions would not render peace impossible, we owed it in good

Lastly, I remarked that in the memorandum to which Count Buol aud

This expression had no doubt led to the demand that Austria should appropriate

“Fo resume, L said that Count Walewski was totally mistaken if he supposed 
that, out of deference to the Emperor Her Majesty's Government could subseribe 
to terms which they could not justify to the country. The deference to the

the allics. Unfortunately, it appeared that in many essential points the opinion 
of Count Walewssi differed from that of Her Majesty's advisers. The first thing 
therefore to be done, was to settle these differences of opinion between the two 
Governments ; for how could they run the risk of recommencing negotiations 
with such a wide divergence in their views? The ultimatum of Austria was 

or bad ag it was interpreted: and that it might be interpreted in different

I had not left Count Walewski very long when he ex ressed the wish to see

Lordship, I subsequently Pal in his hands. 

Count Walewski said that before he could act further in this matter, he 
must ask what was the meaning to be attached to the paragraph which stated 
that ‘although Her Majesty's Government do not propose to make any 
material change in the wording of the Austrian ultimatum, which must be 
regarded as chiefly laying down general principles, yet they cannot hold them- 
selves bound by that wording, and must reserve to themselves the right to 
propose such amendments as may appear necessary to guard the great interests 
affected by the ultimatum.” 

Did this passage refer, Count Walewski asked, simply to the observations 
which followed in the sueceeding paragraphs, or was it intended to reserve the 
vight of Her Majesty's Government to propose, before the recommencement of 
negotiations for peace, other amendments than thase now mentioned ? 

The meaning of the paragraph, I replied, when taken in context with 
subsequent parts of the despatch appeared to me to be, that Her Majesty's 
Governnient required certain amendments in the ultimatum in order to render 
it more clear and effective before it was sent by the Austrian Government to 
St. Petersburzh. These amendments were afterwards detailed, and I did not 
conceive that Her Majesty’s Government intended, if these amendments were 
agreed to by the French and Austrian Governments, to propose any further 
alterations in the present stage of the matter. 

Count Walewski then asked whether Her Majesty’s Government under- 
stood that the condition relating to the establishment of Consulates in the 
Black Sea, was to be inserted into the Austrian ultimatum, or whether it was 
alluded to for the information of Austria only at the present moment. He 
remarked that, in the spring, this was one of the stipulations which had been 
most firmly resisted, as derogatory to the Emperor of Russia’s sovereign 
dignity. 

1 answered, that I could not doubt that your Lordship intended to demand 
the insertion of this clause into the ultimatum. At the same time, I said, that 
| would rather refer both this and the preceding question to your Lordship. 
This was agreed to by Count Walewski, who stated that he should take no further 
steps in the matter until I was in possession of your Lordship's answer.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No. 1,371.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, November 29, 1855. 
IN reply to the inquiry made by Count Walswski as to the meaning of a 
paragraph in my despateh No, 1,356 to your anealeey | have to state thut 
Her Majesty's Government were anxious to reserve to themselves the right to 
propose Fick amendments in the Austrian ultimatum as might appear necessary, 
because the wording of the ultimatum is in part extremely vague, and a want of 
precision as to the true meaning of terms may lead to a failure of the negotia- 


22 


tions for peace, and because it is of the utmost importance that England and 
France should either beforehand. clearly understand, or have the right here- 
after to render clear, the engagements they are about to contract, and which 
will not only impose duties Upon them, but will also affect the interests and 
welfure of others. 

It is difficult, however, to arrive at any such understanding without entering 
‘nto details which would seem to be premature, and Her Majesty’s Government, 
therefore, preferred to regard the ultimatum as chiefly laying down general 
principles, or, as it was ealled by Count Buol, a basis of preliminaries, and they 
wish to avoid all modifications of that document that are not absolutely neces- 
sary; but they do consider it necessary to require that the nature and extent of 
guarantees, and the mode of exercising them, should be reserved for future con- 
sideration. Her Majesty’s Government are convinced that the Government of 
the Emperor will agree with them ‘n this matter, because the manner in which 
the Austrian proposal as to the future arrangements for the Principalities ts 
worded, might, if taken literally, seem to imply that the arrangements which 
were proposed on that pont at the Conferences at Vienna last spring should be 


adopted. But to those arrangements grave and valid objections have been 


urged, and they must at all events be a bar to a hasty and inconsiderate pledge 
on the part of England and France to adopt the arrangements to which those 
abjections apply, It would, theretore, be very desirable that the proposition to 
be made to Russia in regard ta the Danubian Principalities, should be confined 
to what has always been considered as the general and fundamental principle of 
the first point; namely, that Russia should not enjoy or exercise any exclusive 
or single right of protection or iterference in regard to the Danubian Principali- 
ties, that the Sultan should by his own sovercien act grant or conlirm to those 
Principalities a satisfactory internal organization, and that such arrangements a3 
may upon full consideration be deemed sufficient, should be made for securing 
to the people of those Provinces the unmolested enjoyment of the institutions 
thus to be conferred upon them. By such a wording all questions of detail in 
regard to which the Porte and the people of the Provinces ought rightfully to be 
consulted, would be left open and reserved tor future consideration, While the 
leading principles upon W ich, ag Her Majesty's Government understand, Great 
Britain, France, Austria, and Russia, ave all agreed, would be formally recorded 
as consented to by the four Powers. 

With respect to the fourth point 1 have to observe, that some ambiguity 
arises ag to the meaning of the paragraph relating to it in the Austrian 
altimatum, in consequence of the use of the expression “ garanties par le présent 
Article.’ ‘This expression might be understood as implying that there is to be 
some diplomatic Treaty guarantees entered into by the Contracting Powers as to 
the privileges and immunities of the Christian subjects of the Sultan. But 
such an arrangement would in fact be to establish, as against the Sultan, on the 
sart of the other Contracting Parties, that very right of interference in the 
‘ternal affairs of the ‘Turkish Empire, which Prince Menchikoff demanded for 
Russia, and it was to enable the Sultun to resist such demands that the present 
war was undertaken. It would, then, be a strange conclusion of this war, that 
the Powers who have made great sncrifices and exertions to assist the Sultan in 
resisting certain demands, should combine with his enemy to impose them upon 
him as the result of a successful contest. 

As the Austrian ultimatum will be proposed to Russia with the sanction 
of Great Britain and France, the wording of the fourth Article should be less 
ambiguous, and it is desirable that it should only state in general terms that 
arrangements should be made by Kngland, France, Austria, and the Porte, for 
securing to the Christian subjects of the Sultan their proper civil and political 
rights, and that Russia should afterwards, be invited to coneur in the arrange- 
ments which would have been thus made. 

With reference to the secand inquiry of Count Walewski, as to whether the 
condition relating to the establishment © Consulates in the Black Sea was to be 
‘nserted in the Austrian ultimatum, T have to ‘nform your Excellency that such 
«. the wish of Her Majesty’s Government, Tt is true that in the spring Russia 
objected to this condition, but she equally resisted every proposal that would 
have rendered peace honourable to the allies and safe for Kurope. 

If it is supposed that Russia will reject the ultimatum of Austria in the 
form in which it was transmitted to Paris from Vienna, there can be mo 


23 


reasonable objection to rendering itas complete as possible, and thereby placing 
on record the conditions which are thought to be indispensable by the belligerent 
Powers; but if, on the other hand, the necessity of peace is so strongly felt by 
Russia, as to induce her to consent to the loss of half of Bessarabia and the 
mouths of the Danube, to the neutralisation of the Black Sea, and to relinquish 
her military and naval arsenals, itis idle to suppose she would resist the infinitely 
less onerous condition of admitting Consuls in her ports of the Black Sea, or 
that she would refuse to treat for peace if she were not allowed to make a 
separate arrangement with Turkey respecting the number of vessels that are to 
be established for purposes of police in the Black Sea. 

Her Majesty’s Government are clearly of opinion that it would be just antl 
honourable towards Russia,and serve to avoid future embarrassments, if the 
Cabinet of St, Petersburgh were made aware by Austria of the several conditions 
that are not contained in the ultimatum, and which will be brought forward 
whenever negotiations are resumed.

to make the transinission-of the ultimatum to St. Petersburgh depend on this 
concession being made to him, Count Walewski will ask whether Her Majesty's 
Government will not in such case yield the point, provided that proper 
precautions are taken in the General Treaty to prevent the possible abuse of the 
Separate Convention, 

Count Walewski supposes that your Lordship’s declaration that ‘Her 
Majesty's Government cannot hold themselves bound by the wording of the 
ultimatum,” means that Her Majesty's Government, while agreeing to the sense 
of the ultimatum, will not be bound to the exact letter of a wording upon which 
they were not consulted. He takes for granted also that the stipulation 
respecting Consuls 1s intended to be one of the reserved conditions, and that it 
is not sought to have it inserted in the ultimatum. 

Upon this point, | said that such was not my understanding of your 
Lordship’s despatch. It appeared to me that the object of Her Majesty's 
Government was to have this stipulation included in the ultimatum. ‘Count 
Walewski replied that ‘f such was the case, it was useless sending any reply to 
Vienna, Austria would never consent to peace such a condition in “the 
ultimatum, although she might agree to its being a desirable mensure, and one 
that might be discussed in future negotiations for peace. For himself, he must 
gay that it was a very delicate question, nearly touching the right of sovercignty 
of the Emperor of Russia, He did not know how far he should be justified in 
putting it forward. 

| rejoined that 1 was surprised to hear his observations, because this was no 
new question. It was one of the points on which both Governments hud last 


year made up their minds to insist, without entertaming a doubt of its 
propriety. 

Count Walewski replied, that all that he desired was, to postpone the 
question. He had not made up his mind whether its refusal by Russia ought 
to bea bar to peace, if all the other points were arranged satisfactorily. He 
had never heard of such a condition being inserted in a Treaty of Peace. 
Admitting the measure to be desirable in itself, he observed, that a promise to 
care Consuls in the Black Sea might be obtained from Russia in some other 
orm. 

Not knowing what might be the ultimate views of Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment on this matter, I wressed it no further, but I observed that in the Treaty 
of Peace signed with the Chinese Government, express stipulations were intro- 
duced for the reeeption of Consuls in certain ports of China, 

Count Walewski then asked in what way your Lordship proposed that 
the answer of the British Government should be conveyed to Count Buol’s 
knowledge. Was he to send to M. de Bourqueney a copy of your Lordship’s 
despatch on the subject, or did you prefer charging Mr. Elliot with the commu- 
nication? I said that I would ask your Lordship’s intentions.

My Lord, Vienna, November 29, 1555. 

SINCE I forwarded to your Lordship my telegraphic despatch of the 
7th instant, Count Buol has again spoken to me on the subject of the wish 
which he understood was entertained by Her Majesty's Government, that the 
whole of the arrangements respecting the neutralization of the Black Sea should 
he comprised in the General Treaty. | 
I told him f was entirely unacquainted with the views of Her Majesty's 
Government, further than that they considered it indispensable that the neutral- 
‘zation should form a part of the provisions of the General Treaty. 

This, he said, had already been agreed to, with the exception of what related 
to the small vessels to be employed m the coast-guard service, the numbers of 
which he persisted in thinking should be settled by a direct Treaty between 
Russia and ‘Turkey, but which would be annexed to the General Treaty, and 
would therefore be as binding on those Powers which signed the latter, as if it 
had formed a part of it, As he looked upon it merely as a question of form, he 
could not consent to adopt a course which rendered certain the rejection by 
Russia of the ultimatum to be sent to her; for the only hope which he had of 
her necehianee ae that a very feeble one—was based upon the poor siatis- 
faction she might profess to derive from being allowed to come to a direct 
understanding with the Porte upon this matter of maritime police, which, as he 
had said before, would be of no practical importance, as it would be annexed 
to the General Treaty. | 

Your Lordship will have already been informed by the French Government 
that, in addition to the introduction into the General Treaty of the prohibition 
af vessels of war in the Black Sea, Baron de Bourqueney has obtained the 
scaniescence of the Austrian Government to the proposal that the same prohi- 
bition should be Pe to the “établigsements militaires maritimes,’ which 
Count Walewski informed him was the form of words desired by Her Majesty's 
Government. : 

Instead of saying that the Imperial Government was “authorized” to 
‘aform the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh that preliminaries would be signed on 
their acceptance of the ultimatum, Count Buol has also consented to substitute 
any word that may be agreed upon by Her Majesty’s and the French Govern- 
ments. 


These modifications having been admitted, Count Buol appears to await, 
with almost feverish impatience, the decision of the allied Cabinets on his 


roposal. .

My Lord, Foreign Office, December 4, 1855. 

1 HEREWITH transmit to your Excellency the copy ofa despatch* from 
Count Walewski, which has been placed in my hands by the French 
Ambassador, 

L told the Count de Persigny that Iwas very glad to perceive that there 
appeared to be such a fair prospect of agreement between the two Governments, 
and that indeed there were only one or two points upon which there now 
existed any difference of opinion. 

The first related to the armed yeasels that were to be maintaiued for 
purposes of police, and upon that 1 begged to observe that if Russia engaged to 
keep no ships of war in the Black Sea, it stood to reason that she should not 
he allowed to make an exception to that engagement without the participation 
and consent of all the belligerent Powers. 

But, [ said, these coast-guard vessels are ships of war; they carry guns, 
they might be of any size, unleas regulated by stipulation, and if we have nota 
controlling voice, they might be of any number, and we should thus run the 
risk of neutralizing the General Treaty by the Separate Treaty which we annexed 
to it, and of thereby rendering our whole proceedings absurd as re rda the 
present, and our guarantees with respect to the future a delusion. We must 


then be parties to any exception that 15. made to the general rule of no ships of 


‘war in the Black Sea: if we were so, and if Eugland and France sanctioned the 
arrangement that might be entered into between Russia and the Porte on this 
most important point, then some meats might be found for embodying the 


arrangement in the General Treaty, and for making it binding on Russia and 


Turkey. 


any sine qué non condition, on whieh she could make: the rupture of her diplo- 


matic relutions with Russia depend, and if she did not think proper to make the 
Consular arrangement a part of her ultimatum, we ought not further to urge it

With respect to the Consuls, | said, that we could not impose upon Austria

upon her; but, on the other hand, Austria ought clearly to comprehend that we 
consider it a condition sine qud non of peace, and that England and France have 
a right to determine for themselves what shall be the conditions on which they

right to interfere. 

_ With regard_to Count Walewski’s inquiry as to the mode in which the

any observations upon it, as he was expecting communication from M. de 
Persigny which would render an answer unnecessary. Since then, I added, I 
had received no official instructions from your Lordship on this matter, the 
communications which had taken. place between the two Governments having 
heen carried on in London. I said, however, that my recollection of your Lord- 
ship’s despatch enabled me to state that Her Majesty's Government were appre- 
hensive that in accepting the wording of the Vienna ultimatum, as regarded the 
first point, they might be considered as agreeing to the arrangements which were 
proposed in the spring by the Plenpotentiaries who attended the V ienna Confer- 
ences; that Her Majesty's Government thought some af those arrangements 
objectionable, and did not wish to be bound by them ; and that with regard ta the 
fourth point, Her Majesty's Government thought the wording ambiguous, and 
that it might imply a real transfer to the four Powers of that protection over the 
Christian subjects of the Porte in general which had been claimed by Russia over 

: Sultan's Greek subjects. 

_ Count Walewski vid that if your Lordship intended to ask the French 


al 


Government to require of Austria to consent to an alteration in the wording of 
her ultimatum, he must decline to attempt the task. If, on the contrary, your 
object was only to reserve the right of discussion with the French Government, 
he was ready to pledge himself to enter into that discussion immediately. In 
respect, however, to the first point, he did not think that either Government was 
prepared for such a discussion ; certainly he was not. Wath regard to the fourth 
point, he agreed entirely in the principle laid down by your Lordship, that it 
would never do to create, in the place of the protection claimed by Russia, the 
recognised protection of the guaranteeing Powers, one of whom would always 
have a preponderating influence, with a constant desire to make use of it. He 
thought, however, that every precaution had been taken in the wording of the 
ultimatum to prevent any danger of the kind. 

It would be useless to trouble your Lordship with the details of a somewhat 
lengthened conversation which ensued. I endeavoured to point out to Count 
Walewski the advantage which might be taken of the present wording of the 
Austrian ultimatum to produce those evils which Her Majesty’s Government 
sought to avoid. I could obtain no other answer than that although quite 
ready to come to a distinct understanding with Great Britain, a failure in which 
was not to be apprehended, Count Walewski, after having expressed to Count 
Buol his approval of the Austrian ultimatum, could not call for further changes.

THE correspondence whieh has passed between this office and Mer 
Majesty’s Embassy at Paris, together with the copies of Count, Walewski's 
despatches to Count de Persigny respecting the ultimatum which the Austrian 
Government proposes to address to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, have been 
transmitted to Mr. Elliot; I now incloge the copies of two further despatches* 
which 1 have addressed to Lord Cowley, and you will thus be in complete 
possession of the views of Her Majesty's Government upon this important 
matter. 

| regret that some delay has taken place in sending 8 definitive answer to 
Vienna, but this delay has been unavoidable, as Her Majesty's Government 
considered it their duty to come to an agreement with the French Government 
respecting the true interpretation and meaning of certain terms of the ultimatum, 
+n order to guard against future misunderstandings which might endanger the 
suecess of the negotiations, upon which Her Majesty's Government will enter with 
the earnest hope and desire that they may lead to the restoration of te 

You will express to Count Buol the regret of Her Majesty’s Government 
at this delay, and you will assure his Excellency that the amendments and 
alterations suggested have had no other object than to render clear certain 
conditions in the ultimatum which appeared liable to mnisinterpretation, and to 
give more complete effect to the intentions of the three Governments to guar 
jurope against & renewal of the present complications. , 

For the purpose of more convenient reference, I inclose a copy of the 
ultimatum, and | have stated ina parallel column the Articles to which Her 
Majesty’s Government agree, and those to which they suggest that some amend- 
ments should be made; the reasons which have induced Her Majesty's 
Government to suggest them will be found im my despatches to Lord Cowley. 
You will communicate the amendments to Count Bucl, and express to 18 
Excellency the anxious desire of Her Majesty’s Government that he may see fit 
to adopt them. 

Count Buol has already been made aware by the French Government that 
among the conditions which the belligerent Powers reserve to themselves the 
right of proposing beyond those which are contained in the ultimatum, are that 
no fortifieations shall be restored or erected in the Aland Islands; that Consuls 
uhall be admitted at the Russian ports of the Black Sea; and that the future 
position of the territories on the east of the Black Sea shall be open to 


consideration. | a . 
Her Majesty’s Government having no wish to put forward conditions which 


® Nos. 16 and 18. 


33 


are not necessary in the permanent interests of peace, and having no motive for 
disguising their intentions, would have preferred that these terms should form part 
of the ultimatum, but they feel that they have no claim to press upon Austria the 
oe on which the rupture of her diplomatic relations with Russia shall 
On the other hand, however, Austria will admit that the belligerent Powers 
have a clear and indisputable right to decide upon what conditions they will 
consent to make peace; and as Her Majesty's Government do not think it 
would be just or honourable towards Russia that she should be allowed to enter 
upon negotiations for peace in ignorance of the terms to which her assent will 
be required, Her Majesty's Government trust that Count Buol will see the 
propriety of making these terms known to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, for it 
would be far better not to enter upon negotiations at all, than that they should 
be broken off upon the ¢ und that Russia had been unfair! treated, and 
that the real intentions of the belligerent Powers had been kept from her 
knowledge.

My Lord, Foreign Office, December 10, 1855, 

_ YOUR Excellency will have already received the entire correspondence 
which has passed between this office and Her Majesty's Ambassador at Paris 
respecting the proposals which the Austrian Government are desirous of making 
to Russia for the restoration of peace. 

_ My despatch to Sir Hamilton Seymour of the 6th instant, with its inclosure 
will place your Excellency in possession of the amendments to the Austrian 
ultimatum which have been made by Her Majesty’s Government, and which

i ee eS eS (Telegraphic.) Vienna, December 12, 1855, 


COUNT BUOL agrees to your Lordship’s amendments, with the following 
slight changes, which must still be submitted to the Emperor: 

In the second paragraph the words “will not enlarge”’ are omitted for 
grammatical reasons. 

Inthe third paragraph, after the word “satisfaction,” will come the words 
« with the assent of the guaranteeing Powers.” 

All that regards the Black Sea is agreed to. 

On the fourth point the first paragraph of the original Austrian ultimatum 
ig insisted on. The English text is accepted in the following terms: “ arrange- 
ments being made by Austria, France, Great Britain, and the Porte, for the 
purpose of seenring to the Christian subjects of the Sultan their civil and 
political rights. Russia will be invited, after the peace, to be a party 
to them.”

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl af Clarendon.—( Received December 13.) 


(No. 6. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 9, 1855. 

COUNT VALENTINE ESTERHAZY’S carriage is already packed ; he 
hos received his last orders, and should the final instructions from London, 
which are looked for with such intense anxiety by the Austrian Cabinet, reach 
Her Majesty's Mission to-night, and be of the nature which is expected, 
to-morrow night will find him on his way to St. Petersburgh. 

Every step which is to be taken after the dispatch of the ultimatum has 
been settled beforehand with the utmost precision: letters, already prepared, will 
be immediately sent off by the Emperor to the Kings of Prussia and Bavaria, 
apprizing their Majesties of the measure which has been taken, and calling upon 
them as advocates and lovers of peace to urge upon the Court of St. Petersburgh 
an acceptance of the terms which are now within thetr reach. 

After the interval of two days, by which time it is supposed that Count 
V. Esterhazy will have reached Warsaw, Prince Gortchakolf will receive a 
summons to the Foreign Office, and will then be told that Count Esterhazy has 
been furnished with instructions calculated to bring about a peace. He will, of 
course, inquire what the nature of the instructions may be, but will receive no satis- 
faction upon that point, Count Buol intends to acquaint him that he is not at 
liberty to divulge a seeret which belongs to him only in part, and that he must 
resign himself to waiting fora few days. The term during whieh the Russian 
Envoy's patience must needs be employed will coineide with the probable date 
of Count Esterhazy's arrival at St. Petersburgh, when Prince Gortehakoff will 
again be invited to repair to the Foreign Office, and will learn from Count 
Buol the precise nature and, | believe, words of the ultimatum. 

As regards Count Esterhazy, it has been enjoined him to see the most 
influential persons of the Russian Court, and to endeavour to obtain their 
assistance in determining the Emperor to accept the ultimatum, 

In the event—the probable event—of the ultimatum being at once rejected, 
the Austrian Envoy is diveeted to leave St. Petersburgh directly, with the whole

be not returned before the expiration of that term, peremptory orders will leave 
him no option as to demanding passports for himself and the whole of the

So the affair stands at present, and such has been the secrecy observed with 

regard to the whole affair, that when Count V. Esterhazy called upon me 

esterday, to converse upon Russian eubjects, it became at once manifest that he 
had no idea of the intentions of his Government, and of the nature of the 
instructions which he was about to receive. 

It appears to me that a little less reserve towards the Minister of an ally 
with whom the Austrian Court would reluctantly break might perhaps have 
better served their views, but I reflect that foreign Cabinets must know best how 
to deal with one another. 

With regard to the Austrian intentions towards us, | must freely admit that, 
after all that has occurred, it is natural that Her Majesty's Government should 
have acted with full caution before being drawn into fresh negotiations. With 
the openness, however, which it is my duty to employ in addressing your 
Lordship, Ido not hesitate to express my firm conviction that the Austrian 
Cabinet means fairly by us. Such has been my belief from the moment that I 
learned the Austrian scheme for stripping Russia of a considerable portion of 
her ill-gotten possessions in Bessarabia, because this is an offence which Russia 
will never pardon, and because, losing the Northern alliance, Austria must 
perforce endeavour to secure that of England and France. 

Nothing that the Austrian Cabinet can do or say would embitter the 
feelings of Russia towards Her Majesty's Government. ‘The statements which 
Her Majesty's Government have it in iheir power to make, and the acts which 
they can adduce im evidence, would cause Austria to be regarded with more 
enmity by all Russia than are those Powers which are in open hostility 
against her. 

The policy of the Imperial Cabinet, however, is seen to have become of late 
somewhat impulsive; and 1 will not conceal from your Lordship my eager desire 
that it may have been found possible on our part to unite caution with such 
rapidity of decision as may preclude the chances of any further abrupt change 
of purpose on the part of Austria, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Wlarendon.—( Received December 13.) 


(No, 11.) 
My Lord, Fienna, December 10, 1855. 


I HAVE but few particulars to add to my telegraphic message of the 7th 
instant, respecting the overture made by Prince Gortchakoff to Count Buol. 

Prince Gortchakoff’s tone was that of a man about to bring forward a 
proposal which must be accepted with eagerness. “*C’est la paix que je vous 
apporte,”’ was his exclamation upon entering Count Buol’s room, The terms of 
the Russian proposal will be found in the inclosed paper, which is copied from 
4 memorandum made by Count Buol after the Prince had left him, 

Count Buol acquaints me that upon receiving the communication, he 
merely observed that he had no answer to return beyond this, that he would 
take care that it should be made known to the Emperor, and to the English and 
French Governments. 

In speaking to me upon the subject, his Excellency expressed his doubts 
whether the proposition emanated from St. Petersburgh, or whether it originated 
with Prince Gortchakoff himself. In the first of these suppositions, Count 
Buol imagines the proposal to be a kind of echo to the appeals which have been 
made to the Emperor Alexander by the Courts of Bavaria and Saxony, 

M. de Bourqueney, from whom I had the first knowledge of Prince 
Gortchakoff’s overture, saw therein a fresh motive for coming to an under- 
standing respecting the ultimatum with the least possible delay. 
| observed to M. de Bourqueney, as | have since done to Count Buol, that 


47 


I was as little disposed as he would be to any waste of time, but that I must 
remark that Prince Gortchakoff’s proposal tended to set us at our ease; that a 
weapon ceased for the moment to be a weapon as soon as it was discharged ; and 
that the proposal made on the part of the Russian Cabinet only tended to establish 
the wide difference which existed between the sacrifices which Russia was 
prepared to make, and those which, in the interest of a permanent peace, must 
be required of her. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

WE learn with satisfaction that an agreement is nearly arrived at, ‘The 
words ‘will not enlarge” are not in the second paragraph, and we do not under- 
stand to what they allude. We cannot bind ourselves at this preliminary stage 
to guarantee internal institutions, or to give to any one of the Contracting | arties 
a power of veto upon the organization which the Sultan may give to the Princi- 
palities, which would be the case if their assent was required, In order, how- 
ever, to meet the wishes of Austria, we are ready, instead of the words “ with 
the assent of the guaranteeing Powers,” to insert the words “ concerted with the 
Contracting Powers.” 

We agree to the version you have sent as to the fourth point: the amend- 
ments required by the Emperor of Austria are not yet arrived.

COUNT COLLOREDO has reall to me a despatel: from Count Buol, 
together with the instructions which his Excellency proposed to address to the 
Internuncio, to enable him to discuss with the Ambassadors of England and 
France and with the Porte the arrangements that it might be desirable to make 
for the future government of the’ Principalities, and for ameliorating the condi- 
tion of the Christian subjects of the Sultan. 

Count Buol stated that it was by no means his intention to consider these 
instructions as definitive, nor did he propose them for the adoption of Her 
Majesty’s Government, but he thought they might furnish the bases of arrange- 


ment, and facilitate discussion upon matters the speedy settlement of which was 
very Important, | 

I thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, and said that I must 
decline offering any opinion upon a subject which involved so many serious 
considerations. Some of the suggestions of Count Buol appeared to me of 
doubtful expediency, while others, 1 thought, would meet with the concurrence 
of Her Majesty’s Government. 

Count Colloredo was not authorized to leave with me a copy of Count 
Buol's instructions to Baron Prokeach, but he had the goodness to allow me to 
make an abstract of them, a copy of which I inclose confidentially for your 
information. 

On a future oceasion I shall communicate to you the views of Her Majesty's 
Government upon the subject, and shall for the present confine myselt to 
observing that it would not be advisable to embody the concluding paragraph in 
a Treaty or other formal Act. If the proposed hatti-sherif were formally 
communicated by the Sultan to the four Powers, it would as a matter of course 
be open to the Representatives of those Powers to complain of any particular 
viokition of the hatti-sherif, as they would of the violation of any law or. decree 
having the force of law; but it would not be consistent with the dignity and 
independence of the Sultan to confer by ‘I'reaty upon the Representatives of 
foreign Powers the right to remonstrate and to claim reparation. 

The establishment of such a right would indeed be tantamount to a 
concession of the principle contained in the demands of Prince Menchikoff.
