Inclosure in No. 41. 
Abstract of Instructions to Baron Prokesch. 


AS regards the first Guarantee : 


In order to secure to the Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia better 
prospects for the future, and the progressive development of their resources, arid 
to enable them to pass, without a shock, from their actual legal position to one 
more in accordance with their true interests, the first step to be taken is the 
revision of the Organic Statute of 18g)." 

This revision, to be effectual, must have for its object not only the modlifi- 
cation of such of the stipulations of that Statute as may be considered the 
constant sources of the evils affecting those countries, but also the complete 
establishment and organization of a regular and prosperous society. With this 
view the Austrian Government recommends the following course of | roceeding. 

The fundamental principles of the proposed reform, after having been 
discussed and agreed upon between the Powers and the Sublime Porte, with due 
regard to the real wants and legitimate desires of the country in question, should 
he promulgated in the Principalities by the authority of the Suzerain Power, and 


* The Moldavian Organic Statuts ns in 1831; the Wallachian, 1840, 


at) 


under the formal guarantee of Europe. ‘The elaboration of the details would be 
left to the authorities of the Principalities themselves, 

The Austrian. memorandum then proceeds to point out what are, in the 
opinion of the Cabinet of Vienna, the principal abuses arising from, and. 
omissions in, the Organic Statute, with the remedies which they consider should 
be applied. These points have reference to : 3 


1. The General and District Assemblies. 


It is proposed to substitute for the General Assemblies, a Senate, whose 
constitution and functions should be such as to fit it to be the Council of the 
Princes, the defender of the interests of the people, and the organ of amendments 
in legislation. 

Instead of the Departmental Assemblies there should be established District 
Committees, with the view of bringing the Government into closer commu- 
nication with its subjects, 


2. The Mode of Electing the Princes. 


In order to preserve to the Principalities their ancient privilege of electing 
their Princes, and at the same time to avoid the inconveniences inherent im the 
present mode of election, it is suggested that the Senate should propose to the 
Sultan on each vacancy three candidates, from amongst whom the Hospodar 
should be appointed for life. 


3, Institutions which favour Corruption ; for example, the Election of the 
Metropolitan and the Bishops by the Boyards, 


The remedy for this corruption is to be found, in the opinion of the 
Austrian Government, in the abolition of such anomalies, the increase of the 
authority of the Prince and his Ministry, and the exercise by the Senate of 
control over the Civil and Financial Administration. 


4. Faulty Social Organization. 


The purchase of titles, and the consequent exemption from public imposts, 
the degradation of the cultivator of the soil, are mentioned under this head, as 
evils which require a remedy. 


5. The Assessment of the Taxes, und the Arbitrary Collection of them from 
the Tow-payers. 


The remedies suggested are, the abolition of the capitation tax, and of 
monopolies of objects of first necessity; the introduction of a land-tax (contri- 
bution fonciére) applicable to all lands, without exception, in the sense of the 


Hatti-Sherif of 1502. 


6. The want of yood Laws relating to Property. 


Reforms upon this subject are considered by the Austrian Government to be 
the sine qud non of all real improvement, j 

It is stated that the attempts made in this direction by the Porte and b 
Russia failed, because the former had not the power to make them cucceel, 
the latter had not the wish that they should do so; and it is added that the 
cooperation of the European Powers will now afford the Porte the support which 
she requires. 

The result of this revision would be a fundamental Statute, of which the 
Powers might assume the guarantee, with the stipulation that in the event of 
differences between the Hospodar and the Suzerain, recourse should be had to 
the guaranteeing Powers, through their Representatives at Constantinople, and 
that no armed intervention by the Porte, or from any other quarter, should take 
place without a previous understanding with the guarantecing Powers. 


Lastly, the Austrian Government consider that it would be necessary to 
reproduce in a Separate Act, between the Powers and the Sublime Porte, the 


engagements entered into by the latter at_ different epochs for the territorial 
integrity and administrative independence of the Principalities. 

In this Act also, would have to be contained the stipulations relative to the 
system of defence to be established in the interest of the Principalities, of the 
Ottoman Empire, and of Europe, 


With regard to Servia, the Austrian Government consider that various 
alterations are required in the actual organization of that Principality. 

Certain institutions—especially, for example, the Senate, as regards its 
constitution and funetions—require to be examined and modified, with reference 
to the principle of the national and independent administration of the country, 
ae the maintenance of the other rights gnaranteed by the Imperial Hatti- 
Sherifs. 

In the discussion of the fourth point, the Powers will have first fo agree as 
to the measures which they may consider necessary to bring about a real amelio- 
ration in the position of the Christians, and afterwards upon the best means of 
carrying out these measures. 

The essential points to be attended to are: 


1. The condition of the Christian Churches, especially of the Greek 
Church. 

9. "The independence and the constitution of the tribunals. 

3. The development of the municipal system, with reference both to the 
principles already established and the actual wants. 

4. Abolition of the principle that the soil belongs entirely to the Sultan. 

5. The right of foreigners to possess landed property. 

§. Admission of Christians to civil and military offices. 

7. Application of the principle of Christians taking their share in the 
military service of the Sultan. 


These measures, after being agreed upon in confidential discussions with 
the Porte, might be carried out by an Iinperial Hatti-Sherit, which should be 
communicated by the Sultan to the Powers. 

If hereafter, in the exercise of the richts thus granted to the Christians, the 
benevolent intentions of the Sultan should be obstructed from any cause whatever, 
the official communication of the Hatti-Sherif to the Powers would form the 
eround upon which the latter might base a demand for a reparation through 
their Representatives accredited to the Porte.

(No. 996. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, Decerber 2, 1859. 

AS | feel strongly the importance of preparing materials for inquiring with 
good effect into the third and fourth points of the Vienna Conferences, a5 s00n 
as the parties more immediately concerned are able to meet for that purpose, [ 
have put into the form of a memorandum whatever has occurred to as calculated 
to throw light upon the question of the Principalities. 

It appears evident to my judgment that the advantage of coming to a deci- 
sion upon that question before the commencement of any negotiations for peace 
outweighs every other consideration, 1am also under a strong impression that, 
in taking that line, the Sultan and his allies would best consult their real interests 
by rendering the two Provinces an effective barrier against Russia, and, if the 
events of the war should not justify them in requiring the return of Bessarabia 
to its ancient connection with Moldavia, that they would do well to proceed on 
the narrower ground of amending the present state of things, and securing the 
free enjoyment of the Danube, without introducing any fundamental changes 
into the arrangement. 

Inclosed herewith is a copy of the paper to which have reterred above: 
and, while I submit it with hesitation to your Lordship’s indulgent attention, I 
beg to reserve the power of adapting it to any more accurate yiews which [ may 
hereafter find reason to entertain. 

With respect to the question of privileges, [ propose to set down my 
thoughts in writing as soon 4s I may have leisure for entering seriously on 60 
extensive a task. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE. 


a 
Inclosure in No. 53. 
Memorandum. 


THOUGH we are sure that the war must, sooner or later, come fo a close, 
we cannot yet determine the form which peace, whenever it is concluded, will 
assume. We may, however, foresee with moral certainty that among its comndi- 
tions will be the establishment of a new order of things in the Danubian Princi- 
palities, “That part of the Turkish Empire has too otten been made a stepping 
stone for Russian encroachment not to require that the causes of its weakness 
should be examined, and, if possible, removed. The ‘Treaties by which the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh acquired or arrogated the right of exercising i 
dangerous Protectorate in the Principalities are dissolved by the war, and imper 
fect indeed must be our success if peace be renewed without replacing them by 
u more salutary arrangement, The allies, in performing that duty, will no doubt 


seek to provide for the future welfare of the inhabitants, at the same time that 


they deprive Russia of a powerful instrument of aggression, and strengthen the 
Turkish frontier on what has been hitherto found its weakest side, ‘The task 


which Providence appears to have assigned to them is no less benevolent in its 
objects than arduous in execution, It rests with them to atone for ages of 
military vexation and misgoverniment to a people entitled, on many accounts, to 


a far better lot than any they have hitherto enjoyed. 


It is nevertheless but fair that the European interest, which is involved in 
the prospects of Moldavia and Wallachia, should be the tirst to receive attention. 
If something must be sacrificed, it is better that the Principalities should give 


way to Europe than that Europe should give way to the Principalities. 


But prior to entering either on the political or on the constitutional question 
affecting them, it is desirable to obtain a clearer view of circumstances which 


bear more or less directly on both, 


NTS, 7 tec oe aaa Aa. tris er Ure 


| gre Lae 
— ae + Be co — ee | ls r 
= | one eae br i a —— - 


The two Provinces, taken together, contain, as is well known, a wile extent 


on 


of productive territory, peopled by several millions, who in general profess the 
same faith and speak the same language, who are influenced by the same 
traditions, and live under the same institutions. 

In geographical position they are situated between the Danube, the Pruth, 
and the Carpathian Mountains, being conterminous with the Austrian Provinces 
of Bukovine, Temesvar, and Transylvania. ‘They are divided from each other by 
the Sereth and a stream which falls into it from the west. f 

_ By the Treaty of Bucharest, Bessarabia was detached from Moldavia and 
added to the Russian Empire. The inhabitants of both are nearly all of the 
same race, creed, and language. Others of the same description dwell within 
the Austrian frontier. 

The whole population comprised under the name of Rouman may amount 
to nearly seven millions, of whom from four to five occupy the two Princi- 
palities im unequal proportions, about three-fifths of the number belonging to 
Wallachia. : 

__. The chief productions of the country are wheat and other grain, salt, 
timber, and cattle, including hides and tallow. Of these articles the quantities 
exported, which are already considerable, might be greatly increased, and manu- 
Beeutee preporsicnally taken in return. With the exception of salt and timber, 
Russia is their rival in trade, and Odessa flourishes at their expense. Their 
great commercial channel with Germany on the one side, and with the Western 
nations through Constantinople on the other, is by the Danube. 

Their political dependence on Turkey dates from an early period, It was 
formed originally on a capitulation granted to them by the Sovereigns of the 
Ottoman Empire. The character of the Convention was gradually modified by 
Treaties which Russia dictated at the close of successive wars to her Mussulman 
neighbour and victim. Privileges extorted by conquest from a dreaded superior 
in the name of religion formed naturally a bond of sympathy between the Princi- 
palities and their triumphant patron, till bitter experience proved that spoliation, 
misgovernment, and oppression, under the name of protection, were the only 
practical results, 

The relations, moral and political, in which the two Provinces stand at this 
moment towards Turkey on the one side, and Russia on the other, may be thus 
described. ‘The privileges conferred by Treaty remain in virtue of the Porte's 
declarations, though the Treaties themselves are no longer in foree. The Sultan 
is recognized as Suzerain by Wallachia and Moldavia, integral parts of the 
Turkish Empire, The Government of both is carried on by the respective 
Hospodars, who hold their authority from the Porte for'an appointed term, and 
administer the public affairs according to the Organic Statute, and the laws 
resulting from it, partly by agreement between the two intervening Cabinets 
and partly by internal legislation. . 

There is reason to believe that the system is far from being unacceptable 
to the leading classes, and that it is susceptible of amendments, which would 
prove satisfactory to the others, and practically beneficial to the whole 
community. Its vices, and their evil consequences, are less attributable 
to the Constitution itself, than to a corrupt and abusive course of administration 
favoured, if not imposed, by Russia. 

Taking the population as divided, with exceptions few and insignificant 
between proprietors and labourers ; and the proprietory, as classed into Boyars 
having some weight of family, and mere officials, including the new Boyars, it 
may be said that the Russian party is confined to those among the Boyars and 
candidates for office, who have either acquired heretofore, or expect hereafter 
power and fortune through Russian patronage. The great majority appear to 
be animated by national feelings, some of popular, some of an aristocratic 
tendency, alive to the dangers of Russian illusion and Russian encroachment 
nor by any means. disinclined to rely upon Turkish connection, approved and 
supported by the Powers of Europe. The most. decided and pervading 
sentiments would seem to be aversion to Austria, as being identified in public 
opinion with the domineering oretensions of Russia unsoftened by historical 
traditions or by religious sympathies. : 

Such, in the shape of a brief outline, are the prominent features of a 
position which, though precarious and imperfect, contains the elements of 
inprovement, whether political or administrative, unmingled with any obstacles 
of an insuperable kind. Benevolence and fair dealing may be expected to work 


56 


out the problem of reconstruction, not without difficulty, but with practical 
success, ‘The most desirable result may be figured as one which would establish 
the Principalities in relations of mutual confidence with Turkey, of disconnected 
independence towards Russia, of frank good neighbourhood with Austria, and of 
cordial intercourse with England. Added to their securities for a peaceful and 
cradual-advancement in prosperity, the improved Constitution should be such 
ne to establish confidence, together with good order, among the several classes of 
society. A free command of the Danube, divested of all unjust and unnecessary 
obstructions, would open a wide and productive field for the exercise of that 
commercial spirit which so many cireumstances concur to encourage I the 
Principalities, and which tends more than anything else to unfold the resources 
of a country, and to strengthen the bonds of political sympathy. he 

In striving to secure this result, the Porte and its cooperating allies will 
have to deal, in the very outset, with questions of paramount importance. 
Among the most obvious are the following: 


Ist. Whether the two Principalities are to remain separate, or to be 
moulded into one. eee 

8nd. Whether the Prince or Princes are to be selected exclusively among 
natives. | hear 

3rd, Whether the Organic Statute is to be taken as the basis of an improved 
system, OF a new system to be formed. : ae 193 

4th. In either case, how the administrative, judicial, and legislative powers 
are to be distributed. Aw, ae 

5th. By what armed force, of whatever denomination, the internal peace of 
the country is to be maintained, ee 

Gth. What military defences are necessary agaist foreign aggression, and 
how they are to be kept up, carrisoned, and supported. 


‘These several points may be examined with most convenience in their 
numerical order oe 

ist. The question of throwing the two Principalities into one may be fairly 
entertained us presenting important considerations on both sides. The present 
arrangement is best for the Porte, in regurd to maintaining her influence. It 
affords her more room for meeting the wishes of expectant adherents, and for 
playing off one of them against another when put in possession of power, This 
advantige would extend, in a measure, to the officials in both communities. 

The country would probably gain by having a single Administration ; and, 
in the sume sense, an union of the Principalities might give them greater force 
asa barrier against Russia, But other considerations must be kept in view, A 
single Government at the head of four or hve millions of subjects, inhabiting a 
rich country, open to an extensive remunerating commerce, would hardly keep 
long within the bounds assigned by the jealousy of its neighbours: Activity 
engenders a spirit of independence ; and ambition is never long dormant when 
there is a sufficient arena for its display. The susceptibilities of Austria—the 
apprehensions of Russia, would be gradually excited: and in due season, making 
common cause, might defeat the purpose of the alliance, and endanger, by fresh 
encroachments, the peace of the Levant. +" 

It is not to be supposed that Russia can reach so extreme a pont of humilia- 
ton as to renounce entirely its long-cherished dream of dominion, and the hope 
of recovering a lost position by the arts of intrigue and the study of opportu- 
nities. Far more likely is it that she would work upon the ambition of a Prince 
confiding in the resources of his Government, and tempt him to look across the 
Danube for instruments and materials of further aggrandisement. 

If these objections were not deemed sufficient to stand agaist the reasons 
for union, it might be as well to give full play to the prnens involved in so 
hazardous a innovation, In that ease, let the idea of a barrier be frankly 
carried out, Let the territorial distribution which existed before the ‘Treaty 
of Bucharest be restored, Let Bessarabia beeome once more a part of the 
ndjacent Principalities. ‘The Danube, with its chain of fortresses from the Black 
Sea to the Carpathian Mountains, would then form the frontier line; the popu- 
lation of Moldavia would obtain a considerable reinforcement of its own rice ; 
and the Danube, unshackled by Russian contrivances, would augment the revenue 
of the new State, at the same time that it conveyed to distant markets the 
vecumuluted produce of Germany. 


oF 


The arrangement thus shadowed out would, perhaps, be preferable to any 
other, if the allies were successful enough to demand it, In the meantime, a 
sober exercise of judgment operates in favour of the existing division, as being 
better calculated, on the whole, to meet the requirements of the case, without 
giving umbrage to any Power whose goodwill it is important to retain. 

2nd. This question turns in part on the selection of the preceding one. If 
the two Provinees were to be formed into a single State, the Government of a 
freign Prince selected from the Sovereign houses in Europe might have its 
advantages. The selection, however, would not be free from difficulty. Preten- 
sions hard to set aside, and hard to accept, would infallibly be advanced. If the 
profession of orthodoxy were required, where but in Russia could the “ right man” 
be found? On the whole, there appears to be no sufficient reason for departing 
from the established practice. ‘The Hospodars sent from Constantinople before 
the Greek Revolution have left no reminiscences to make their return desired. 
Intrigue, cupidity, corruption, and perfidy, were but often the characteristics of 
their Government. It requires no sagacity to perceive that their return to 

sower would be viewed with alarm and disgust. The native families offer few 
individuals worthy of the trust, but national feelings are enlisted in favour of 
national choice, and the recurrence to strangers would no doubt be a cause of 
discontent. 

rd. ‘The Organic Statute is by no means destitute of merit. But it bears 
the stamp of its Russian origin, and is not efficient either for the correction of 
abuses or for the repression of corrupt and arbitrary power. ‘These circum- 
stances would seem to indicate the proper course of proceedmg. Let the 
Organic Statute cease to have legal force after a given term, and let a new 
Constitution be prepared in its place, emanating from the supreme authority 
with the aid and advice of its allies, taking the original Capitulation for its start= 
ing point, and receiving with amendments such portions of the Organic Statute 
as can be fairly approved by the parties concerned. In this manner, whatever 
is vicious in the principle of practice of the present organization would be 
extirpated, and the administration of the Principalities would be established for 
the future on a sound basis, equitable alike for the Sultan and for his tributary 
dependents. 

4th. The questions comprised in the fourth point must of necessity be 
reserved for those special discussions which will naturally accompany the forma- 
tion of a new constituent Act, It will hardly be prudent to exclude the 
suggestions of those who have local experience and loyalty of character to 
recommend them. The best meant decisions, havin for their object the esta- 
blishment of a just, beneficent, and stable system of administration, would ever 
be the stronger for carrying with them a willing obedience formed on the judg- 
ment of leading minds in the Principalities themselves. But however that may 
be, there are landmarks which cannot with safety or prudence be overlooked. 
Such, for instance, are, fidelity to the Sultan, as sovereign and supreme; free 
action for the Prince, and authority made effective by suitable powers and 
adequate meats; a legislation founded on national habits and wants, and ecalcu- 
lated to provide by its enactments for the rights and welfare of all classes ; 
competent and independent courts of justice ; efficient legislative control over 
the taxation und revenue of the State; responsibility of Ministers; religious 
tolerance, with reverential maintenance of divine worship; individual freedom, 
and security under law; @ vigilant and sufficient police under Ministerial 
direction. 

Any Constitution, however named, which ensures a real application of these 
principles, ean hardly finl of giving stability to, the Government and content- 
ment to the nation. The prospect of this twofold result would at once deprive 
every neighbouring Power both of pretext and motive for unseasonable interfer- 
ence, and even any jealous anxicty. 

5th, ‘There is little to be submitted on the fifth point, which is rather a ques- 
tion of detail than principle. No one can doubt the necessity of providing for 
the maintenance of good order by some kind of armed foree, in action or in 
reserve. Constables, watchmen, patrols, gendarmes, policemen, guards, whether 
rural or municipal, are only different names for @ civil force auxiliary to the 
magistrate and answerable for the public pecs A wuilitia is more; it may be 
used inaid of the police. Between that body and a standing army it occupies 
the middle station, This kind of force, which is already employed in both 


a 


5 


Principalities, might be continued, on a moderate scale, with advantage. At all 
events due provision should be made for an adequate police m every town and 
district, the whele affiliated together and placed in connection with a central 
corps at each capital. In an age of steam locomotion and electric communica 
tion, the instruments of order, though separated by distance, may be so prepared 
| for concentration, in case of need, as to secure the peace of society at little cost 
and with still less parade. a dh 

Gth. Opinions can hardly settle down on this point before it be known what 
character will ‘n future belong to the ultra-Danubian Provinces. Continuing as 
hitherto, for some time back, to be merely a delay or battle-ground in case of 
foreign attack, they stand in little need either of armics or of fortresses. It 1s 
only on the supposition of a different system, followimg upen an administrative 
union of the two Principalities, together, if possible, with the recovery of Bess- 
arabia, that a plan of local miltary defence may be brought consistently into 
discussion. In view of such a contingency the existing defences of the Dniester 
would require a standing military force in the Principality to provide garrisons, 
and to support them in resisting the first shock of invasion. The limited reve- 
nues of the State, and also the Supreme Government, would correet any tendency 
to excess in the formation of a local army. Local it would be, of course, in time 
of peace, when no Turkish troops would be stationed in the country. In the 
event of war there would be every motive for keeping it on foot, as auxiliary to 
hy the Sultan’s army, which no doubt would have to advance towards the frontier. 
A Should circumstances lead to the adoption of any such plan, it would be highly 
f desirable that two at least of the principal fortresses on the Dniester should be 

garrisoned from Constantinople, and kept always open (by water, at least) for 
a the admission of reinforcements from the same quarter, 
; In addition to this view of the subject, as 4 whole, there are some detached 
questions which claim a separate notice :— . ; 
tae In what manner is the Danube to be secured from obstruction ? 
Is the passage of the river to be still impeded by an idle chain of quarantine 
stations ? 

[s all protection of the two provinces to cease with that of Russia? 

Is the amount of tribute to remain unaltered ? 

Is no provisional arrangement required for @ better administration of the 
Provinces while waiting for a definitive settlement ? ’ 

There cannot be two opinions as to the importance of thoroughly emanct- 
pating the Danube. More interests than those of Turkey and its dependencies 
are involved in that act of justice. But colemn engagements having failed to 
counteract the machinations of an ambitious policy, it would seem that a 
new territorial allotment can alone supply the requisite guarantees. Every one 
knows what difficulties and dangers beset the channels of Sulina and St. George. 
The Russian authorities were bound to keep the former clear; they often 
pretended to do so, but somehow it happened that the obstructions remained 
to the prejudice of all navigation except that of Russia, The Kilia channel is 
still in her hands. 

Not only was the course of trade by the Danube impeded, but a large tract 
of country along the right bank of that river was condemned to be a barren 
solitude that Russia might not be disturbed in the enjoyment of her monopoly. 
Moreover, the arrangement was wrung from ‘Turkey by foree, unjustly exerted 
against that country in virtue of hostilities which had their source: in Russian 
artifice, $0 had Bessarabia been previously annexed to the colossal Empire. 
In one case, the alliance of England with France, in the other, a deadly quarrel 
hetween those countries, afforded the opportunity which Russi sclzed with 
clandestine address. ; 

How stands the matter now? Victim and dupes are alike engaged in 
rescuing Europe from the snares of a policy no less aggressive than insidious. 
As common danger gives union to their arms, # common interest ought surely 
to animate their negotiation. Suecess in war ts 0 flourish without meaning, 1 
peace be not made to yield the securities Which justice requires, lhe securities 
now in view are as obvious its the need of them. ‘Take them at their lowest 
Russia must recede from the left as Turkey was forced’ at Adrianople to recede 
from the right bank of the Danube, ‘Then will the waters of thut nable river 
hecome, as they ought to be, truly European, and past complianees will receive 
an exemplary, though imperfeet and tardy, atonement. 


[t may further be hoped that the quarantine stations imposed by Russia 
will areenpe with the colours of that Power from the banks of the Danube. 
Serious doubts may be entertained whether any real advantage accrues from 
sanitary frontier establishments. Plague has ceased to infest the Levant, and 
cholera is rather epidemical than contagious. But granting their abstract use 
elsewhere, they are too irregular in practice throughout Turkey to secure any 
effective result, ‘The stations may answer as instruments of police; they may 
offer lucrative places to candidates for public employment,—that is all; and 
those along the Danube were founded by Russia for political purposes. They 
cannot but operate unfavourably on trade, occasioning expense to the State and 
yexation to travellers. 

With respect. to replacing the Russian protectorate by that of any other 
European Power, neither the Sultan, nor his allies, nor even the inhabitants of 
the Prineipalities, are likely to desire it. Russia herself never acquired a legiti- 
mate title to the function. All who take an interest in the welfare of the 
Provinees would recognize in a constituent Act, emanating from the Sultan and 
seconded by his allies, the best and most convenient security as well for the 
sovereian as for the dependent population. 

So long us the Principalities retain liability to tribute, circumstances may 
occur to raise the question of altering its amount. [he great change which is 
now in operation, already threatens to bring it on. The Porte has, no doubt, 
its arguments in favour of an Ierease. The Principalities would probably be 

lad to throw off the burthen altogether. ‘The amount at present is light, butas 
the Porte has no share in the expenses of administration, it may be asked on 
what ground she is entitled to any part of the revenue? But as she has 
commanding voice in the question of improvements, it would not perhaps be 
wise to cast a doubt upon her claim to tribute, especially as the charge of defen- 
sive operations, in case of invasion, would principally devolve wpon her. 

If the ideas thus brought together for reflection are sound in themselves and 
at all likely to be realized, the parties whom they immediately concern will have 
to consider at what period the settlement they relate to, may be most advanta- 
weously fixed, The Organic Statute, irrespective of passing events, will soon 
reach the term at which it may either expire or be revised. Then will arise the 
question of provisional or definite arrangement, Important, perhaps insurmount- 
able, objections will be offered to the latter course. To some, it may appear that 
the time for a settled and final constitution is not yet come. Opinions as well as 
events may be thought likely to prove more conducive to a complete and durable 
settlement hereafter, A delay of some few years may be jooked to as promising 
a better race of legislators and functionaries in the provinces. Much certainly 
depends upon the character of our future pacification, 

These and similar considerations are not to be lightly thrown aside. But 
how are they to be reconciled with the urgency of completing a final arrange- 
ment, while Russian influence is necessarily excluded from the deliberations ? 

How can the Provinces be kept indefinitely under a doubtful and provisional 
Administration without prejudice to their best interests ? 

Risk and inconvenience attach to both contingencies. It remains with the 
Sultan and his allies to determine in which of the two cases they are likely to be 
least. 


The following appears to be the result of the recommendations in this 
memorandum : 


|. It is desirable to maintain the existing division of the Prineipalities. 

4. It is, on the whole, desirable to continue the existing practice of selecting 
the Hospodars from among the natives of the Provinces. 

ob. it is desirable that the Organic Statute should be replaced by a new

the allies, but based on the original Capitulations between the Provinces and the 
Porte, and comprising such portions of the Oreunic Statute as, after amendment, 
can be fairly approved by the parties concerned. 

4, In providing for the administrative, judicial, and legislative powers, 
regard must be had to securing fidelity to the Sultan, a8 Sovereign and supreme ; 
free action for the Prince, and authority made effective by suitable powers and

No. 55. 
Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon, —(Received December 19.) 
No. 18. 
ue va Vienna, December 12, 1855. 


UPON receiving yesterday your Lordship’s despatch of me a pene 
marked No. 7, 1 at once proceeded to the house of the i inis idee i 
secured his cooperation in endeavouring to obtain Count ee aS ia 
of the amendments proposed by your Lordship in the Austrian ultimatum. 


61 


I then waited upon Count Buol and read to him your Lordship’s despatch, 
together with the amendments. | 

As had been agreed upon, I was soon rejoined by the Baron de Bourqueney, 
whose promises of assistance were much more than redeemed by the ready and 
indefatigable manner in which he came to my support in proposing the suppression 
of passages of an act, drawn up by himself, an the substitution of others, to 
which he felt obliged to acknowledge some verbal objections. 

Count Buol made comparatively little difficulty as to admitting the first 
three corrections of the ultimatum ; but when we reached the passage proposing 
that arrangements should be made by Austria, France, Great Britain, and the 
Porte, “afin d’assurer aux sujets Chrétiens du Sultan leurs justes droits civils et 
politiques, et la Russie sera ensuite invitée \ adhérer aux arrangements qui seront 
ainsi faits,”’ he laid down the paper and observed, that it was quite impossible 
that Austria should make herself a party to an intimation s0 unnecessarily 
insulting to Russia. 

Baron de Bourqueney, after observing that “justes droits” was an express 
sion which in his eagerness to adhere to a correct “redaction” he could never 
support, made, with infinite judgment and temper, various suggestions, all of 
which the Minister for Foreign Affairs listened to with attention, and with the 
most manifest desire of rendering the sense and text of the passage conformable 
to the views of Her Majesty's Government. 

After a lengthened deliberation, in the course of which Count Buol expressed 
a doubt whether the intention of Her Majesty's Government might not possibly 
be to shut the door against negotiation, and to ensure the immediate and positive 
rejection of the ultimatum by Russia, this suspicion was successfully combated, 
and it was finally agreed that your Lordship’s despatch and inclosure, together 
with memoranda of amendments drawn up so as to adhere as closely as possible 
to the English version, should remain in Count Buol's hands and be taken at 
once into consideration. 

By this time it was past 4 o'clock, and Count Buol took leave of us, request- 
ing that we should call upon him again five hours later, before which time, 
besides reflecting upon the course to he followed, he should have had an oppor- 
tunity of submitting the rjuestions pending to the Emperor, whose return to 
Vienna might be looked for in a couple of hours. 

Upon leavivg the Imperial Chancelleric, | hastened to send off a telegraphic 
message to acquaint your Lordship with the very manifest wish exhibited by the 
Austrian Minister to comply with the wishes of the Queen's Government. 

In the course of a long diplomatic life, 1 have never felt greater anxiety than 
has been pressing upon me for some hours and days: . 

For above a twelvemonth I have entertained this belief, I might say the 
conviction, that the neutral position of Austria must, in the long run, become 
‘tolerable to her, and that she would ultimately escape from it by an abrupt 
determination to act, probably against, but: possibly with, her northern ally. 

This point has been reached ; Austria has taken a decision which, if acted 
upon, must, it appears to me, enibroil her irretrievably with Russia; but the same 
desire to cut through difficulties which appear not to admit of solution, may, if 
the present plan be not acted upon, very possibly compel her to try some course 
‘which no attention would be paid to the interests and wishes of Her Majesty's 
Government. : 

She is prepared, I firmly believe, to break, if needs must, with Tussia, but 
the resolution of permitting the rupture to be attended with forms which would 
be offensive to her old ally would, it is clear, be most painful to her. 

The sum, then appears to be, that if there is danger in neglecting any 
precaution which may ensure the carrying out of that poliey which Austria 1s 
apparently resolved upon adopting, there is, at least, equel danger in exposing 
ourselves to the chance of her being driven to some other course of action. 

Intent us there is: reason to believe both Austria and France to be upon 
peace, if the caution of England should prove an obstacle, there might be danger 
of the two Governments endeavouring to carry out their object with the assist- 
ance of that Power which has suffered the most severely from the war. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

(No. 19.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 12, 1859. 

LAST night, Baron de Bourqueney aud myself resumed our conversation 
with Count Buol. 

1 am willing to believe that the result will be considered by your Lord- 
ship as satisfactory, 4s the alterations in the amendments of Her Majesty's 
Government, which were insisted upon by Count Buol, are less considerable 
than I had expected. 

These alterations (translated into English) were at once transmitted to your 
Lordship by telegraph. 1 have now the honour of inclosing them as they were 
written out by Count Buol. 

Game of the objections raised to our text were made upon the grounds of 
style; “‘ trés satisfaisante,” although allowed to stand, was considered as an 
‘nvorrect. translation of “satisfactory whilst “ne jouira” was suppressed 
as a neuter verb which could not properly be coupled with “exercera,’’ and 
“justes,”” as an epithet which cannot in French be applied to“ droits.” 

‘The difficulties in our way, then, are, 0s regards the Minister of Foreign 
Affairs, In a great measure surmounted. 

It remains to be seen whether his Excellency’s proposed alterations will 
receive the Emperor's sanction. 

This 1 may possibly learn to-day from His Imperial Majesty himself, to 
whom 1 am about to have the honour of presenting my letters of credence. 

I ought to observe to your Lordship, that when | quitted Count Buol last 
night, he appeared to be as much averse as ever to making any allusion i his 
ultimatum, either to the Alond Islands, the right of sending Consuls to the 
ports of the Black Sea, or the consideration of the Russian territories to the east 
of that Sea, and that, as before, he pointed out the full reserve which had been 
made in his own ultimatum for that and any other demands which the Powers 
at war with Russia may think fit to make upon her. 

[should likewise remark upon the great stress laid by the Minister of 
Foreign Affairs upon being apprised whether Her Majesty’s Government adhere 
to the arrangements made by himself and Baron Bourqueney, and recorded in 
ve apes dated the 14th November, to which their initials (‘‘ paraphe”) were 
affixed, 

To this point Count Buol attaches great importance, as he regards that 
document as “ the basis” of the present proceedings. 

Desirous, however, as his Exeellency is of being informed upon this point, 
he has full confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and is ready to receive a 
answer to his inquiry in any shape which Her Majesty’s Government may 
consider the most convenient. 

I ought to state to your Lordahip that Prince Gortchakoff called yesterday 
upon Count Buol, for the purpose of inquiring whether any step had been taken 
upon his overture. 

Count Buol informed him that it had been brought to the kuowledge of the 
Emperor, and had been mentioned to the English and French Ministers, when 
the conversation closed without any questions being asked by the Russian 
Envoy as to the negotiations of which so many persons suspect the existence, 

ite only asked what day was fixed for Count V. Esterhazy’s departure for 
St. Petersburgh, and was told in reply that no decision was yet taken upon this 
point, and that Count Esterhazy’s mother was suffering from illness. 

1 ought, before concluding my despatch, to state to your Lordship my 
belief and conviction that the alterations in the ultimatum now proposed are, 
after the concessions made by Count Buol, to be simply accepted or refused, 
have every reason to imagine that no further corrections would be admitted by 
the Austrian Cabinet.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clurendon.—(Received December 15.)

My Lord, Vienna, December 13, 1855.

objections of the Austrian Chancellerie to any mention of the Aland Islands, or

the Black Sea, remain insurmountable. 

Both his Excellency and M. de Bopequoney continue to maintain the entire 
right reserved to England and France to bring forward these points as soon as 
negotiutions are opened—these or eny others which a continuance of the war may 
render expedient. 

They likewise argue that a distinct mention of these two points might have 
the effect of closing the door against any further sacrifices which it may be found 
necessury to impose upon Russia,

they seck no advantage for themselves, and they require only guarantees for the 
future peace of Europe—guarantecs which Germany is even more interested in 
obtaining than England and France; and Her Majesty's Government do not 
doubt, therefore, that. Baron Manteuffel will see the expediency of supporting the 
ultimatum in the interests of peace, for which the Prussian Government has 
always shown itself so solicitous, and, it may be added, in the interests of Russin 
also; for that Power will assuredly not again have the opportunity of accepting 
terms go little onerous if the war continues, and the costs and sacrifices: of 
another campaign are imposed upon the allies.

No, 72. 
Circular addressed to Her Majesty's Representatives abroad. 


Sir, Foreign Office, December 20, 1555. 

I TAKE the earliest opportunity to acquaint you with the result of the 
communications which have recently taken place between Her Majesty's 
Government and those of France and Austria respecting a proposition to be 
made by the last-named Power to the Court of St. Petersburgh, which if accepted 
in sincerity and acted upon in good faith, may possibly lead to the re-establish- 
ment of peace. 

The communications between the three Courts which have led to this state 
of things originated in an overture made some time back by Count Buol to 
Baron Bourqueney, then on the point of leaving Vienna for Paris, which 
indicated a disposition on the part of Austria to adopt a more decided course of 
policy towards Russia than she had hitherto pursued; and the subject having 
been renewed on Baron Bourqueney’s return to Vienna, an offer was made to 
send to St, Petersburgha proposition in the shape of an ultimatam, the rejection 
of which by Russia, or its non-acceptance within a specified time, would be 
followed by the immediate interruption of diplomatic relations between Austria 
and Russia. ‘This proposal was embodied in a memorandum which bears date 
the I4th of November, and to which Count Buol and Baron Bourqueney 
respectively affixed their initials. 1 inclose a copy of this memorandum for your 
information.t ; 

To this memorandum was appended the draft of the ultimatum which the 
Austrian Government was prepared to address to that of Russia. 

The terms in which that ultimatum should be framed have formed the 
subject of serious deliberation and well-weighed discussion between the Cabinets 
of London, Paris, and Vienna: and the further paper which | now inclose will 
fully explain the nature of the terms upon which the three Governments have 
agreed as bases of negotiation for peace. 

Her Majesty's Government have learnt, by a telegraphic message from Sir 
Hamilton Seymour, that Count V. Esterhazy, the Austrian Minister at the 
Court of Russia, would leave Vienna for St. Petersburgh, as the bearer of the 
ultimatum, on the 16th instant. By a previous despatch from Sir Hamilton 
Seymour, Her Majesty's Government were informed that Count Esterhazy is 
instructed, in the event of the ultimatum being at once rejected by the Court of 
Russia, to leave St, Petersburgh directly, with the whole of his Mission. But if 
no immediate answer is returned by the Russian Government, Count Esterhazy 
ia directed, on the expiration of ten days from the delivery of the ultimatum, to 
state to the Russian Minister that unless a favourable answer is returned before 


* No. 68, i. } Inclosuro 3 in No, 2. 


’ ’ - . 


70 


the expiration of a further term of nine days, he must demand passports for 
himself and the whole of the Austrian Mission. 

You will observe by the last clause of the ultimatum, that the right is 
reserved to the belligerent Powers of bringing forward in the general interest of 
Europe other conditions over and above those specified in the ultimatum, Her 
Majesty's Government would faye much preferred that those conditions shoulil 
have been specified in the ultimatum itself, but they felt that they had no right 
to press upon Austria the conditions on which the rupture of her diplomatic 
relations with Russia should depend. 

The Austrian Government, however, has been made aware that the 
following are among the conditions which the belligerent Powers reserve to 
themselves the right of proposing, beyond those contained in the ultimatum, 
namely, that no fortifications shall be restored or erected in the Aland Islands ; 
that Consuls shall be admitted to reside at the Russian ports of the Black Sea; 
and that the future position of the territories on the east of the Black Sea shall 
be open to consideration ; and Her Majesty's Minister at Vienna has been 
directed to acquaint the Austrian Government that Her Majesty's Government 
trust that Austria will see the propriety of making these terms known to the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, as Her Majesty's Government consider that it would 
be far better not to enter upon negotiations at all, than that such negotiations 
should be broken off upon the ground that Russia had been unfairly treated 
and that the real intentions of the belligerent Powers had been kept from her 
knowledge. 

Her Majesty’s Government trust that the course adopted by the Govern- 
ments of England and France at this juncture is well calculated either to bring 
about the reestablishment of peace on. terms honourable to the belligerent 
Powers, and advantageous to the general interests of Europe, or to demonstrate 
to the world that Russia is not yet prepared to listen to such reasonable terms 
pf accommodation as will afford security to Europe against renewed attempts of 
agerandizement on her part.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received December 21.) 
(No. 24.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 17, 1855. 


I DID not mention to Count Buol the amendment in the Austrian 
ultimatum suggested by your Lordship’s telegraphic message of the 1dth 
December, because at that time I did not know whether some changes in the 
wording desired by the Emperor might not be demanded by Her Majesty's 
Government, 

This not being the case, as was proved by your Lordship’s telegraphic 
despatch of the 14th instant, I at once waited upon Count Buol and explained 
to him that we were now quite agreed, if, as I presumed, he had no objection to 
substituting the words “concerted with the Contracting Powers,” for those of 
“the assent of the Guaranteeing Powers.” 

Not the slightest difficulty having been made by Count Buol, your Lord- 
ship's amendment was admitted as far as it could be without the [operial 
sanction, which his Excellency felt certain of receiving the same evening upon 
the Emperor's return from a shooting party. 

Upon this result being obtained, I sent off to your Lordship the telegraphic 
message of which I have the honour of inclosing a copy. 3 

Before I took leave, Count V. Esterhazy, who had been summoned, had 
arrived at the Foreign Office, that he might receive orders as to making his final 
preparations for his departure for St. Petersburgh, 

Again, I would take the liberty of calling your Lordship’s attention to the 
instructions which will be placed in the hands of the Minster. 

I learn, with surprise, from Paris, that the dispatch of Count Esterhazy 1s 
viewed by many as a certain sign of approaching peace. ‘That the step now taken 
by the Austrian Cabinet may conduct ultimately to peace is very probable, and for 
that reason | regret that it was not resorted to months ago; but as to immediate 
results, these, unless 1 am much mistaken, are much more likely to be the 
rupture of diplomatic relations between Austria and Russia, i 

In the same way, although | will not shut my eyes to the reluctance 
which would be felt by Austria in becoming a party to the war, { cannot bring 
myself to the belief of her present course having been taken in bad faith, 

It is easy to see, from the speculations of the newspapers, that some persons 
surmise that the step about to be taken by Austria has been concerted with the 
Russian Cabinet. | 

"This suspicion | cannot share; and to believe that Russia is a party toa 
proposal, the effect of which would be to strip her of the half of Bessarabia, 
appears to me to allow mistrust to get the hetter of cool judgment. 

It is, however, of little use to speculate upon a point which is about to be 
submitted to a decisive proof, 

| am obliged indeed to infer that Russia is still unpr. pared for the sacrifices 
about to be demanded of her; Prince Gortchakoff’s language with regard to 
the proposal lately made by him to Count Buol being, that it has been a great 
embarrassment to the parties who were negotiating at Vienna (“ un baton qu'il 
leur avait jete dans les roues”). 

‘The embarrassment was unperceived, and the supposed impediment did not 
prevent Count V. Esterhazy’s departure on the night of the 16th instant. 

‘To return to my narrative; on the evening of the 15th, Count Buol having 


signified to me the Emperor's approbation of the last amendment proposed by 


Her Majesty's Government, the first was communicated tg your Lordship in the 
telegraphic message of which | beg to melose a copy, © 


72 


Count Esterhazy, not being in strong health, has obtained leave to stop 
twice on the road, and will probably reach St. Petersburgh on the 24th instant. 

There is one point respecting his instructions which, probably on account 
of a misapprehension on my part, requires to be made clear. | - 

Count Esterhazy will present his proposals as soon as he reaches, but will 
add nothing in the shape of threat as respects non-compliance with them. 

He will wait ten days, and only at the expiration of that term signify that 
he will be obliged to quit St. Petersburgh in ten days in the event of their not 
being accepted. ;

be received fram Berlin and Munich which will produce a favourable impression 
upon the mind of the Emperor Alexander. j

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Reeeived December 25.) 


(No, 25.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 17, Too. 

| UNDERSTAND that a circular despatch has heen addressed by the 
Imperial Government to their diplomatic servants, the object of which is to 
counteract the effect of the statements which have gove abroad us to the 
reductions in the Austrian army. 


‘The circular, if | am correctly informed, sets forth that the extent of these 


reductions has been greatly exaggerated; that they have borne, not upon the 


very considerable force already under arms, but upon the extraordinary additions 
made thereto; that such arrangements have been made as would enable the 
extraordinary force to be brought back to its highest standard in the course of a 
very few weeks; that the very measure of economy resorted to, had for its 
object the means of giving more efficiency to the resources of the State, and 
that the army is in the highest state of efficiency. 

_ Upon this latter point I received some naturally partial but satisfactory 
evidence from an English officer who had passed through several Austrian 
garrison towns on his way from Turkey. 

He had found large bodies of troops in these towns, and he assured me he 
had never seen men better clothed, fed, and armed, or ina more complete state 
of readiness for taking the field whenever their services may be required. 

Were only the financial condition of Austria on a par with her military 
resources, she would be well prepared for the eventualities which loom at 
perhaps no great distance ; as it is, it must be manifest that the resolution of 
drawing the sword will be attended with almost as much danger at home as can 
be affronted abroad. 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 77. 
Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 25.) 
(No. 28.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 17, 1855. 


COUNT BUOL has taken more than one occasion of reminding me how 
desirable it is that measures should be concerted, without further loss of tine, as to 
the future organisation of the Principalities, and by his language gives it to be 
understood that the delays in considering that question have proceeded rather 
from Her Majesty’s Government than from his own Cabinet. 

Austria, he says, has been occasionally suspected of a wish to favour 
Russian interests, and of a too exclusive regard of her own. ‘Uhe wish felt by 
her to proceed at once to an arrangement of the important questions to which 
he is anxious that the attention of Her Majesty’s Government should be 
directed, proves the injustice of such suspicions. 

Were she only intent upon her own objects, Austria could desire nothing 
more than a prolongation of the actual “ état provisoire,” as, besides her usual

men, which would be doubled were there any urgent need of an increase of 
force, . 

She wishes, however, to act with her new allies; is prepared to enter upon 
the task without the concurrence of Russia, and to leave to that Power only the 
faculty of associating herself to resolutions already taken, should the task be 
completed before she has resumed her place in the European Council. 

It is clear to me that Count Buol sees, in the course which he recommends, 
an additional incentive to Russia lending herself to these arrangements for peace, 
which would be so grateful to Austria and the whole of Germany. He does not, 
indeed, hesitate to observe that Russia cannot fail of perceiving that she will loge 
a great advantage if she should hereafter be unable to claim her share in the 
labours by which a satisfactory and definitive organisation has been worked out 
for Provinces of which it hus been her special object to represent herself as the 
sole Protectress.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 25.) 


(No. 352, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 22, 1855. 

I REPORTED last week the expected arrival of Count Miinster, the 
the Prussian military agent at St. Petersburgh; he was the bearer of despatches 
from Baron Werther, which do not,as 1 have heard from Baron Manteuffel, hold 
out the expectation that the Emperor Alexander will be in any way disposed to 
accept the terms of the ultimatum. His Imperial Majesty had received an urgent 
appeal, which had been lately addressed to him from Berlin, in favour of peace, 
with much apparent goodwill, but had said nothing to the Prussian Minister 
which indicated that His Imperial Majesty was disposed to make any serious 
concession, 

Count Miinster, I understand, describes the Emperor as having returned 
from the Crimea in raptures with the condition of his army, which appeared 
to want nothing, and considers that its improved condition will be a 
powerful argument in favour of resistance rather than of concessions. Count 
Miinster says that Count Nesselrode, Count Orloff, and the older persons 
about the Emperor, would be disposed to listen to overtures of peace, but 
that the younger persons of influence at Court, at the head of which is the 
Empress, are for a continuance of the war ; and that a large and fanatical party 
are for doing so at any cost: that they have no fear, if even the European Powers 
were all allied against them, that Russian would materially suffer, convinced as 
ithin herself, and that her prosperity 


they are that she has boundless means w1 
would not severely suffer, if she was even cut off from all communication with 
the rest of Europe. 

Count Minster brings a very unfavourable account of the health of 
the Dowager Empress of Russia, Baron Manteuffel, tn speaking to me to-day 
on this subject, said that though Her Imperial Majesty had rallied from a severe 
attack of illness it was not expected that her life would be prolonged many 
months,

His Prussian Majesty received him in the presence of Baron Manteuffel, and 
spoke in a calm and studied manner. He expressed his thankfulness for the 
letter of the Emperor of Austria, and the communication which it contained. 
He gave Count Esterhazy to understand that he would suppurt it at 5t. Peters- 
burgh, but that before doing so he should wait to hear on the subject from 
London and Paria, alluding at the same time to proposals which he understood 
had emanated from the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. 

Count Esterhazy assured me that throughout the audience the King 
repeatedly spoke of his readiness to assist in promoting the interests of peace 
but he added that he left His Majesty under the impression that His Majesty 
would do nothing to compromise his present attitude on the Bastern question, 
and that the support which he might give to the ultimatum would have no weight 
in making it acceptable at St. Petersburgh, | a ee 

The King promised, after giving the subject the most mature consideration, 
to send an answer to the Emperor Francis Joseph, observing that the most 
important thing he had now to say was, that “he hoped Austria would not 
forget that she belonged to Germany +” meaning that the policy of Germany should 
be peace, and that the adoption of an opposite course was not called for under 
present circumstances, and would not be congenial to the interests or feelings of 
the German community. 

‘The Austrian Minister told me that he read to the King a copy of the 
instructions which had been addressed to Count Valentine Esterhazy, but that 
he carefully abstained, as directed by his Government, from divulging the course 
which would be followed if the ultimatum was rejected, and which would end in 
the withdrawal of the Austrian Legation from St. Petersburgh.

A CONVERSATION respecting the communication made by the Austrian 
Government to that of St. Petersburgh has taken place between Count Buel andl 
the Russian Eavoy: . 

It appears that Count Buol called yesterday upon Prince Gortchakotf und 
informed him that Count Esterhazy had been the bearer of certain propositions 
with the nature of which he had not been at liberty to acquaint him. He had 
been the less disposed to do so as the Prince might have been expected either to 
approve or disapprove of them, to urge their acceptance or to counsel their 
rejection. ‘That in the one supposition it had, of course, been desired to avoid 
Prince Gortchakofl’s sl eaarae) while, on the other, it had been hardly con- 
sidered fair to call upon him for support to proposals which possibly might not 
be altogether acceptable to his Court. 

Prince Gortchakoff replied that he could, of course, only feel flattered at 
any resolution which was based upon the conviction of his being devoted, heart 
and soul, to the interests of Russia; and that his only regret at not having been 
consulted, proceeded from the belicf of its being possible that the suggestions 
which it would have been in his power to make, would have increased the 
probability of the Austrian terms being acceded to by his Government, 

Before the conversation closed, Count Buol took an opportunity of 
expressing the hope that no attempt would be made to modify proposals to 
which it was the wish of the Imperial Government that a simply affirmative or 
negative answer should be returned.

The Earl of Clarendon to Sir Hamilton Seymour. 
(No. 49.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, December 26, 1855. 

IN reply to your despatch No. 28 of the 17th instant, reporting a conyer- 
sation held with Count Buol relative to the affairs of the Danubian Principalities, 
I hare to instruct you to assure Count Buol that Her Majesty's Government 
entirely concur with him as to the importance of immediately settling the future 
organisation of those Principalities as far as it may be practicable, 

I inclose a copy of a memorandum® on this subject as the basis on which 
such organisation might, in their opinion, be arrranged, and Her Majesty’s 
Government have the satisfaction of thinking that it does not, in any material 
degree, vary from the project which was communicated to them by the Austrian 
Government, except that it avoids placing too many matters under European 
euarantees. Her Majesty's Government are desirous to avoid this— 

Ist’ Because such guarantees appear to be unnecessary ; no danger from the 
Porte having ever threatened the privileges and immunities of the Principalities, 
nor being likely to arise ; and 

Qndly, Because these guarantees of the internal affairs of the Provinces, and 
the working of the institutions that may be given to them, are likely to create 
dissensions between the Guaranteeing Powers, and seriously to embarrass the 
Local Governments. 

Her Majesty's Government desire to submit these views to the favourable 
consideration of the Cabinet of Vienna.

The Bart of Clarendon to Sir James Hudson. 
(No. 154.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, December 19, 1855. 

THI time has arrived when Tam able to authorize you to make known to 
the Cabinet of ‘Turin the result of the communications which have recently taken 
place between Her Majesty's Government and those of France and Austria, 
respecting a proposition to be made by the last-named Power to the Court of 
St. Petersburzh, which, if accepted in sincerity and acted upon in eood faith, 
Wveny possibly lead to the reestablishment of peace. 

Phe communications between the three Courts which have led to this state 
of things, originated in an overture made some time back by Count Buol to 
Baron Bourquency, then on the point of leaving Vienna for Pans, which 
indicated a disposition on the part of Austria to adopt a more decided course of 
policy towards Russia than she had hitherta pursued; and the subject having 
Leon renewed on Baron Bourqueney’s return to Vienna, an offer was made on 
the part of Austria to send to St, Petersburgh a proposition, in the shape of an 
ultimatum, the rejection of which by Russia, or its non-aceeptance within A 
speciiivd time, would be followed by the immediate interruption of diplomatic 
relations between Austria and Russia. “This proposal wis embodied in a 
niemorandum which beara date the 14th of November, and to whieh Count Buol 
and Baron de Bourqueney respectively affixed their initinls. Linclose a copy 
of this memorandum® for your information, and for communication to the 
Sardinian Government. , 

To this memorandum was appended the draft of the ultimatum which the 
Austrian Government was Benita to address to that of Russia, ‘The terms 
on which that ultimatum should be framed have formed the subject ol 
serious deliberation and well-weighed discussion between the Cabinets of London, 


* Inclosure 3 in No. 2, 


81 


Paris, and Vienna; and the further paper which I now inclose, and which you 
will also communicate to the Sardinian Government, will fully explain the nature 
of the terms upon which the three Governments have agreed as bases of nego- 
tiation for peace. 

You will farther inform the Sardinian Government that [Her Majesty's 
Government have learnt by a telegraphic message from Sir Hamilton Seymour, 
that Count V. Esterhazy, the Austrian Minister at the Court of Russia, would 
leave Vienna for St. Petersburgh as the bearer of the ultimatum, on the 16th 
instant. 

By a previous despatch from Sir Hamilton Seymour, Her Majesty's 
Government were informed that Count Esterhazy ts instructed, in the event of” 
the ultimatum being at once rejected by the Court of Russia, to leave St. Peters: 
burgh directly, with the whole of his Mission. But if no immediate answer is 
returned by the Russian Government, Count Esterhazy is directed, on the 
expiration of ten days from the delivery of the ultimatum, to state to the Russian 
Minister that unless a favourable answer is returned before the expiration of a 
further term of nine days, he must demand passports for himself and the whole 
of the Austrian Mission. 

The Sardinian Government will observe that by the last clause of the 
ultimatum the right is reserved to the belligerent Powers of bringing forward in 
the general interest of Europe other conditions over and above those specified 
in the ultimatum. Her Majesty's Government would have much preferred that 
those conditions should have been specified in the ultimatam itself; but they 
felt that they had no right to press upon Austria the conditions on which the 
rupture of her diplomatic relations with Russia should depend. 

The Austrian Government, however, hus been made aware that the following 
are among the conditions which the belligerent Powers reserve to themselves 
the right of proposing, beyond those contained in the ultimatum ; namely, that 
no fortifications shall be restored or erected in the Aland Islands ; that Consuls 
shall he admitted to reside at the Russian ports of the Black Sea; and that the 
future position of the territories on the cast of the Black Sea shall be open to 
consideration; and Her Majesty’s Minister at Vienna has been (lirected to 
acquaint the Austrian Government that Her Majesty's Government trust that 
Austria will see the propriety of making these terms known to the Cabinet of 
St, Petersburgh, as Her Majesty's Government consider that it would be far 
better not to enter upon negotiations at all, than that such negotiations should 
be broken off upon the geound that Russia had been un uirly treated, and that 
the veal intentions of the belligerent Powers had been kept from her knowledge. 

The explanations which I have given in this despatch and the documents 
which [ have instructed you to place in the hands of the Sardinian Government, 
will, Her Majesty’s Government trust, satisfy the Cabinet of Turin that the 
course adopted by the Governments of England and Franee at this juncture, 1s 
well calculated either to bring about the reestablishment of peace on terms 
honourable to the belligerent Powers and advantageous to the general interests 
of Europe, or to demonstrate to the world that Russia is not yet prepared to 
listen to such reasonable terms of accommodation as will afford security to Europe 
against renewed attempts of aggrandizement on her part. 

Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

WITH a view to carry out the instructions contained in your Lordship’s

Qur conversation fell naturally on the all-absorbing subject of the ultimatum 

which has been forwarded from Vienna to St. Petersburgh, and considering that

his approval of the terms which the Austrian Government had been authorized

peace.

T then urged on Baron Manteuffel to impress on the King the hope

My Lord, Paris, December 26, 1855. 

IF Lam to believe the reports which reach me, M. de Seebach, before his 
departure from Paris, gave out that he was going to St. Petersburgh with the 
Emperor's sanction, and that he had an audience of His Majesty, at which he 
had ascertained that His Majesty was not indisposed to facilitate the signature 
of peace by concessions to Russia. 

Although I felt certain that no such assurance had ever been given by the 
Emperor, | was not the less sorry that such rumours should prevail, because 
their existence is sufficient to excite speculations in the money market, which 
are too likely to end in disappointment, Having, therefore, a fair opportunity 
for so doing, I alluded to them this afternoon to Count Walewski, expressing 4 
hope that his Excellency would, whenever an occasion offered, contradict 
them. 

Count Walewski replied by repeating to me what I had the honour to state 
in my confidential despatch No. 1,597 of the 10th instant respecting M. de 
Seehach's departure, but with this important modification, that after he had 
announced to M. de Seebach that the proposals of Russia were insufficient, and 
that she would learn through Vienna on what terms peace could be made, that 
ventleman had asked whether he could not see the Emperor; that Count 
Walewski had asked His Majesty's orders, and that M. ce Seebach had been 
received by him; that at this audience M, de Seehach had recommenced the 
old story of the friendship und admiration of the Czar for the Emperor, and of 
his desire to come to a direct understanding with France ; that the Emperor had 
replied that he was sensible of the courteous dealings (‘bons procédés’”’) of 
Russia, but that this was not the time or place for them, and that he could give 
no other advice than that the Czar should accept the terms now offered to him, 
for he might be sure that the allies would not i satisfied with less—that with 
the enormous resources of the allies, another campaign must add to the 
disasters of Russia, while the terms of peace would not be less rigorous, anc 
would probably be more severe, 

This, Count Walewski stated, was the general tenour of the Emperor's 
observations to M. de Seebach, who came to him alter the audience, and said 
that his conversation with the Emperor had been so important that he should 
like to convey it himself to St. Petersburgh. Count Walewski represents 
himself as having neither encouraged nor discouraged the journey thus suggested, 
as he considered that M, de Seebach was the best judge of its utility. The 
journey was then determined ee but only us far as Dresden in the first 
instance. It appeared, however, that M. de Secbach had there found an invitation 
to proceed to St. Petersburgh.

No. 102. 
Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Recetved December 31.) 


(No. 45. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, December 25, 1895. 


THAT a very important step has at length been taken by Austria—a 
step which is caleulated to bring her into closer cooperation, a8 it already has 
‘nto closer contact, with the Western Powers—cannot, I think, be denied by the 
most sceptical politician. . 

If nothing else is abtained, it-can hardly be otherwise than that the altered 
policy of Austrin must have the effect of alienating her effectually from Russia. 

That, at least, will be secured ag soon as the ultimatum is made known 
officially at St. Petersburgh. 

T apprehend that any ex jlanations which would refer the change to which 1 
allude to a single cause aoa be incorrect. As usually happens, Various causes 
have conduced to obtain a result. 

It appears certain that, from the beginning of the war, the wishes of 
Austria were in favour of the allies, but that various considerations prevented 
these wishes from being backed by cooperation. 

An undue estimate of the strength and resources of Russia had been taken, 
and her open hostility was greatly feared, and the more so as the allied forees 
had undertaken a task which, according to the opinion of some of the best 
Austrian, and, indeed, German officers, it was impossible should be performed. 

The fall of Sebastopol disproved these opinions, quieted thetr apprehensions, 
and proved, no doubt, the turning point of the policy of the Austrian Cabinet. 
‘Ag reflection came, it probably struck the Imperial Ministers that if there was 
anything to fear from fiestas resentment, that of the allied Powers might prove

Inclosure 1 in No, 104, 


Count Buol to Sir Hamilton Seymour. 


(Translation.) Vienna, December 20, 1855, 

THE Undersigned, Minister of the Imperial House and of Foreign Affiirs, 
while acknowledging the receipt of the note of Her Britannic Majesty’s Envoy 
Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, Sir H. Seymour, of the 15th 
instant, referring to the Article of the “ Oesterreichische Zeitung,” against the 
British Consul-General at Bucharest, takes the liberty of adding a few remarks 
which appear to him to correct in essential points the character given to the 
affair in question. 

It is, first, the duty of the Undersigned to remark that the interpretation of 
the 22nd Article of the Press Law of the 27th of May, 1852, as it is given in 
the said note of Her Britannic Majesty’s Envoy, would contain within it a 
limitation of the legitimate freedom of the press which does not belong to the 
spirit of the law; while the legislator in drawing it up certainly never intended 
(and in such a sense no proceedings have ever been taken) to place attacks of 
public journals on the character of a private individual, or of an official in the 
service of a friendly Power, under the category of “offences against public 
morality and the principles of civil society,” and to put in force the 22nd Article 
of the Press Law. 

When, therefore, the said note expresses the desire of Her Britannic 
Majesty’s Envoy that some steps may be taken against such excesses of the 
Austrian press, because by them the friendly relations between Governments 
and the communities represented by them might be weakened, the Under- 
signed would wish nothing more heartily than that the idea which forms the 
basis of that desire should find universal recognition. Most undoubtedly the 
hest and most earnest endeavours of Governments for the attainment of a friendly 
and cordial understanding are but too often weakened by excesses of the press 
against friendly Powers, which the Government in question may indeed ignore, 
but which but too often leave among the public an impression difficult to remove. 
This evil may evidently be averted by reciprocity, which the Austrian Legislature 
have adoptedl as a basis for such efforts, when in the Code of Criminal Punish- 
ments (ch. 66) they demand reciprocity as a condition for the punishment of 
injurious language towards Sovereigns of foreign States. But even in the 
Austrian States the principle of demanding reciprocity is never carried out so far 
ab to permit, or allow to pass unnoticed, that a journal should contain injurious 
language against the persons of friendly Sovereigns, because in the other country 
such language is daily used with impunity against His Majesty the Emperor; 
and this is done apart from the conditions positively laid down by law in cases 
like the present, hut the principle cannot be so entirely abandoned ag that in the 
one place the sacred person of the Sovereign should be exposed with impunit 
to all the slanders of the daily press, but in the other insinuations of journals 
against inferior forcign officials should ex officio, and by the Administration, be 
visited with severe blame. 

The Imperial Government feels conscious of not having been led away in 
the slightest degree from their friendly feelings towards Great Britain and her 
Government, by the unrestrained excesses of the English press against them and 
their illustrious Sovereign, which, especially in latter times, has passed all bounds, 
on account of a State Treaty which in no way touches England, They, there- 
fore, expect, with confidence, that Her Britannic Majesty's Government will not 
allow their friendly relations with Austria to be weakened by the humble amount 
of freedom which is granted by law to the Austrian press in its remarks. 

The Undersigned, &ec. (Signed ) BUOL,
