Inclosure 2 in No. 104. 
Sir Hamilton Seymour to Count Buel. 


Vienna, December 22, 1855. 

THE Undersigned, in acknowledging the receipt of the note under date of 
the 20th instant, which Count Buol-Schauenstein, &c., has done him the honour 
to address to him, is desirous of offering the following observations, which are 
rendered necessary by the misapprehension to which his note of the 15th 

ve given rise, 
PN tine aenvedls could be more remote from the intentions of the Under- 
signed than to call upon the Imperial Government to render more stringent the 
law regulating the press, or to ask for any undue application of the law at 
present in force, ; 

His object was only to point out (with the reluctance which belongs to a 
person who treats a subject with which he is not familiar) that if the writer in a 
newspaper exposes himself to the admonition or the censure of the police 
authority by any offence against public morality and the principles of civil 
society, that correction or that censure may be considered as justly incurred by 
the author of the article in the ‘‘Ocsterreichische Zeitung” to which the 
attention of the Imperial Government had been called by Her Majesty’s Mission. 

The reason appears to him to be obvious. ‘The flagrant attack upon the 
private character of a functionary, contained in the article in question, 18 not 
only calculated to proveke a breach of the peace (as between individuals), but, 
besides injuring the person against whom it is directed in his private capacity, 
is calculated to interfere with the efficient discharge of those duties whieh he is 
called upon to perform as the servant of an allied and frendly Government. 

No one more than the Undersigned deplores the exeesses which may be 
objected occasionally to the press in those countries in which (like his own) the 
press is wholly unrestricted. The greater the value which he attaches to the 
perfect freedom of the press, the more sincere his regret that this value should 
ever be diminished by casual abuse. ‘ 

He would however observe that that description of abuse or excess 
consisting in virulent, and it may be groundless attack, which is productive of 
no effect when directed a Government, may become extremely effective when 
aimed against private character. in | 

From his residence in England, and from his knowledge of English customs 
and English law, Count Buol must be well aware that no reciprocal engagements 
can be taken by Her Majesty's Ministers with the Governments of other coun- 
tries for the restriction of the public press. That institution has grown up with 
the growth of England, and is as much a part and parcel of the English system 
as the geographical configuration of the country, ; ; 

All that Her Majesty's Government can do as regards England ts, to notice 
those offences of the press against foreign Governments or their servants which 
are amenable to the law, and to deplore those which are not. As regards foreign 
countries, the endeavours of Her Majesty's Government must be confined to 
endeavouring to procure the employment by their Governments of such means as 
inay be legally at their disposal for the prevention of similar offences, the effects 
of which are the more mischievous when directed not against poblie acts, but 
against private reputation ; not against personages whose exalted station, parti- 
cularly when joined to elevation of character, places them beyond the reach of 
attack, but against those persons whose comparative obscurity exposes them the 
more readily to the assaults of calumnious writers, NARS | 

The Undersigned, &e. (Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, Vienna, December 26, 18955. 

COUNT BUOL, whom I have just. left, is not satisfied with the reports 
which he receives from Berlin, He imagines the King to be less well-disposed 
than he was upon the receipt of the Emperor's letter. He augurs ill of the 
calenlated withdrawal of Baron Manteuffel from the capital, and 1s very anxious 
that the full support of the English and French Missions should be given to 
representations which it will be Count George FEsterhazy’s province to make im 
a seeond audience of His Majesty. Count Buol desires that no threat should be 
made to the King of Prussin; but that it should be made perfectly clear to hin 
that his admission into the Councils which will negotiate the conditions of peace, 
will depend upon the Austrian proposal being warmly supported by His Majesty 
at St. Petersburgh. 

Upon this point Count Esterhazy’s declaration to His Majesty will leave no 
shade of doubt. 

Count Buol’s language upon the great affair of the day 1s as decided and 
resolute as 1 could desire. 

He has resolved to acquaint Colonel Manteuffel, upon his arrival here, that he 
cannot enter into any discussion with him as to the overtures whieh may be 
made by the King: Austria being engaged in negotiation in concert with Great 
Brita and France, whilst his decision with regard to Baron Seebach’s mission 
is equally decided. 

Count Valentine Esterhazy is informed that any support which ean be given 
by Baron Seebach to the ultimatum will be weleome; but that on no account 
must the Saxon Minister be permitted to assume the position of a mediator. 

Of Count Valentine Esterhazy’s progress since he left Warsaw, nothing is 
known here, It is, however, expected that le will reach St. Petersburgh to-day. 

Count Buol is well pleased with the reports which he receives from Munich, 
He considers M. Van der Pfordten’s language satisfactory, and reckons upon 
the support which the propositions will meet with from the King of Bavarii, 

From a private source J learn that Prince Gortehakoil’s language is to the 
rejection of the propositions is less decided than it was two days ago. 

My informant observed to me that the feeling which was the most apparent 
from Prince Gortchakoff’s conversation was, that of soreness at not having heen 
sonsulted during the deliberations which preceded Count Valentine Esterhazy’s 
departure for St. Petersburgh. If this report be correet, the change in the 
Russian Envoy's language is very abrupt, as I heard of lis saying, yesterday, 
that he should probably be obliged to quit Vienna, but that he should not take 
his departure before he had stated to Count Buol what he thought of his conduct,

No. 107. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received December 31.) 


(No. 367. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 29, 1855. 

ON the receipt, at Vienna, of Count George Esterhazy’s report of his 
audience with the King of Prussia, the substance of which was conveyed to 
your Lordship in my despatch No. 353 of the 22nd instant, Count Buol 
‘nstructed the Austrian Minister at this Court. by telegraph, to seek an inter- 
view with Baron Manteuffel, for the purpose of urging the Prussian Government 
to lose no time in coming to decision as to the course they will pursue at 
St. Petersburgh; for on it might depend the admission of Prussia to the delibe- 
rations amongst the Great Powers which may ensue if Russia accepts the bases 
that will have been presented to her. 

Count Esterhazy was also directed to state to his Excellency that the 
Bavarian Government had already announced their intention of supporting the 
Austrian communication; to explain that the direct communication sald to be 
made to London and Paris, and which the King had alluded to in his interview 
with Count Esterhazy, was of no value, and by no means answered the objects 
of the Alliance; and that the journey of Baron Seebach to St. Petersburgh 
would have no effect in diminishing the extent of concession which had been 
agreed upon, and which the three Powers must obtain if negotiations for peace 
were to be opened, 

Count Esterhazy was instructed further to say that, much as the aequi- 
escence of Prussia was desired, and gratifying as it would be to Austria if she 
supported their communication at St, Petersburgh, the refusing to do so would 
have no effect on the ulterior resolutions of the Austrian Government. 

Baron Manteuffel had left Berlin for the Christmas holidays when this 
‘natruction arrived at the Austrian Legation, and as it was put in the most 
pressing form, Count Esterhazy considered the best means of executing his 
orders without delay—for Baron Manteutfel’s return was then fixed for the 29th— 
was to request another audience of the King, which he did by addressing a letter 
to Count Keller, the Marshal of the Court. Twenty-four hours elapsed belore 
any notice was taken of this application, and Count Esterhazy then received a 
reply from Count Keller expressing regret that he could not take on himself the 
responsibility of asking for an audience of the King, as such applications could 
only be sent through his Minister for Forcign Affairs, but that his letter had 
heen forwarded to Baron Manteuffel, from whom he would hear further. This 
letter brought Baron Manteuffel to Berlin, and Count Esterliazy was requested, 
on his Excellency’s arrival, to call on himat the Foreign Department. 

At this interview Count Esterhazy explained the nature of the instructions 
which he had received, and urgently pressed the Prussian Minister for Foreign 
Affairs to exhort the King to lose no time in writing to St. Petersburgh. 

The Austrian Minister has told me that he explained to Baron Manteutfel 
the instructions whieh he had received in the most Ane and precise terms, and 
that as his Excellency requested him to repeat the most important parts twice 
over, he had no doubt the communication would be accurately conveyed to the 
King of Prussia, 

Count Esterhazy mentioned to me that at this interview no question was 
asked. and no observation made to him, except in reply to his inquiry whether 
the King’s answer was likely to be favourable or hostile, to which Baron 
Manteuttel answered, Certainly not hostile.” 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received December 31.) 


(No. 364. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, December 29, 1855, 

COUNT ESTERHAZY has just called upon me to say that Colonel 
Manteuffel had been to see him to-day, and informed him of the mission he was 
to be charged with to Vienna, for which place he would probably start on 
Sunday. The Austrian Minister endeavoured to learn the nature of the com- 
munication of which he was to be the bearer, and was. told, to lis great surprise, 
that the King would not do more than urge on the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh 
the advantages of peace in general terms. 

Count Esterhazy then observed that the King had receded from the 
assurances which he hud given him at his audience, when His Majesty said that 
he would recommend the Austrian proposal to the adoption of the Russian 
Government. 

On this, Colonel Manteuflel appears to have spoken in no very measured 
language against the conditions which the allies sought to inypose on Russia, 
saying, that he should never believe that an Emperor of Russia could consent 
to give up half of Bessarabia; rather, he exclaimed, carry on the war against 
United Europe than submit to anything so degrading. 

In fact, said Count Esterhazy to me, an aide-de-camp of the Emperor 
Alexander could not have advocated the interests of Russia in stronger terms 
than did this Prussian Colonel. 

Whether these words pourtray an exact picture of the state of things here, 
I cannot say, but they are not encouraging or indicative of any improvement in 
the attitude likely to be assumed by the Prussian Government in the present 
crisis. 

L have, &c, 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD, 


No, 109. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Harl of Clurendon.—j{ Received December 31.) 


(No. 369.) 


My Lord, Berlin, December 29, 1855. 

1 SAW Baron Mantenffel last night, and inquired if the King had yet taken 
any decision upon the Austrian communication to St. Petersburgh, and whether 
any instruction on the subject had been sent to Baron Werther, observing that 
it was most important that no time should be lost, for that Count Nesselrode 
must now be in possession of the proposed bases of peace. His Excellency said 
that intelligence of Count Valentine Esterhazy’s arrival at St. Petersburgh had 
reached him by telegraph; the more necessary then, [ said, for you to make up 
your minds as to what you will do, 

Buron Manteuffel then gave me to understand that his cousin, Colonel 
Manteuflel (who had been sent for by the King some days ago, and who, as 
your Lordship is aware, has frequently been employed in unprofitable missions 
to Vienna and St. Petersburgh, and is by no means a favourite at the Austrian 
Court), would convey the King's answer to Vienna, but what that answer would 
be Baron Mantenffel did not even shadow forth, and upon my further pressing 
him to let me know what the King would write to St. Petersburgh, all 1 could 
learn was, that his communications would be better than we perhaps expected 
they would be. 

Our conversation afterwards turned on the passage through Berlin of Baron 
Seebuch on his way to St. Petersburgh. 1 asked if he could tell me what 
he carried to the Imperial Court, and that [hoped at all events it would not be 


words that would encourage resistance to the Aust-ian proposals, His Excellency 


99 


replied that he believed Baron Seebach would endeavour to impress Count 
Nesselrode with the true state of feeling of the Emperor Napoleon, the French 
Government and people, on the great question of the moment, and that he 
would urge the neceseity of making large concessions, if peace was seriously 
desired in Russia, for he was convinced that though there might bea powerful 
peace party in France, trifling concessions would not be listened to. 

I usked Baron Manteuffel if it was true that Baron Seebach had seen the 
Emperor Napoleon before leaving Paris. He said that Count Hatefeldt believed 
that he had had a private audience of His Imperial Majesty after his interview 
with Count Walewski, but that even if it were so, he possessed no information 
as (o what had occurred on this occasion. 

He then told me that Baron Budberg had been to see him in the course of 
the day, and had requested to be furnished with a copy of the proposed bases of 
peace, which he declined giving, as the communication had not come from the 
‘Austrian Government, but from the Emperor Francis Joseph, He said they had 
conversed on the subject, and that Baron Budberg told him that though his 
Government might agree to most of the conditions proposed, as far as he was 
acquainted with them, the question of the cession of part of Bessarabia could not 
be entertained. 

Baron Manteuffel added, as from himself, that he thought resistance on 
this point certain; but that Russia might not be indisposed to give up the 
‘lands at the mouth of the Danube, 1 then told Baron Manteuffel that [ had 
heard that the Russian Minister had been endeavouring to raise a ery against 
‘Austria for the condition regarding Bessarabia, and had endeavoured to lay at 
her door the whole responsibility of this part of the question, but I could assure 
him that England took as much interest in this point as in any other, and that 
the bases proposed formed a whole, and that England, Austria, and France 
were prepared to take their stand equally on ewch; but I said the free navigation 
of the Danube was a question which particularly regarded Germany, and, 
therefore, ought to deserve the fullest support of Prussia. 

I have, &c. 
Signet) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lord, Vienna, December 30, 1855. 

A MESSENGER, dispatched by M. de Bourqueney, gives me an oppor- 
tunity for writing a few lines to your Lordship. 

Count Buol is very much disappointed by the accounts which he has 
received from Munich. 

M. Von der Pfordten began by saying that he had no knowledge of the 
terms proposed by Austria, and upon being made acquainted with them stated, 
that although he was ready to give them a general support they were not of a 
nature to bring about peace, or tobe worth enforeing by war. 

Count Appony has been instructed to communicate the ultimatum officially 
to M. de Pfordten, and in the most energetic manner to call upon the Bavarian 
Government for its support of them. 

The conduct of Count George Esterhazy offers a striking contrast to that 
of Count Appony, and the spirit with which he has acted upon his instructions 
appears to have produced an effect upon the Court of Berlin. 

Count Walewski has signified by telegraph the full approbation of the 
Emperor, his master, of the orders sent from hence to St. Petersburgh, and of the 
firm resolution taken by the Austrian Cabinet not to admit of any mediation on 
the part of Baron Seebach. 

The intention of the Porte to send Prince Callimachi to Vienna with the rank 
of Ambassador is embarrassing to the Austrian Government and very unaccept- 
able to the French Mission. As an Envoy M. de Callimachi would, it is felt, be 
able to discharge all the duties assigned to him, whilst his diplomatic rank would 
secure him against the jealousies and embarrassments .o which a higher grade 
would subject him. 

Colonel Manteutfel is expected to arrive here to-morrow. 

Were his mission to be indefinitely postponed, little inconvenience would, 
| imagine, acerue to the service of the King of Prussia.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl af Clurendon.—(Received January 4, 6 P.M.) 


En évitant ce double inconvénient, on (Telegraphic.) Vienna, January 4, 1856, 2 a.m 


THE interview between Count Buol and Colonel Manteuffel has proved at 
least as satisfactory as could be expected. 

Count Buol was very unbending. and said plainly that the omission of a 
single comma would be equivalent to a refusal. 


it 


with satisfaction the instructions which had been given by the King of the 
Netherlands to his Envoy, M. Gevers. 

{ understand that fresh instructions have been sent to Count V. Esterhazy, 
reiterating the injunction laid wpon him to listen to no counter-propositions, 
modifications of terms, or qualified acceptance ; and such is the rule which 
Count Buol has laid down for his own guidance, in the event of Prince Gort- 
chakoff resorting to any of these expedients. 

Up to a certain point the resolution of the Austrian Cabinet appears to be 
irrevocably fixed ; beyond this, all is yet uncertainty and hesitation: and 
reluctance to advance must, I conceive, be looked for, if Austria is to find herself 
with a hostile Russia in her front and a Russianized Germany behind her. 

It is satisfactory meanwhile to observe that some of these philo-Russians to 
be found in the ranks of German diplomacy, are beginning to be aware that 
the interests of Russia suggest a compliance with the terms at present within 
her reach. 

Count Buol’s language upon this point (but he, at least, is free from any 
predilection of the kind to which I allude) is perfectly explicit. 

Lam willing, he observed to me yesterday, to affirm upon oath that Russia 
could have obtained better terms last May than she could do now; and though I 
could net swear it, | can conscientiously express my conviction that the con- 
ditions now within her reach are more favourable than those which she would 
obtain after a third campaign. 

It has been whispered to me that one at least of these diplomatists who, 
although not ostensibly in Russian employment and pay, are to all intents and 
purposes her agents, has suggested that it would be hard to deprive Russia of 
any part of Bessarabia, but that possibly the cession might be acquiesced’ in 
wore she to receive some Slight territorial compensation in another quarter. 

From this and other trifling indications, as well as from the time which has 
elapsed since the presentation of the Austrian ultimatum, it may, I think, be 
inferred that the conditions of peace are such, in the opinion of the Russian 
Cabinet, as to deserve, at least, very mature consideration, 

I have, &e.

quarter; that he did not believe that any decision had yet been taken by the

‘ndicated what would be the result of the communication, but that his own 
impression was that the Emperor would not accept the bases of peace as sub- 
mitted to him. | said that I was grieved to hear that this was his Excellencys 
opinion, for | had hoped that, in the interests of Russia, it would have been 
prudent to accept them rather than expose that Empire and Europe to a con- 
tinvation of the war; nay, Lsuid, to un extension of it, for if peace was not 
signed, the Baltic would probably be the seene of hostilities on a very different

to our views than on former oceasions ; that we had reason to believe that she

of Austria, the minimum that we could be satisfied with, Baron Manteuffel 
endeavoured to defend himself from the accusation of going backwards, or of

Sir R, Abercromby to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 7.) 


(No. 1. Confidential.) 


My Lord, The Haque, January 3, 1856. 

_ OAL the request of M. Van Hall, 1 called upon him yesterday evening, at 
his private residence, where he confidentially communicated to me the proposuls 
which Count Esterhazy has been instructed by his Government to carry to 
the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, and also a despatch which he has himself 
addressed to the Netherland Chargé d’Atfaires in Russia on the subject of 
price. 

| found that the report of the proposals which M, Wan Hall had that 
morning received from the Netherland Minister at Vienna corresponded with the 


107 


printed copy of the Austrian ultimatum, as transmitted to me in your Lordship’s 
despatch marked “ Confidential,’ No. 60, of the 26th of December, 1855; but 
his Excellency was not aware of the nature of the additional conditions attached 
by Great Britain and France to the ultimatum, as detailed in the body of your 
Lordship'’s confidential despatch ; and I accordingly abstained from communt- 
eating them to the Netherland Minister for Foreign Affairs, nor did | allow his 
Excellency to perceive that I had had any previous knowledge of the contents of 
the ultimatum itself. 

After M. Van Hall had read to me the propasals, 1 asked him what was his 
opinion of them, when Ins Excellency replied that he considered them to be 
acceptable by Russia. 

In answer to my question as to what he thought of the proposal respecting 
the territory to be ceded by Russia in Bessarabia, he observed that, according to 
the information he had received, the population of the ceded territory did not 
exceed 400,000 souls, and that he did not apprehend Russia would object to 
the cession. 

On further conversation, however, I perceived that his Excellency had not 
referred to a map of Bessarabia, and fiat he was not aware that by the 
proposed throwing back of the Russian frontier, Russia would have to abandon 
the important fortress of Ismail and the military port of Reni, which holds the 
Turkish fortress of Galatz in check, besides having to relinquish the line of the 
Pruth. On becoming acquainted with the full importance of the cession required 
from Russia, M. Van Hall appeared to entertain some doubt as to the willingness 
of Russin to consent to such terns. 

His Excellency, however, said that in the present position of Russia, he was 
af opinion it would be for her interest to make peace, as it was evident that 
another campaign might bring with it results most prejadicial to the welfare of 
Russia ; and, in support of this opinion, his Excelleney alluded to the formidable 
preparations now making, both in England and in France, for the vigorous 
prosecution of the war ‘1 the Baltic and in the South, in the ensuing spring. 

When expressing to his Excellency as my own private and individual 
opinion that the ready acceptance by Russia, as af present situated, of the 
Austrian ultimatum might give rise to some doubt as to her sincerity in thus 
finally acquiescing in the required abandonment of her aggressive policy in the 
East, by entering honestly and in good faith into engagements to renounce for the 
future those objects of ambition which had formed the basis of Russian policy 
for the last seventy or eighty years, his Excellency considered my apprehensions 
to be unfounded: but his subsequent conversation proved that in fact we did 
not in reality differ as to what might be the secret intentions of Russia, for he 
proceeded to remark that a Russian Minister might gladly avail hinselfof the 
first opportunity to make peace, because he might feel that so long as Great 
Britain and France were united together by the common interests af the present 
war, little or no chance existed of seeing the cordial alliance between the two 
countries either broken or diminished ; whereas, under the calmer influences of 
peace, circumstances tight possibly arise, of policy or of interest, which might 
lead, if not toa rupture, at least toa diminution of that intimate friendship and 
mutual confidence which at present forms the great power of the Western 
Alliance ; and that a period of peace might enable Russia, by profiting from the 
experience she had acquired daring the present war, to make fresh preparations 
for the future, and to provide against a repetition of such faults or omissions as 
had occurred in the course of the present hostilities. 

Such arguments your Lordship will, I think, be of opinion, sufficiently 
justify me in feeling that in reality M. Van Hall and myself view the 
possible policy of Russia much in the same light—namely, that Russia, to avoud 
becoming more effectually crippled, and ultimately forced to abandon her 
ambitious projects, from utter inability to pursue them, may only uccede to the 
present proposals of the allies, for the purpase of waiting for a more fayourable 
opportunity to renew them, and not from a sincere and fixed determination tw 
eonfine her foreign policy within such limits as may effectually secure the 
cerenien of neighbouring States und the future repose and tranquillity of 
SUrope. 

In thus reporting to your Lordship what dropped from M. Van Hall in the 
course of a confidential conversation as to what might be the result of the 
communication which Count Esterhazy is charged to make to the Cabinet of 


108 


St, Petersburgh, and as to a course of policy which might possibly suggest itself 
to the mind of a Russian Minister, 1 shoula be representing M. Van Hall in an 
invidious light, were 1 to lead your Lordship to believe that he anticipated that 
such would in reality be the motives which are to govern the decision of the 
Russian Government, and his hope is, that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, 
appreciating as it deserves, the advice that has been tendered to it from so many 
different quarters, from feelings of sincere friendship, and measuring to their full 
extent the dangers and humiliations to which an obstinate prolongation of the 
present contest with the Western Powers may eventually expose the Russian 
Empire, will embrace, in a-spirit of honesty and sincerity, the opportunity now 
offered of restoring peace to Europe: i 

The impression which my conversation with M. Van Hall has, however, 
left upon my mind is, that his hope rather than his conviction leads him to 
entertain visions of the possibility of an approaching peace,

nication, that he, M, Van Hall, now renewed, of his own free will, and not at

ON the receipt of your Lordship’s instruction inclosing the Austnan

and to be supported by the French Ambassador at Vienna, | settled a time for 

meeting with M. de Thouvenel. We met, in consequence, on the 22nd instant; 

and after communicating freely with each other on the subject and its attendant 


considerations, we agreed to apni Fuad Pasha, by a simultaneous message, of 


the proceedings which had taken place, and to put him in possession contiden- 
tially of the memorandum which T had received from your Lordship. 

In coming to this decision 1 am guided by two motives, both equally in 
aceordance with the interests of the case and the views of Her Majesty's 
Government, | was not only at liberty, but directed, to make a full communi- 
cation to the Turkish Ministers. It was evidently desirable for me to make the 
communication in concurrence with the French Ambassador. 

Yesterday, in execution of our agreement, the principal interpreters of the 
two Embassies, acting under similar instructions, waited on the Ottoman Secre- 
tary of State together, and read the ultimatum, with its modifications, preficing 
their communication to his Exeellency with a brief statement of the preliminary 
facts, and of the reasons which had prevented any previous reference to the 
Turkish Government, 

Fund Pasha, after listening to the whole with deep attention, expressed the 
eatisfaction which he had derived in general from the terms of pacification 
sunctioned by the allied Governments, particularly in what respected the removal 
ofthe Russi frontier from the Danube, and the neutralization of the Black 
Sea, He declared that for peace, as for war, the Porte was prepared to move in 
concert with her allies; reserving only the faculty of submitting her remarks at 
the proper time, and drawing attention to such considerations as might arise 
with reference to the question of privileges, constituting the fourth point or 
basis of negotiation, and that of the Danubian Principalities, which wus comprised 
in the first. 

In conformity with your Lordship’s instructions, I propose to send Iuad 
Pasha a copy of the Memorandum marked B, as requested by his Excellency.

No. 150. 
The Karl of Clarendon to Sir Hamilton Seymour. 


(No. 16.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, January 8, 1856. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has informed me that the Austrian Govern- 
ment were desirous of knowing whether Her Majesty’s Government adopted the 
memorandum which had been” paraphe” by Count Buol and M de Bourqueney 
on the 1th of November. 

I told Count Colloredo that there were portions of that memorandum to 
which Her Majesty’s Government were not disposed to adhere, as the discussions 
which had taken place between the two Governments since the date of that 
memorandum had materially altered some of its provisions. 

With respect to the second paragraph im the memorandum, which professed 
to give an account of what had passed with respect bo ihe propositions, I begged 
to observe, although the matter was not of much importance, that there was an 
‘aaccuracy, for although it was true that M. de Bourqueney, when at Paris, had 
confidentially communicated to Lord Cowley what had passed between himself 
and Count Buol, yet Her Majesty s Government had limited themselves to 
stating that they could give no opinion upon any proposals for peace until they 
were before them in writing. 

In the fourth paragraph of the memorandum the right was. reserved to the 
belligerents to bring forward such further conditions as they might think proper, 
but Count Buol expressed the hope that those conditions would not offer an insur- 
mountable obstacle to the re-establishment of peace, and it was clear, therefore, 
that any such further conditions which were insisted upon by the belligerents, and 
were rejected by Russia, would, ipso facto, become an insurmountable obstacle to 
peace, and Count Buol having expressed his hope that no such obstacle would 
be raised, he would be entitled not to support the demands of the Western 

Powers, and the same disagreements might then be expected with the Austrian 
Government which took place last year, and the recurrence of which Her Majesty's 
Government believed it was the firm intention of Count Buol to avoid, Her 
Majesty's Government according!y, having no policy to conceal and no motives 
to withhold from Russia the conditions they meant to bring forward beyond 
those contained in the Austrian ultimatum, had at once made known to the 
Cabinet of Vienna that they should insist upon no fortifications being restored 
or erected upon the Aland Islands, upon the power to appoint Consuls at the 
Russian ports in the Black Sea, und the right to consider the state of the 
countries on the eastern shores of the Black Sea ; they further desired that these 
conditions should form part of the Austrian ultimatum, and upon this having 
heen declined by Count Buol, Her Majesty's Government felt that they had no 
right to preseribe to Austria the conditions on which she should muke the 
rupture of her diplomutie relations with Russia depend, but, on the other hand, 
they claimed to be the judges, in conjunction with the French Government, of 
the conditions on which alone they would consent \ negotiate for peace, anid 
they again requested that those conditions should be formally announced to the 
Cabinet of Vienna. 

‘To that request, however, t remarked to Count Colloredo, that Her 
Majesty's Government lad as yet hal no answer, and they were at this moment 
in ignorance as to whether the additional conditions had or hud not been made 
known to Russia, and under these eircumstances Count Buol, | telt sure, would 
erceive that the pure and simple acceplance by Russia of the Austrian pro- 
posals, which the Austrian Government wished to be followed by the signature 
of the preliminaries of peace, would not be the acceptance of all those conditions 


upon Which alone England and France would consent to sign preliminaries of 


118 


peace, The signature of such preliminaries, therefore, and definitive negotiations, 
and a general armistice, must all depend upon the acceptance by Russta of the 
conditions which’ the memorandum reserved to the belligerents the right of 
bringing forward, but which they had at once made known, in justice to Russia, 
and in order to avoid misunderstanding with Austria. 
Her Majesty’s Government, I said, would gladly agree to a Treaty between 
Great Britain, Austria, and France, which should complete the stipulations of 
ace, by guaranteeing the integrity and independence of the Ottoman Empire, 
and establishing as a casus belli, any ‘nfraction on the part of Russia of the 
stipulations of the said peace. 
In the event of the conditions proposed by Austria being refused by Russia, 
it was proposed in the memorandum that the allied Powers should meet ("se 
réuniraient”) for the purpose of cor certing measures to coerce Russia; but 
l observed to Count Colloredo, that the ordinary means of communication 
between the three Goyernments would be sufficient, and that no conferences, 
specially established for that purpos?, would be necessary. 
You are instructed to communicate this despatch to Count Buol, and to give 
a copy of it to his Excellency. 
Lam, &c.

No. 135. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No, 44) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 9, 1856. 

1 HAVE to state to your Excellency, m reply to your despatch No. 35 of 
the Gth instant, that M. d'Azeglio read to me, and placed in my hands, a copy 
of the Sardinian note respecting the consexuences to Italy of peace being 
concluded upon the terms proposed by Austria to Russia; and I made to him 
much the same answer that Count Walewski appears, from your Exeellency’s 
despatch, to have given to M. de Villamarina. 

I said that the views, or rather the fears, of the Sardinian Government 
appeared to be founded on a misapprehension of facts, and a notion that Austria 
would, by the aid of England and France, obtain the Protectorate of the Princi- 
palities hitherto exercised by Russia, and thus become all-powerful in Germany 3 
but so far was this from being the case, that we had taken special care, in the 
wording of the ultimatum, to avoid pledging ourselves to anything of the kind; 
and [saw no reason to think that Austria would hereafter exercise more influence 
in the Principalities than that which she must always derive from her geographical 
position ; and that, with regard to the increase of power which Austria would 
obtain in Germany, it was likely rather to be diminished than increased, owing 
to the jealousy and hostile feclings of Prussia, and the disunion which prevailed 
between Austria and the minor States, and evidence of this was already existing, 
ag these States had declined to support the Austrian ultimatam, 

I farther told M. d’Azeglio that if negotiations for peace were now entered 
upon, it was not easy to see in what way the condition of Italy could be brought 
under the serious consideration of the Plenipotentiaries ; but that Her Majesty's 
Government took a decp interest in the question, and would, on all fitting 
occasions, use their best efforts to promote a better state of things in that 
country. 


Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

been the combining Aches to produce this apparent improvement in the 
disposition of the Prussian Government,

LT HAVE the satisfaction of informing your Lordship that the Treaty of 
Defensive Alliance signed on the 2lst November last between the Western 
Powers and Sweden, has been received exceedingly well throughout this 
country. All the provincial papers agree in estimating highly its importance, 
and in’ praising its purport, and they describe the feelings of the people in their 
respective neighbourhoods as being those of entire satisfaction and hearty 
enthusiasm. | 

In Stockholm also the effect has been on the whole decidedly favourable, 
though not as general as the advantages secured to Sweden might have led us 
to anticipate. A certain number of persons belonging to the higher class of 
society, and whose organ in the press is the “ Svenska Tidning,’” have thought 
fit to cavil at the Treaty, and to underrate its importance. They pretend that 
the dignity of their native land suffers by its being put under the “protection” 
of the Western Powers, and they deny that Sweden is in need of any such 
“ protection.” "Those persons would, notwithstanding, he the first: bo cry out 
for large guarantees, and considerable subsidies, in the event of the United 
Kingdoms joining the allies in the present war. The * Attonblad,” in a 
temperate article, answers by reminding them that a hundred and fifty years have 
passed since Sweden was a great Power, which could give protection instead of 
having to seek it from others, and that the dream of a new great Scandinavian 
Power had not yet been realised, Tt advises its readers to be content with having 
changed one protection for another, and declares that the gain by the exchange 
must be clear to the blindest. ‘This is the opinion of the middle classes. “They 
have received the news that Sweden has allied herself with England and France 
with entire goodwill, and they are content to have gained such protectors, and 
to have thrown off the yoke of Russia, Still they only look on the present 
Treaty as a step, but one at all events in the right direction ; and they earnestly 
desire and hope that it is mercly a prelude to another, which will put an end to 
the neutrality of the United Kingdoms, and make them take an active part in 
the present war against Russia. 

A remarkable article, of which I have the honour to inclose a translation, 
appeared in the official “ Post Tidningen," in reply to the cavils of the Svenska 
Tidningen ;” and, as it is supposed to have been inspired by a high source, and 
puts the advantages of the Treaty ina clear point of view, is deserving of your 
Lordship’s perusal. 

| have, &e. 
(Siened) ARTHUR €. MAGENIS,

Inelosure in No. 1435. 
Extract from the“ Post Tulningen” of December 22, 1855. 


(Translation, } 


_ THE “Svenska Tidning™ says that “our independent position would have 
cained if we had not been obliged to place ourselves under the protection of the 
Vestern Powers,” 


119 

We have to call the attention of the “ Syenska Tidning” to the fact that no 
such werd as “ protection,” or the least allusion to such a thing, is to be found 
in the whole Treaty. That Treaty simply consists of an alliance concluded 
between independent States, founded on miutual respect and reciprocal adyan- 
tages, by which England and France (for whom it must be of immeasurable 
importance that Russia should not succeed in obtaining a firm footing on the 
North Sea) have promised to come forward as allies, if the United Kingdoms 
should be attacked, and to furnish the Sovereign of those realms sufficient forees 
to cooperite with our own. We learn from history that the enfecblement of 
Sweden, in spite of the heroie resistance of her sons, was caused by the 
indifference, not to say blindness, with which the affairs of the north have 
hitherto been regarded by Europe. It redounds to the honour of the Cabinets 
of the Western Powers, that they, with noble resolution and great foresight, 
have resolved to make good that which has for ages been neglected. It would 
be childish to attempt to deny the dissimilarity which exists in the means and 
resources over which we and the Powers now allied to us can command; but the 
more the sister-nations of the north show their patriotism, the eloser they unite 
to one another for the protection of their mountains and plains, and the more 
warmly their hearts beat for the cause of humanity and civilization, the higher 
they will raise themselves in the eyes of their allies. Moral worth equalises the 
differences in material force. 

The Svenska Tidning” promises to give a fuller account of the “small 
differences which have arisen with regard to the frontiers of Finmark.” We 
hope that the “Svenska Tidning ” will then perceive that these differences are 
not so unimportant, and that they contain seed for future complications, as 
dangerous for the Seandinavian Peninsula as for the peace of Europe. The 
many copious articles which have appeared on that subject in foreign journals, a 
part only of which have been taken up by our own press, May serve asf guide 
in that inquiry. We shall also take an opportunity of more clearly explaining 
this delicate question, which has hitherto been treated only too superficially. 

«The Treaty,” adds the “Svenska Tidning,” “is without doubt advan- 
tageous to us, inasmuch as in ease of a Russian aggression taking place in our 
time, it assures us a powerful alliance—the most powerful that can be given us 
by two States in our quarter of the globe. With regard to the future, on the 
other hand, its security rests on the security of the alliance between England and 
France themselves, which we trast may, for the welfare of Europe, be of long 
duration.” 

We join our heartfelt wishes for this to those of the * Svenska Tidning,” 
but we must also call its attention to the fact that the Treaty has not been 
concluded with England and France as collective Power, but with each of 
these Powers separately, and that the ratifications which were respectively 
signed in London and Paris have also been separately exchanged. 

We hope that these explanations will calm the apprehensions of the 
Svenska Tidning,” and we are convinced that it, as Well as every true patriot, 
will now rejoice at the conclusion of a Treaty which in so high a degree secures 
our future independence, without in the smallest degree wounding our national 
feclings.

HER Majesty’s Government entirely approve the language which your 
Lordship states in your despatch No. 7 of the Sth instant, that you held to 
Baron Manteuffel on the proceedings of the Prussian Government with regard 
to the Austrian proposals at St. Petershurgh. 

[have received no communication from Count Bernstorff upon the views 
and intentions of the Prussian Government, and not even the acknowledgment 
which in courtesy might have been expected to the request which, in the interests 
of peace, had been addressed by Her Majesty's Government to the Cabinet of 
Berlin, that the fair and moderate proposals transmitted to St. Petersburgh by 
the Austrian Government might receive the support of Prussia, But the 
silence maintained upon this subject, and upon the instructions sent to the 
Prussian Minister at St. Petersburgh; the active measures adopted to induce 
the German Powers not to take part with Austria; and the enormous facilities 
afforded by the Prussian Government to Russia for carrying on the war, are but 
too manifest indications that the sympathies of the Prussian Government are on 
the side of Russia and against the Western Powers, and Her Majesty's Government 
feel it their duty to declare that the great and partial assistance afforded by 
Prussia to the Russian Government in regard to the supply of munitions of war, 
cannot be considered consistent with the obligations of a neutral Power. 

Your Lordship will read this despatch to Baron Manteutfel.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received January 16.) 


(No. 28. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, January 11, 1856. 

THE Swedish Minister has been kind enough to read me a private letter 
(dated the 2nd instant) which he had received from his colleague at St. Peters- 
burgh, who has written to ‘aform him of the manner in which the Russian 
Government have expressed themselves with regard to the Treaty signed on the 
®Ist November, 1855. 

With respect to the Emperor Alexander, General Nordin states that his 
manner is perfectly unchanged towards him. His Imperial Majesty received 
General Nordin with the same cordiality as before, and had only taken nt 
opportunity of expressing a hope that nothing would ever impair the gonil 
relations which had so long existed between the two countries. 

The observations made: by the Chancellor seemed, on the contrary, to show 
that the late act of the Swedish Government had made a deep iipression upon 
iis mined, 

He likewise had pointed out the expediency of cultivating triendly relations 
between Russia and Sweden; but upon General Nordin’s assuring him that his 
efforts would not be wanting, observed that what had passed constituted a crack 


133 


(“fissure”), that care must be used to prevent the crack being widened into a 
breach, ‘Already,’ he said, “you appear to have one foot in the enemy's 
camp. Be careful that you do not altogether quit your neutral position.” 

«There is,” said General Nordin, “a precaution which would give security 
against any change of the kind.’ “ And that is?” inquired Count Nesselrode. 
‘That is, returned General Nordin, “ to make peace as soon as possible.” 

The conversation, although carried on in amicable terms, did not conclude 
without the Swedish Envoy having adverted to Finland, as the cause of feelings 
which still prevail or exist among his countrymen; to which allusion the 
Chancellor replied, by begging it might be remembered with what. pertinacity the 
Russian Government had pursued an object of procuring for Sweden a compen- 
sation for her loss. 

My colleague appears to be very forcibly struck with the altered tone of 
the Russian Government in speaking of an affair which in previous times they 
would have considered as a grievous offence, as one, probably, which would 
have led to the breaking off of diplomatic relations. 

Great attention to form had been, he candidly remarked, at-all times obser- 
vable in the diplomatic proceedings of the Russian Cabinet; still, upon any, 
the slightest cause of offence, a bitterness of language, an assumption of supe- 
riority, were discernible, of whieh, upon that recent occasion, no traces are 
allowed to appear. 

It may be hoped that a country like Sweden, which has once enjoyed the 
happiness of having recovered from the pressure of such an incubus as Russia 
has long been to her, cannot be otherwise than well disposed to the use of the 
exertion required for converting temporary relief into permanent security. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, Vienna, January 12, 1856. 

COUNT BUOL’S courier, who is the bearer of this despatch, will carry to 
Count Colloredo the two papers which form Count Nesselrode’s reply to the 
Austrian ultimatum. 

My knowledge of these documents was obtained by the hasty perusal which 
enabled me to send your Lordship the short telegraphic despatch which, by this 
time, must be in your Lordship's hands. 

It did not, however, require a close examination to ascertain that, although 
the Russian Cabinet have made some advance in the right direction, a con- 
siderable distance still remains between the point whieh they have reached, and 
that which would constitute compliance with the demands made upon them, 
A crisis has thus arisen for the Austrian Cabinet, and what I am at this moment 
eager to state to your Lordship is, that not the slightest suggestion on the part 
of Baron Bourqueney or myself was called for to remind Count Buol of the 
course which he had to pursue. 

He intimated tome indeed that were the Governments of England and 
France disposed to make any slight concession to Russia, such facilities for 
securing peace could not but he acceptable to the Emperor's Government. At 
the same time, however, he felt strongly the necessity of conforming atrictly to 
engagements, of making acts closely conformable to words, and the more 50 a8 
Austria, from not taking part in the war in whieh her Western allies are engaged, 
was the more bound not to recede from the position which she had taken up in 
their support. | 

Under these circumstances he had, he said, requested Prince Gortchakoff 
to call upon him to-morrow (this day) at 1 o'clock, when it would be his painful 
duty to inform him that, the answer from Count Nesselrode not being a direct 
compliance with the demands set forth in the ultimatum, he had no choice but 
to send him and the persons composing his Mission their passports on the 17th,

unless, before that time, he (the Prince) should be able to obtain by telegraph 
an unconditional acceptanee from his Court. 

{ did not conceal from Count Buol that, had I remarked any hesitation on

of his engagements, he was obliged to call upon Prince Gortchakoff for 4 plain 
acceptance or refusal, but that the straightforward course which he had at once 
adopted, rendered all remarks on my part unnecessary, and that T had but to

It had not escaped Count Buol’s observation that, whilst difficulties are 
raised by the Russian Cabinet as to the two points to which Austria and Great 
Britain may be supposed to attach particular importance, a hint is thrown out 
of the expediency of a mode of settlement which might be more exclusively 
acceptable to the Government of France. . 

He alluded to the notice of a Congress heing assembled, which Baron 
Bourqueney likewise considers to have been put forward with a view to producing 
a difference of opinion among the allies. 

With regard to the tract of country demanded of Russia, Count Buol 
aurmises that there would be comparatively little difficulty in obtaining the 
cession of the flat and waste land lying near the Danube, but that the Russians 
are very unwilling to part with the line of mountains which would form & strong 
frontier for the Province. 

[t may well be conceived that any precaution against fresh altacks upon the 
Principalities must prove unacceptable to those whom similar incursions had long 
been familiar. 

Having been unable for the last three or four days to leave my house,

a hurry that 1 am very imperfectly acquainted with their contents, My great 
object during Count Buol’s short visit. was to learn what was the immediate 
result to which they were to lead. 

This, as your Lordship will see, is closely conformable to the expectations 
to which my correspondence must have given rise. 

I may again state that supposing no direct consent, whether conveyed by 
telegraph or drawn from some reserved portfolio, to be sent in im the course of 
the next two or three days, Count Esterhazy will receive renewed orders for 
leaving St. Petersburgh with the whole of his Mission on the 17th instant.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 

(No, 63.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 16, 1856, 

| HAVE to state to your Excelloney that Her Majesty's Government have 
read with some surprise that a communication so important as that referred to 
in your Execellency’s despatch No. 1,055 of the 24th of December, namely, the 
terms of the ultimatum addressed by Austria to Russia, which might have 
required explanation and might have led to discussion, should have been made 
to the Porte merely through the channel of the English and French Dragomans. 

It has, no doubt, been the practice at Constantinople to proceed in this 
manner, and the practice has probably arisen from the circumstance that formerly 
the ‘Turkish Minister not speaking any European language, and European 
Ambassadors not speaking Turkish, conversation was necessarily carried on by 
mutual interpretation, and, to save ne and trouble, messages were sent by 

‘ 


142 


Dragomans. But now the Turkish Ministers speak French, and conversations 
can be held with them without the intervention of interpreters, and it is clear 


that it must be infinitely better, with a view to a satisfactory settlement of 
questions, that principals should meet and discuss together, rather than that 
such questions should be treated by means of messages sent through interpreters. 


er Majesty’s Government, however, desire to be informed by your 


Excellency what is the custom in this respect, and upon what occasions it 1s 
usual for Ambassadors to communicate personally with the Turkish Minister for 
Foreign Affairs, and on what occasions Dragomans are sent to convey thew 
messares,

No. 178: 


The Earl of Clarendon to Sir Hamilton Seymour. 


(No, 30.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, January 17, 1856. 

IN a despatch which Count Colloredo has read to me, Count Buol expresses 

his satisfaction that the views of Her Majesty's Government concerning the 

organization to be given to the Danubian Principalities, as stated in the menio- 

randum whieh you had communicated to him, were upon so many points in 

accordance with the memorandum on the same subject communicated by the 

‘Austrian Government to Her Majesty's Government, 

With respect to the guaranty of the Principalities, Count Buol remarks, 
that such a guaranty had always been put forward in Pe negotiations, a 
necessary to prevent any one Power from interfering with the Principalities, and 
also to secure the inviolability of the institutions of those Provinces, ut Austria 
nevertheless will not insist upon a formal act of guaranty. : 

At the same time the Austrian Government considers it necessary that tt 
chould be made clear that the Contracting Powers, by assisting in the work of 
reconstituting the Principalities, will have thereby acquired & just claim to the 
acceptance of their joint ‘iterrention, if at any time serious differences should arise 
between the Principalities and the Porte: and this object they think would be 
attained by inserting the proposals made to Russia in the preliminaries of peace. 

Count Buol further observes, that the Austrian Government are not 
convinced of the advantage of excluding the Porte—as he understands Her 
Majesty’s Government to propose—from the confidential deliberations respecting 


143 


the Principalities, in which the Representatives of the three Powers at Constan- 
tinople are to take part. The Austrian Government fears that the suscepti- 
bilities of the Porte will be wounded by this mode of proceeding, whilst the 
advantage will be lost of being able to aseertain through the Porte the wants and 
wishes of the Provinces which will be the subject of these deliberations ; and for 
these reasons it would appear better, Count Buol remarks, to admit the Ministers 
of the Sultan to the deliberations on the first point, declaring at the same time 
that these deliberations have no conclusive character, being only intended to 
furnish the respective Governments with grounds for definitive decisions, 

| expressed to Count Colloredo the satisfaction with which Her Majesty's 
Government would learn that no material difference existed between them and 
the Austrian Goveroment with respect to the arrangements for the future 
overnment of the Principalities, and | said that I did not apprehend any 
difficulty as to admitting the Porte to the deliberations which were to take place 
upon the subject at Coustantinople. 
Lam, &e. 


(Signed) CLARENDON.

No 180. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 18.) 


(No. 89. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 17, 1856. 
DURING a shooting party, to which the Emperor did me the honour to 
invite me yesterday, His Majesty took an opportunity of stating to me what had 
passed at the audience which | informed your Lordship, in my despatch No. 85 
of the 18th instant, he intended to give to M. de Seebach; and, although the 
statement of His Majesty has lost much of its interest from the news reeeived 
here last night that the Hussian Government had accepted the Austrian 
ultimatum, I do not hesitate the less to put your Lordship in possession of it. 
M. de Seebach, His Majesty said, had assured him of the sincere desire of 
the Russian Government to make peace, and had expressed the opinion that 
it would not be innposssible to obtain of them the conditions put forward in’ the 
Austrian ultimatum, if those conditions were submitted to them under another 
form, and if their success at Kars was taken ‘ato consideration, In other words, 
that which could not be conceded to an ultimatum might be obtained by discus- 
sion; that the Emperor of Russia had charged him to propose to the French 
Government that Plenipotentiaries from England, France, Austria, and Russia, 
should mect in Paris to exchange opinions. A day or two would suffice to 
prove whether they were in a position to come to any agreement, If such was 


144 


the case, the negotiations for peace would be continued at once; if nol, the 
Plenipotentinries would separate, and hostilities would continue, 

This, the Emperor stated, was, in a few words, the purport of M. de 
Sechach's communication, who added that if it was favourably entertained the 
Government of Russia would immediately address a proposal founded upon it to 
the different Governments interested, 

_ ‘The Emperor stated further that he had desired Count Walewski to inform 
M. de Persigny of what had occurred, and to instruct him to state to Her 
Majesty's Government that His Imperial Majesty considered that it merited 
serious consideration, He could not, however, permit the Plenipotentiaries to 
meet at Paris. It would expose him to suspicions of all kinds, and he should 
prefer Tirussels. 

I observed to the Emperor that the atmosphere of Brussels was supposed 
to be very Russian. His Majesty rejoined that he had indicated Brussels, 
first, because it was almost within equal reach of London and Paris: and, 
secondly, because the advice of the King of the Belgians might be useful in 
settling contested points. . S 

I said, further, that there was another point of far greater consequence than 
the place of negotiation, and that was, the choice of negotiators. The Emperor 
replied that this had already occupied his attention, and that he thought that 
he could not do better than employ M. de Bourqneney, who was so well 
aequaimbted with all the subjects which must come under discussion. 

It appears to be the intention of the Emperor of Itussia to name Count 
Orloff and M. de Brunnow, 

asked the Emperor why His Majesty considered this preliminary meeting 
of Plenipotentiaries to be necessary. It would surely be more simple to state, 
in writing, the terms on which the Western Powers would make peace, and 
not to begin negotiations until, from the acceptance of those terms by Kussia, 
it became necessary to work out the details. His Majesty replied that he had 
inade a similar observation to M.de Seebach, and that he gathered from that 
Minister’s reply that the Russian Government thought that an understanding, 
respecting the bases of negotiation, might be more easily attained if the attempt 
was made a distanee from St. Petersburgh, 

[t 13 impossible not to remark that this proposal of Russia has greatly taken 
the Emperor's fancy. His Majesty considers it, of all those that have yet been 
brought forward, as the most likely ta lead to peace. I repeated what I have 

so often said before, that, ere we go into negotiations with Russia, we must first 
understand each other, and that, as every day brought fresh evidence that the 
intention of Russia, whatever might be her ulterior object, was to negotiate, we 
ought to lose no time in making this necessary commencement. His Majest 
answered, as he invariably does when this subject is touched, that such was his 
opinion also, 
_ LF asked the Emperor whether, in the course of his conversation with M. de 
Seebach, His Majesty had obtained any information respecting the internal state 
of Russia-and the feelings of the Russian nation. 

His Majesty replied that M. de Seebach’s remarks tended to establish that 
there was a sincere wish for peace in the higher classes, but a fanatical desire to 
continue the war amongst the lower ranks. M. de Seebuch attributed this state 
of the public feeling to the fact that the lower orders did not so much feel the 
pressure of the war; for it was an extraordinary fact that, while all the articles of 
luxury had greatly increased in value, the price of bread in Russia was very low, 
Fis Majesty added, that the impression left upon his mind, not so much from 
the assurances given by M. de Seebach, as from the general tone and tenour of 
his remarks, was, that Russia was intent upon peace. For instance,” said His 
Majesty, “M. de Seebach made the following observation to me: ‘The Emperor 
Alexander counts upon the Emperor Napoleon HT taking the same interest in 
his fate us his uncle, the Emperor Alexander, took in the fate of Napoleon I.' 
But,” added Mis Majesty, “in order to vender the cases similar, it must be as 
necessiry for Russia to make peace now, as it wis necessary for Mrunce to make 
it in 1814," . ‘

WITH reference to your Excellency’s despatch No. 84 of the 1th instant,

the 14th of November, I have upon each oceasion held the same language to his 
Excelleney, and assured him that Her Majesty’s Government. had no desire or

the straightforward course towards Russia which Her Majestys Government 
had all along recommended had been pursued, and that the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh had been informed of the additional conditions which it was the 
intention of England and France to propose; but as that course had not been 
adopted, and that for some reason unknown to Her Majesty’s Government 
a mystery had been and still was observed upon the matter, Her Majesty's 
Government felt that it would not be safe to leave these important conditions to 
the chance of negotiation, and that a clear understanding must consequently be 
come to with Russia respecting them before any Preliminary Treaty of Peace was 
signed. ‘This precaution, | told M, de Persigny, appeared now to be all the 
more necessary as Count Walewski was not prepared to say whether the 
Government of the Emperor considered these particular conditions sine quibus 
yon to peace or not.

My Lord, Stockholm, January 11, 1856. 

M. DASCHKOFF, the Russian Minister at this Court, communicated on 
the 7th instant to Baron Stierneld the despatch which he had received the 

receding evening from Count Nesselrode, in reply to the communication of the 
Defensive Treaty signed on the 21st of November last, between Great [ritain, 
France, and Sweden, which General Nordin had made to his Excellency on the 
18th ultimo. 

As the Swedish Government forward by post this day to Baron Hochschild 
copy of Count Nesselrode’s despatch for communication to your Lordship, it is 
unnecessary that [ should enter into details, or do more than mention the chief 
points touched on by the Russian Chancellor, 

His despatch is dated the 44 December, and commences by alluding: to the 
explanations which Baron Stierneld had directed General Nordin to make when 
communicating the ‘Treaty, namely, that it in no way changed the position of 
Sweden, or the neutrality which that Power had laid down, assurances © dont 
I’ Empereur prend acte.” His Imperial Majesty hoped, also, that tt would in no 
respect alter the relations of friendship and good neighbourhood which had so 
long existed between the two countries, relations which His [mperial Majesty on 
his side regarded “comme un legs précieux de ses augustes prédécesseurs.” 

With respect to the apprehensions which had induced Sweden to conclude 
the ‘Treaty of November 21, although the Emperor could not admit that they 
were well grounded, nevertheless he would have been willing to have offered her 
every guarantee on the subject, had he not supposed that that the neutral 
position which Sweden had observed, and had hitherto so“ loyally’ maintained, 
rendered such guarantees unnecessary, 

Count Nesselrode’s despatch is drawn up with studied moderation, and 
betrays in no part of it the surprise which General Nordin reports he showed 
when the communication of the ‘Treaty was made to him; but notwithstanding I

have reason to believe that the Treaty of the 21st November has produced a 
considerable impression both on the Imperial Government at St. Petersburgh, 
and on those Cabinets which are nuppoet be favourably inclined to Russia.

My Lord, Paris, January 19, 1856. 

__ TAM most happy to be able to report to your Lordship a decided 
improvement in Count Walewski’'s language respecting the coming nego- 
tiations. 

[ called upon his Excellency this afternoon, and although [ found him stiff 
and reserved on first touching the subject, yet he gradually assumed a more 
cordial and finally a friendly tone. As I have reason to know that the Emperor 
has expressed himself very strongly to his Excellency, and in disapprobation of 
his iate conduct, I have no doubt that this amendment is to be traced to that 
SOnUrCe, 

I read to his Excellency your Lordship’s despatch No. 99, of yesterday's 
date. He asked me whether | could tell him that Her Majesty's Government 
would be satisfied if he made the declaration to which your Lordship alluded, 
namely, that the acceptance of the particular conditions was sine qua non to 
pence: [ told him that it would be much more satisfactory if he would say that 


he was prepared to require their insertion, as also the eventual evacuation of 


Kars by the Russians, in the preliminaries of peace. lL remarked, that I thought 
such a course would be easy if the present state of the question was fairly stated 
at Vienna. Count Buol was too sensible and too reasonable to insist on that 
which was no longer practicable, and it was clear that peace must be eventually 
made, not as Austria wished, but as the allies determined, 

_ Some further conversation ensued, anc eventually I stated it to be my 
opinion, reserving, however, the ratification of it for your Lordship's superior 
decision, that if the preliminaries of peace contained, in addition to the terms 


already agreed upon between the two Governments, the further stipulations that 
+ return for the evacuation by the allies of the places and territory in Russia 
now held by them, Russia should abandon the left bank of the Danube with the 
fortresses situated thereon, should restore Kars and the country belonging to 
Turkey now in the possession of her troops, should undertake not to refortily 
the Islands of Aad and should come to some een (“s'entendre oe was the 
word employed) respecting the provinces east of the Black Sea; if these additions 
were made, I said that | thought Her Majesty's Government would be 
satisfied. | 

‘ount Walewski assured me that if such should prove to be the case, he 
would endeavour to bring the Austrian Government into this arrangement, and 
that at all events he would engage to make the question of the Aland Islands a 
sine gud non to peace, 7 | 

| congratulate your Lordship on this sudden change of language, which, I 
frankly confess, I did not expect. 

Count Walewski told me that he ‘ntended sending M. Baudin to-night to 
London, for the purpose of better explaining to M. de Persigny the intentions of 
the [Imperial Government.

~ Baron Bourqueney alluded to the reserve whieh it had been necessary for 
him to observe upon his retuen from Paris, at 1 time when it was so desirable

Emperor expressed his warm satisfaction at the results which had been obtained

The words were heard, as probably they were intended ta he, by some of 
the foreian Ministers who were standing in the circle, and conveyed the impres-

energetic part than he has hitherto done in the great question by which Hurope

Baron Bourqueney, they have been not less so to the Minister for Foreign

conducted by Prince Schwartzenberg,

merits, 

Prince Schwartzenberg possessed an unbounded influence over his youthful 
snaster, Count Buol had to establish his influence firmly before he could apply

My Lord, Vienna, January 16, 1856. 

THE violence of the language used by the Russian Mission and the Russian 
party is extreme at the answer received from St. Petersburgh being met by an 
intimation of its being incomplete, and of the intention of the Austrian Govern- 
ment to send away Prince Gortchakoff and his staff should a distinet acceptation 
ol the ultimatum not be received by the 16th instant. 

Chere are very indisereet apceches attributed to Prinee Gortchakolf and his 
staff, which they probably never made; 1 know. however, for certain of his 
having said, “ L’Autriche vient de ereuser une abime entre elle et Ia Russie qu'il 
ne sufira pas de cinquante ans i combler, Quant au jeune Empereur il vy tombera 
le tout premier, Avant trois ans il versera des larmes de sang sur la faute qu'il 
vient de commettre,” : 

The indignation of Count Aron, Colonel Manteutiel, and the Prussian 
party, is, a8 Lam told, expressed in language equally energetic. They speak of 
the contemplated expulsion of the Russian Envoy as an act of brutality, and 
declare openly that the Austrians are much mistaken if they imagine that 
Prussian Mission will ever be recalled from St. Petersburgh in support of 
demands made in so coarse a manner upon the Emperor of Russia. 

2K 


It is not a little deplorable to see any awakening energy Which can be 
mustered by the Prussian Government put forth for the purpose of confirming 
Russia in a resistance to the demands so justly made upon her. 

Tt had been Prince Gortchakoff’s intention upon quitting Vienna to take 
up his residence at Dresden. He has now received a telegraphic order enjoining 
him, when he leaves his post, to repair to St. Petersburgh. 

Some of his friends here understand, as I believes he desires that it should 
be understood, that he is about to enter the Ministry. Should this prove to be 
the case, it will show that the orthodox party are in the ascendant.
