No, 196. 
Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 21.) 


(No. 44. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 16, 1856. 

NOTHING which has ever happened in my professional life has given me 
such painful perplexity as the decision which I have been called upon to take 
respecting the communication of your Lordship’s despatch No. | i of the 8th 
instant to the Austrian Government. 

On the one hand, the impulse is always strong to pay unhesitating and 
“mmediate obedience to your Lordships directions ; on the other, the motives 10 
favour of a reconsideration of my instruction appear to be so cogent that 1 could 
not bring myself to act as I had been ordered to do without reference to your 
Lordship, 

This struggle between simple obedience to orders, and the desire to guard 
against dangers which struck me as being of a very serious nature, led to the 
telegraphic messages which I had the honour of forwarding to your Lordship on 
the 19th instant and yesterday, the latter being sent after the receipt of your 
Lordship’s telegraphic despatch of the 14th instant. 

We are now in the midst of the crisis produced by Count Buol’s announce- 
ment to Prince Gortchakoff, and although a reference has been made by the 
Prince to St. Petersburgh, according to all probability the Russian Government 
(however great their desire for peace may be} will hardly make up their minds to 
purchase that advantage by a math and unconditional acceptance of the Austrian 
ultimatum. 

If they do, the disabled condition of Russia, and the reserve made in the 
ultimatum, afford the allied Governments the means of negotiating with 
advantage. 

If they do not, on the LSth or the 19th instant Prince Gortchakoff and his 
Diplomatic staff will receive their passports, and the diplomatic rupture between 
Austria and Russia is complete. 

In the meantime, however, not only is the indignation occasioned to the 
Prussian party much greater and much more openly expressed than was to be 
anticipated, but the opposition to Count Buol’s policy is likewise seen to be 
most powerful, not only among a purty always known to be favourable to Russia, 
but even in the Cabinet itself. 

The fact is so well established, that even a newspaper conducted under the 
‘afluence of the Finance Minister, docs not hesitate to express its warm (lisap- 

robation of the deplorable manner in which the conciliatory concessions of 
‘ussin have been met by the Imperial Government, 

It is not to be doubted that a portion of the Cabinet, possibly the Emperor 
himself, would be glad of a motive or an excuse for undoing what lias lately 
been done, and such excuse or motive would be afforded by the declaration 
that Her Majesty's Government decline all recognition of the memorandum of 
the 14th November. 

Tam far from being able to wssert that such a declaration to this. effect 
might not be followed by # reconciliation between the Austrian Government and 
the Russian Mission, Little more might possibly be required than that the 
Minister for Foreign Affairs should request Prince Gortchakoil to consider the 
declarations of the last days as “ non avenues.” 


165 


With regard to the point how far the ultimatum and the memorandum of 
the 14th November are to be considered as binding upon Her Majesty's 
Government, I have avoided discussion upon it, but I know perfectly well the 
arguments by which Count Buol supports his view of their constituting a0 
engagement from which we should not be at liberty to free ourselves, and I 
must confess my inability to meet them. 

The promise to break off diplomatic relations with Russia in the event of 
their not complying with the demands presented in the ultimatum, was recorde 
1 that memorandum, and in my despatch of the 12th December, No, 19, the 
following passages are to be found: “I should likewise remark upon the great 
stress laid by the Minister for Foreign Affairs upon being apprized whether 
Her Majesty's Government adhere to the arrangements made by himself and 
Baron de Bourqueney, and recorded in the paper (lated the 14th ultimo, to 
which their initials (paraphés”) were affixed. To this point Count Buol attaches 
great importance, as he regards this document as the basis of the present 
proceedings.’ 

As regards myself—although certainly [had no wish to express the opinion— 
I must admit, as I did lately in my despatch No. 19 of the Oth instant, that no 
doubt existed in my mind as to Her Majesty's Government having adopted the 
arrangements of the memorandum upen the consideration of the advantages 
which they offered outweighing those parts to which objections were entertained. 

When called upon, accordingly, a few hours before Count V. Esterhazy’s 
departure for St. Petersburgh, to declare whether Count Buol “ was to consider 
that Her Majesty's Government adhered to the plan traced out in the memo- 
randum of the }4th November,” I replied, “that I lad no instructions upon the 
point, but that 1 had no hesitation in expressing my firm belief that such was 
the case; that, slightly modified, Her Majesty's Government had agreed to the 
ultimatum, and that T inferred, therefore, that the paper which had led to it 
was included in the sanetion.” 

The declaration may have been indiscrect, but at least it was not unjusti- 
fable, as without it the whole proceedings would at once have fallen to the 
ground, The ultimatum would have become waste paper, and the diplomatic 
relations between Austria and Russia would have remained where they had been 
since the outbreak of the war. 

As it was, Count Buol was satisfied with the declaration of my confident 
belief, Count Esterhazy was dispatched on his mission ; and a certain advantage, 
with the chance of a more important contingent advantage, was at once 
obtained. 

If it be now said that the advantages, actual and remote, were too dearly 
purchased, I would respectfully submit to your Lordship that the reflection comes 
too late; the conditions of the ultimatum must, I think, be considered the condi- 
tions of the English Government, after this paper having received several correc- 
tions suggested and insisted upon by your Lordship ; whilst there will remain some 
difficulty in disconnecting this document from the paper to which it owed its 
existence. 

That it was the wish of Her Majesty's Government that no concealment 
should be used; that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgl should be made aequainted 
with the full extent of their demands, is certain; but [ submit that the point was 
not peremptorily insisted wpon, 

That it was not, appears from your Lordship's despateh No. 7 of the 6th of 
December, in which after stating “ that this delay has been unavoidable, as Her 
Majesty’s Government considered it their duty to come to an agreement with 
the French Government respecting the true interpretation ane meaning of 
certain terms of the ultimatum, in order to A acainst future misunder- 
standings,” your Lordship directed me “to assure Count Buol that the amend- 
ments and alterations had no other object than to render clear certain conditions in 
the ultimatum.” Ina later passage of the same despatel, the expediency and 

ropriety of making known to Russia the conditions upon which the two 
Vestern Powers insist are urged with great foree; but again | venture to 
remark that their setting forth is not made a peremptory condition. The 
expression used is, “that Her Majesty's Government trust that Count Bual 
will seo the propriety of making these terms known to the Cabinet of St. 
Petersburgh.” 

Lf [turn to your Lordship’s circular despatch of the 20th ultimo, explaining 


————————E 


156 


to Her Majesty's Missions abroad the position of the Russian question, I find a 
similar expression; in this it is said, ** Her Majesty’s Government would have 
mueh preferred that these conditions should have been specitied in the ultimatum 
itself, but that they felt that they had no might to press upon Austria the condi- 
tions on which the rupture of her diplomatic relations with Russia should 
depend.” And again, that ** Her Majesty's Minister at Vienna had been directed 
to acquaint the Austrian Government that Her Majesty's Government trust that 
Austria will see the propriety of making these terms " (regarding the Aland 
Islands, the Consuls in the ports of the Black Sea, and the conditions respecting 
the territories on the east of the Black Sea) “ known to the Cabinet of St. 
Petersburgh,” 

It may then be said, I think, that the ultimatum, as finally agreed upon 
and sent off, is to be regarded as a sort of compromise between the Power with 
which it in fact originated, and the Power which gave it its somewhat reluctant 
adherence. 

It was less explicit than was wished by Her Majesty's Government, in 
consequence of the warm desire felt by the Austrian Cabinet that it should be 
accepted by Russia; it was agreed to by Her Majesty's Government, notwith- 
standing its want of explicitness, on account of its offering the great chance of 
proving the cause of a rupture between Austria and her northern ally, and of 
her being brought into closer alliance or even cooperation with the Western 
Powers. When I say cooperation, however, | observe that this was to be looked 
to in virtue, not of the articles of the altimatum, but of the stipulations of the 
memorandum to which it owed its birth, 

I owe your Lordship apologies, and 1 offer them in great sincerity, for 
having expressed myself with perhaps unbecoming freedom; when, however, I 
see such dangers as I think may be made out a-head, T should be unworthy of the 
confidence which you have been wont so largely to bestow on me, if I allowed 
any consideration to induce me to keep silence. 

1 have observed the dispositions of the Austrian Cabinet to very little 
purpose, if Lam mistaken in’ supposing that, besides. great offence being given 
hy the communication of your despatch No. 16, the effect of the communi- 
cation will be, to throw Austria unhesitatingly into the armsof France In that 
event, as | have quite as little doubt that the displeasure would have been to 
some degree shared by France, & great risk would be incurred of the approxi- 
mation of the two countries ending, and possibly at no very distant period, in 
a disposition to come to terms with Russia without the concurrence and with 
little reference to the interests of Great Britain. 

I have, &e.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetwed January a.) 


(No. 48.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 16, 1856. 

IN obedience to your Lordship’s orders, I have this day placed in Count 
Buol’s hands a copy af your despatch No. 16 of the Sth instant. 

Count Buol’s feelings of regret at receiving this eammunication were 
manifestly very strong, although expressed in more measured language than I 
had expected. He had considered Austria pledged to Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment, he had considered that he held the pledge af Her Majesty’s Government 
in return, and he would ask me, Did I not understand that strong moral obliga- 
tion had been contracted by the Cabinets ? 

He would further inquire whether or not Her Majesty's Government had 
insisted upon certain alterations being made in the ultimatum, and whether by 
their acceptance the ultimatum had not beeome bond ide an English as well as 
an Austrian document? 

The English Government had desired that provision should be made for the 
admission of Consuls into the Black Sea; that proviso was accordingly to be 
found in the ultimatum, If Her Majesty's Government had laid such stress 
upon a specific mention of the Aland Islands and a consideration of the terri- 
tories of the Black Sea, these points should have been made a condition sine qua 
non, aud Her Majesty’s Government should not have allowed the ultimatum to 
be sent off in its present shape. 

After a pause Count Buol preceeded to say that he found it difficult to 
express What he had to say after one reading of your Lordship’s despatch, but 
that he should make some observations upon it in a despatch which he should 
address in the course of two or three days to Count Colloredo, 

He added that the French Government having repeatedly made known their 
intention of carrying out to their full extent the engagements which they had 
undertaken, it would be to the French Cabinet that he should look for support 
to the observations which he wished to offer to Her Majesty's Government. 

In conclusion, Count Buol intimated that as the rupture with Russia was 
now so nearly brought to a crisis, no deviation would be made from the course 
which had been struck out, but that, were this rupture to be averted by the 
unconditional acceptance by Russia of the terms of the ultimatum, it was to 
France that he must look for inducing Her Majesty's Government to stand by 
engagements which he must consider to be binding upon them. 

] have, &c. 


(Signed) G, H, SEYMOUR.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed January 21.) 


(No, 22.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 16, 1856. 


L CALLED to-day on Baron Manteutfel with the object of hearing if any 
news had arrived from St. Petersburgh as to the effect produced by the last 
communication from Vienna, and whether the Russian Government was likely 
to persist in its rejection of the ultimatum, His Excellency read to me at once 
a telegraphic despatch which he had just received from Baron Werther, stating 
that he had seen Count Orloff and other persons, and that he hatl still hopes, 
though slender ones, that it might be accepted purely and simply ; that he was 
doing everything in his power to obtain a solution of the question in this sense, 
and was strenuously supporting the efforts of his Austrian colleague. I then 
observed that there never was a more favourable moment for Prussia to step 
forward, and to declare at St. Petersburgh that she heartily joined with Austria, 
and would withdraw her Minister if Russia persisted in her refusal to accept the 
offered terms. 

Baron Manteuffel said that he had been duly informed of all that was 
intended by the Cabinet of Vienna, and that he thought if negotiations for peace 
were opened the security against a renewal of the present complications would 
be greatly increased by all the Powers becoming parties and guarantees to any 
Treaty that might be made, but that he felt reluctant to come in at the tail of 
Austria, giving me to understand that it would have been more congenial to 
him to have come forward at the invitation of the other Powers. 

I replied that we had already had several conversations respecting the 
course which we hoped to see Prussta pursue with regard to the ultimatum ; that 
his Excellency had never given me a clear and explicit answer on the subject; 
that the mere support of the question at St, Petersburgh was insufficient, and 
that, as Count Buol had explained, Prussia was required to reeall her Minister 
from St. Petersburgh if Count Esterlazy left the Russian capital. Limplored him, 
in the interests of peace, to add the weight of Prussia in the scales ; that it was 
evident from what he had just told me that Russia was giving way, and that. if 
she felt she had no longerany support toexpect from Berlin, she must yield ; and 
that not a moment was to be lost in sending instructions by telegraph to ot. 
Petersburgh, which would remove all doubt as to the position of Prussia. His 
Excellency rejoined that he had felt the gravity of the present moment, and that 
as to recalling Baron Werther, the question certainly hail been entertained,—" je 
ne vous dis nioui ni non :”’ evidently wishing me to believe, as | have already had 
the honour to inform your Lordship this afternoon by telegraph, that somethin 
on the subject had been sent off; but the observation was so qualified that { 
doubt his having addressed any instructions to Baron Werther that will compra- 
mise the Prussian Government if Russia finally rejects the ultimatum, but enough 
on the other hand, if it is accepted, to enable Prussia to put in a claim for acdmis- 
sion to the negotiations. 

She clings to her position as a great Power, but will incur none of ite 


159 


-responsibility, and will play the game of indecision to the last moment. She has 


no wish frankly to join us, neither has she; I believe, any desire openly to unite 
her policy with Russia. Her jealousy of Austria is undisguised and unabated ; 
but she is afraid to separate from her, and the force of circumstances may vet 
impel her into the right course.

No. 203. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January Pa 


(No. 26.) 


My Lord, Berlin, January 17, 1856. 

THE news arrived here to-day of the acceptance by Russia of the Austrian 
ultimatum, and I called on Baron Manteutiel to endeavour to learn from his 
Excellency the impression which had been made on him by this important 
intelligence. 

He seemed well pleased at the prospect now held out of approaching 
negotiations, but he did not appear to participate in the universal feeling existing 
here, that peace must necessarily follow, or that serious ditticulties might not yet 
arise in the course of the discussion. He possessed no details, and evidently 
considered that it would be prudent to wait for further intelligence before giving 
an opinion, 

I observed to his Excellency that he would perhaps now regret that Baron 
Werther had not been instructed to take the same course as Count Esterhazy 
had done. His Excellency said that os Prussia had had nothing to do with 
drawing up the ultimatum, it was hard to expect that she should at onee step 
forward and adopt as her own a project compiled by the three Powers; but he 
would observe that Baron Werther had greatly contributed to the success which 
had just been obtained. 

If so, I rejoined, why did you not communicate the instructions under 


160 


which he was acting? His Excellency answered, that he did not do so because 
he wished to avoid their becoming public, which he imagined would have 
happened if they had been communicated, and a knowledge of this would have 
done more harm than good at St. Petersburgh. 

I then asked if Baron Werther had been ordered to leave if Russia refused. 
His Excellency said that such a possibility was shadowed forth, and that Baron 
Werther had been ordered to let Count Nesselrode know that this might be the 
consequence if Russia rejected the Anstrian ulumatum. 

We spoke for some time on this matter, but I elicited nothing new, and 
only obtained a confirmation of the opinions which I have already haa the 
nonour to report to your Lordship in my despatch No, 22 of the 15th instant. 

It is clearly evident that the desire of the Prussian Government is to be 
admitted to the future Conferences, but I doubt, if that were the case, whether 
she would bind herself to guarantee, in conjunction with the other Powers, the 
due fulfilment of the conditions that will be imposed on Russia in a Treaty to be 
hereafter negotiated. What Prussia wishes to hold out to the allies, is that her 
being a party to the Treaty would strengthen it, and be an additional security 
for the maintenance hereafter of the peace of the world. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

are on the side of Tussia, and against the Western Powers, that Her Majesty’s

had certainly not chosen to follow in the line potnted out by three Powers, she 
had nevertheless played a useful part at St. Petersburgh, and Vrussia was far 
from being the tool of Russia, as was frequently reproached to her. 

As to the assistance which Prussia is secused of affording to the Russian 
Government in supplying munitions of war which the British Government 
considered inconsistent with the duties of a neutral Power, this was an cxagge- 
ration of the real fucts; but he added nothing to disprove the statement, and 
our conversation ended without my being able to obtain from him any assurances 
of a satisuctory nature.

My Lord, Berlin, January 17, 1856. 

COUNT ESTERHAZY has informed me confidentially that he received 
this morning a despatch from Count Buol, giving an account of an interview 
with Colonel Mantenffel, in which he urged him to use all his influence with 
the Prussian Government to adopt another position towards Russia; that her 
assistance would be of the greatest value, and that he hoped Baron Werther 
might yet be instructed to leave St. Petersburgh in the event of the rejection of 
the ultimatum. | 

Count Buol's despatch then states that in the event of Russia's refusal, 
war will certainly be carried on in the Baltic on a different scale from what has 
hitherto been the case, and that it would be impossible for Prussia to maintain 
her present neutral and passive attitude; that if complications arose Austria 
would remain faithful to her alliance with the Western Powers, and that Prussia 
must not look to her for assistance. 

Count Esterhazy left this despateh with Baron Manteuffel for communica- 
tion to the King, but has been unable to learn from his Excellency whether any 
fresh instructions had in consequence been sent to Baron Werther, His 
impressions on the subject of his former instructions coincided with those which 
I have reported to your Lordship in my other despatch No. 26 of this day; but! 
have no doubt that the Prussian Government has in its own way endeavoured 
to. render service to the cause of the allies, though the form in which this has 
been done is concealed from us.

Lord Bloomfield to the Bart of Clarendon.—(Received January 21.) 


(No, 36, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 19, 1856, 

THE prospect of peace is a source of great satisfaction to the public of 
Berlin: but 1 cannot say that the Court party feel otherwise than humiliated by 
the unconditional acceptance by Russia of the terms of the ultimatum. 

The most zealous of this party have always maintained that Russia could 
make no concession that would meet the demands of the Western Powers. 
At first they disbelieved the counter-propositions ; and when the telegraph 
announced the pure and simple acceptation of the ultimatum, many considered 
the news to be false; and the Kreuz Zeitung" did nor even favour its readers 
with an article on the subject the evening the news arrived; and the President 
Gerlach, the principal anager of the journal, pretended to doubt the authenticity 
of ay announcement that was known to the whole town. 

[ think it right to inform your Lordship that the principal consideration of 
the Prussian Government at the present imoment is, us to how they are to gain 
admission to the Conferences which may be held. 

The Austrian Minister, who has been most bitter in his invectives against 
this Government and country, has, I hear, suddenly come round, and now 
presents himself as the general protector and peace-mitker, He states, 1 hear, 
that France and England have no wish to see Prussia in the Conference; but, 
after ull that has lately passed at Vienna, there is an end of former differences, 
and that Austria will willingly exert her influence with the Western Powers to 
amooth the way for her admission. 

Baron Manteuffel has already hinted to me, as I have stated to your Lord- 
ship in my despatch No, 22 of the 15th instant, the advantage which he 
considers it would be for the peace of the world if Prussia were a party to the 
future Treaty; and he has this morning spoken in a still stronger sense to my 
French colleague. ) 

Baron Manteuffel has also alluded, in conversation with M, de Moustier, to 
the rumour that Vienna is objected to as a seat for the Conferences, antl lias 
mentioned Dresden and other places; and I apprehend that his jealousy of 
Austria is such, that if no place in Germany were seleated, lie would prefer that 
u Conference were established in London or Paris. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

No, 215. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received January 22.) 


(No, 113.) 


My Lord, Paris, January 21, 1855, 

THE haste in which I am constantly obliged to write to your Lordship, 
often renders my despatches less complete than I could wish them to be. On 
looking over my confidential despatch No. 90 of the 19th instant, reporting the 
discussion respecting the preliminaries of peace which took place on the 
18th instant in the Emperor's presence, I find that I omitted to mention an 
argument put forward by Count Walewski, which appeared to weigh more than 
any other with His Majesty as a reason for signing preliminaries on the basis of 
the Austrian ultimatum. 

It was clear, Count Walewski said, that there had been a reciprocal 
engagement contracted between Austria on the one side and the Western Powers 
on the other. It was not to be supposed that Austria had engaged to break 
with Russia if Russia refused her ultimatum, unless she had been assured on 
the other hand that the acceptance of the ultimatum by Russia would lead to the 
conclusion of peace. 

I observed in reply, that there would be more force in this argument if 
Austria had been left in ignorance of the intentions of the Western Powers 
concerning the particular conditions, but that those conditions had been fairly 
stated to her, and she could have been under no delusion (at all events as far 
as Her Majesty’s Government were concerned) as to the determination that 
existed to make peace dependent on their acceptance ; such being the case, and 
Her Majesty’s Government being desirous above all things that negotiations 
should not be renewed for the mere purpose of being broken off, it became 
essential that the consent of Russia to the principle of the particular conditions 
should be obtained before Plenipotentiaries met to convert the preliminaries into 
a definite Treaty of Peace. In fact the moral contract which existed between 
Austria and. the Western Powers, went no further than this—that if Austria 
sent an ultimatum to Russia, the Western Powers would consider the terms of 
that ultimatum as their own, and would not make peace until they were obtained; 
in other words, they were bound not to be satisfied with less, but by no 

rversion of reasoning could it be maintained that they were not entitled ta 
Insist On more, 
L have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


No, 216, 
Lord Stratford de Redelijfe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 22.) 
(No, 29.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, Junuary 9, 1856. 


THE weeting appointed for a preparatory consideration of the question, 
known to Europe as the fourth point, relating to the privileges of the Sultan’s 
non-Mussulman subjects, and connected with the still broader question of 
administrative reform, took place this morning at the Grand Vizier’s house, In 


2U 


166 


addition to his Highness and myself, the French Ambassador, the Austrian 
Internuncio, and Fuad Pasha, were present. me 

[ should have proposed a previous interchange of opinions, by means of a 
confidential meeting between the Representatives of the three Powers more 
immediately engaged in the war, as calculated to elicit and put into tram their 
jnint views, itrespective of those which may be entertained elsewhere. I had 
indeed suggested this mode of proceeding to my French colleague, as ppp 
to the question of the Principalities also, which it 1s evidently desirable, with 
reference to the eventualities of negotiation, to bring under deliberation without 
delay. But M. Thouvenel preferred the course which we are now following, 
under an impression, as he stated, that by acting separately, though confidentially, 
we might give umbrage to Baron Prokesch, at the same time that we could not 
make progress without knowing whether the question of the Principalities was 
to be treated on the principle of a barrier against Russia, or on that of a simple 
improvement of their eondition. Not thinking it worth while to lose time in 
maintaining a discussion on points which could not be set aside as wholly 
insignificant, I acquiesced in the course which was finally adopted by common 
consent. aD 

It affords me the liveliest satisfaction to state that in general the disposition 
manifested by my two colleagues, and also by the Turkish Ministers, was such 
us to warrant a sanguine hope of our ultimate success in the great twofold work 
to which our exertions are now more particularly directed, Our consultation 
was carried on for the most part in a conversational form, as best suited to a 
frank and mutual expression of our respective ideas. We all in turn expressed 
a desire to bring the various classes of the Sultan’s subjects into harmony and 
confidence with cach other us a source of prosperity to the Empire, whose 
Government would find its advantage, both internally and externally, m acting 
no longer on the principles of religious exclusiveness or predominance of race, 
but on those broader, sounder maxims, which have only to be carried out 
with perseverance in order to produce a full measure of national unity and 
strength. a er 

Some other important points appeared to offer little or no diversity of 
opinion. ‘Those which recur to my recollection may be stated here without any 
ungeasonable pressure on your Lordship’s time, er 

We all agreed that Ottoman ascendancy could not be dispensed with in 
tle Government: that there was less room for extension of privilege to the 
Christians than want of security for the enjoyment of those which had been 
eranted, and neglect on the part of provincial authorities in causing them to be 
respected ; that a good system of administration, applying equally to all classes, 
would be found more practically remedial than fresh immunities conferred upon 
any separate class; that the initiative of any improvements to be adopted in 
future belongs to the Sultan; that by “ initiative ” was meant the promulgation 
of them in the shape of a firman; and that finally, by anticipating in that 
respect the conclusive act of negotiation to the exclusion of Russia as a dehibe- 
rative party, the Porte would raise itself in the estimation of foreign nations, 
and acquire a stronger hold on the affections of its own subjects. 

To these may be added the general belief, whether shown by assertion or 
by admission, that the present course of Ottoman administration is really so 
defective in action, and so liable to abusive influences in every department, as to 
require a searching aud comprehensive reform. 

‘The points on which difficulties are principally to be foreseen, as appearing 
from the language employed in our deliberation, may be thus enumerated; On 
the part of the Turkish Ministers, we may expect procrastination, on the ground 
of respect for religious antipathies, popular prejudices, and unassociating habits, 
moral and physical; incompleteness in carrying out laws and regulations for the 
enforcement, of necessary measures; deficiency of will for bringing the long- 
alicnated classes into closer communion with each other; and a very natural 
inclination not to limit the process of reform to the Mussulman and dominant 
population; on the part of my colleagues, u certain reluctance to admut. the 
distinction which, however, exists between protection by Russia and admonition 
by Europe; and, consequently, an enti want of agreement as to the terms 
in which it will be desirable to consign the result of our conferences to the 
future Treaty of Peace. 

On this last point we only touched, agreeing to consider it as one not 


167 


pressing for immediate solution, and fit to be reserved for the decision of our 
respective Governments. 

The French Ambassador argued with energy in favour of the right to 
repair and erect places of worship in Turkey, without other check than that of 
an administrative character. He acknowledged the readiness with which his 
application for churches and church-bells had been recently granted by the 
Turkish Government. He expressed a confident hope that the Sultan's liberality 
would be carried still further; and [need not assure your Lordship that T joined 
with Baron Prokesch in supporting these views with cordiality, in the hope that, 
if so much had been conceded toa single ally, the Porte would not find it easy 
to resist. the united importunities ofall. | 

With respect to a gradual and retarded process of reform, I reminded the 
Turkish Ministers that sixty years had already elapsed since the necessity of 
reform had been openly “ete upon in Turkey, and many more since the period 
when the Ottoman Empire first gave signs of meaning to associate itself with 
the Powers of Christendom. Admitting that the whole scheme of reform could 
not be accomplished in a week, I urged the rapid movement of human society in 
the present age, the favouring circumstances of the time, and the importance of 
anticipating the conclusion of peace, as so many stringent considerations for 
hastening the work in hand. On the question of religious difficulties, I endea- 
voured to show the absolute necessity of not being stopped by them, and the 
impracticability of realizing a plan of efficient reform while the wheels of the 
State continued to be clogged, and the avenues of justice to be choked by obser- 
vanees which were wholly irreconcileable with the known wants of the Empire 
and the established principles of equity. 

It remains for me to state that the meeting closed with an understanding 
that the Turkish Ministers would present a statement of existing privileges, 
spiritual and civil, ancient and modern, together with an enumeration of such 
additions as it occurred to them to propose. In answer to an inquiry on my 
part, whether the intended statement was to be left open for new suggestions 
and amendments, the Grand Vizier replied in the affirmative, and seemed not to 
have any definite limitations in view, 

Weare to meet again ina week, and Prince Callimachi is to assist at our 
deliberations. 1 proposed an earlier day, but the whole interval was thought 
indispensable for preparing the statement and talking over its contents, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No, 125.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, January 23, 1856, 
COUNT DE PERSIGNY, on the 18th instant, read to me a despatch 
from Count Walewski, stating that as Count Nesselrode had notified to the 
Austrian Envoy at St. Petersburgh the unqualified acceptance of the propositions 
contained in the Austrian ultimatum, the signature of preliminaries of peace 
must forthwith be proceeded with; that it could not be doubted that the 
memorandum of the 14th of November rendered it morally obligatory to pursue 
the course therein laid down, but that the Imperial Government, after deliberate 
consideration, did not consider it contrary to the moral engagements contracted 
with Austria to make known to Russia, even before the commencement of 
negotiations, the nature of the particular conditions. The Imperial Government 
would have preferred not making those conditions known to the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh until the time for discussing them arrived, The fifth paragraph 
of the ultimatum could leave no doubt as to the power reserved to the belligerents 
of bringing forward further stipulations in addition to the principal conditions, 
and by apprizing Russia beforehand of what it was intended to put forward, they 
in some degree impaired their right to bring forward others at a Jater period. 
However, this did not much signify, and the Imperial Government was disposed 
to waive the point in order to defer to the views of the British Cabinet, and it 
was therefore ready to make known to the Cabinet of Vienna that it was. 
proposed to communicate tu the Russian Government the particular conditions 


as specified in my despatch to your Excellency No. 1,856 of the 24th of 


November, namely, that no military or naval establishments shall be restored or 
ereated in the Aland Islands, and the right to consider the state of the territories 
on the east of the Black Sea; and Count Walewski added that he tirmly trusted 
that Austria would adinit that this mode of proceeding involved nothing at 
varianee with the course laid down in the memorandum of November 14, 

I told M. de Persigny that Her Majesty's Government would learn with 
great satisfaction the course which the Government of the Emperor was ubout 
to pursue, and which T hoped would lead to the immediate acceptance by Russia 
of the additional terms. 

M. de Persigny called here on the 2lst instant, to inform me that the 
communication to Russia announced in Count Walewski's despatch had not

My Lord, Paris, January 23, 1856. 

COUNT WALEWSKI mentioned to me yesterday that he had been 
informed hy M. de Hiibner that there appeared to be very little difference of 
opinion between the Austrian Government and that of Her Majesty, as to the 
future organisation of the Principalities. His Excellency added that the Austrian 
Minister had invited him to let him know as soon as possible the views of the 
Imperial Government on this important question. 

Count Walewski went on to say that he had examined the memorandum 
which I had given him some time back as containing the opinions of Her 
Majesty's Government, and that uthonge it did not coincide with the opinion 
of the Imperial Government, who would prefer, for instance, the union of the 
two Principalities in one Government, that if Her Majesty's Government urged 
the adoption of their proposals he should not be disposed to oppose them. 

There was something in Count Walewski’s language which made me 
apprehend that this apparent conciliatory offer might be made use of hereafter 
to oblige Her Majesty's Government to cede on questions on which it might suit 
the French Government to make a stand, T said, therefore, to Count Walewshi, 
that | had not understood your Lordship to do more than submit the memo- 
randum to the consideration of the other Governments interested in the question ; 
that I was quite sure that your Lordship would be ready to consider and discuss 
any other proposals which the French Government might like to bring forward. 
The Conference would then decide upon the merits of the several propositions 
laid before them, 

Count Walewski said that in that case he should probably draw up a 
memorandum embodying the views of the French Government,

No, 225, 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 24.) 


(No, 126.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 22, 1856, 

M. DE HUBNER has, by Count Buol’s desire, informed Count Walewski 
that the Prussian Government have made overtures at Vienna to be admitted to 
the negotiations for peace. 

Count Walewski stated to me that the Emperor was not at all disposed to 
comply with the wishes of the Prussian Government, but that it would be 
difficult to exclude Prussia, as a great Power, from any arrangements touching 
the general equilibrium of Europe. 

I observed that Prussia had voluntarily withdrawn from the Councils of 
Europe on the Eastern question, and had been informed that she would not be 
readmitted into them but on certain conditions, which conditions she had not 
fulfilled: that the allies therefore, unless they intended to stultify themselves, 
and offer as it were a premium in future to other States who might conduct 
themselves as Prussia had done, could not deviate from the course which Prussia 
had baought upon herself; but that this need not prevent her adherin hereafter 
ta the Treaty which, it might be hoped, would be the result of the impending 
negotiations. 

This course would, I think, be cordially agreed to by the French Govern- 
ment. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 24.) 


(No. 180.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 23, 1856. 

COUNT WALEWSKI read to me yesterday a despatch which had been 
placed in his hands by M, de Hiibner, and which contained a copy of the note 
addressed by Prince Gortchakoff to Count Buol, announcing that Russia accepted 
the Austrian ultimatum as containing a“ project of preliminaries of peace.” 
Count Buol expressed the hope that the French Government would fulfil the 
engagement which they had contracted by signing preliminaries at once, to be 
followed by an armistice. 

Same conversation followed between Count Walewski and myself respecting 
the place and manner of signing preliminaries whenever the two Governments 
had decided what the preliminaries were to contain. 

Without troubling your Lordship with details, 1 may say that Count 
Walewski appeared to coincide in the opinion which I expressed, that if the 
preliminaries were to be in the form ofa Treaty, and subject to discussion, that 
discussion could hardly be separated from the discussion of the final Treaty, and 
niust be conducted at the place where it was determined that the principal 
negotiations should be carried on. He elung, however, to the opinion that the 
preliminaries might be signed at Vienna, without further discussion, in the form of 
a protocol, the substance of which might almost be communicated by telegraph. 

| asked his Excellency in what way he conceived that the protocol might 
be drawn up. He replicd that he had sent a project of a protocol, whieh he 
thought might answer the purpose, some days ago to Count rene: but that 
he had not instructed him to communicate it to your Lordship, as he did not 
wish to appear importunate. 

At my request, however, his Excellency furnished me with a eopy of it, 
which I do myself the honour to inclose. 

On reading it, it appeared to me to offer the least objectionable mode of 
proceeding if it is eventually determined that Vienna is to witness the acceptance 
by the belligerent Powers of the preliminaries of peace. I asked Count 
Walewski whether the Austrian Government would be satistied with an act of the 
kind proposed, His Excellency seemed to hope that she would ; and in reply to a 
further question which | put to him, he said that he was ready to insist on the 
signature of the preliminaries elsewhere, if Count Buol objected to this propo- 
sition. 

Your Lordship will understand that I have not compromised myself in any 
way towards Count Walewski in regard to this new suggestion, 

L should remark, further, that I drew his Excellency’s attention to the term 
‘“nraject of preliminaries '" employed by Prince Gortchakoff as indicating an 
intention on the part of the Russian Government to raise some sort of 
discussion. 

Count Walewski’s idea is, that when the preliminaries have been signed, 
un armistice, to terminate on a given day, not later, however, than the Ist of 
May, should be signed. his, his perleay thinks, will prevent the Russian 
Government from unnecessarily lengthening the discussions. In the meantime, 
the preparations for continuing the war should be vigorously prosecuted, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

tain the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, it would be impossible ta make Pete 
leaving Russia in occupation of any part of the Turkish territory; and this 
proposition is so self-evident that the omission of any allusion in the Austrian 
conditions to the withdrawal ofthe Russian armies from any ‘Turkish districts of 
which they might have temporary possession during the progress of hostilities, 
can in no degree militate against the right of the allied Powers to insist upon tt 
as an indispensable condition to the conclusion of peace. Ihave further to 
observe that if the allies had not occupied any portion whatever of Russian terri- 
tory, the engagement which they have contracted to maintain the integrity of the 
Turkish Empire would have made it incumbent upon them peremptorily to 
require that as asine qud non condition of peace the Russian forces should evacuate 
any andevery portion of the Turkish territory which they might have happened 
‘1 the course of hostilities to have occupied: and it cannot be contended that 
because the course of events has been more favourable to the allies than 1t would 
have been in such a supposed case, they should on that very account be bound 
to uccept less favourable terms from Russia in regard to the portions of Turkish 
territory momentarily occupied by a Russian force. 

But even if the allies were not to take their stand on this ground, which is, 
however, indisputable, and if they were willing to treat the question of Kars on 
the principle of equivalents, it is to be remembered that if Kars has been oceu- 
pied by the Russians, Mingrelia is occupied by the Turks ; and that the position 
now held on Russian territory by the army of Omer Pasha would enable the 
allies in the spring to take up a position which would give them the command 
not of Mingrelin only, but also of lineritia, Guriel, and Georgia, and that conse- 
quently the allies by retiring from Mingrelia would give to Russia o full equiva- 
lent for their evacuation of the territory of Kars, 

Your Excellency will read and give a copy of this despatch to Count 
Walewski.

HER Majesty's Government approve the language held by your Excellency 


to Count Walewski, as reported in your despatch Iho. 124 of the 23rd instant, 
relative to the future organization of the Principalities. Her Majesty’s Govern- 


175 


ment have no wish and no interest in this matter beyond sccuring to the 
Principalities the best form of government attainable under present circum- 
stances. 

Her Majesty's Government were disposed to think, as Count Walewski 
does, that the union of the two Provinces would be the best arrangement, but 
they have come to the conclusion that this could not be effected without great 
delay, which on every account it is desirable at this moment to avoid, and that 
local feuds and rivalries would probably prevent the solid amalgamation of 
the two countries, and might hereafter furnish the pretext for foreign inter- 
ference.

I HAVE learned with great satisfaction by your Excellency’s despatch 
No. 29 of the 9th of January, the good disposition evinced by the Turkish 
Ministers in the first meeting respecting the fourth point, which was held at 
Constantinople on the 9th instant; and 1 have to instruct you, in the event of 
the Turkish Ministers continuing to display the same laudable spirit, to inform 
them of the pleasure with which Her Majesty's Government have learned their 
mode of proceeding upon the great questions of toleration and reform, respecting 
which, for the welfare aud prosperity of the Ottoman Empire, Her Majesty's 
Covernment feel an anxious solicitude, and the settlement of which the Powers 
of Europe are entitled to expect, now that Turkey 1s to become an integral part, 
of the European system. 

Your Excellency cannot too strongly impress upon the Turkish Ministers 
the importance of avoiding delay in coming to an arrangement with respect to 
the first and fourth points, in anger that Russia may have no pretext for taking 
part in the discussions on those matters at Constantinople when the negotiations 
for peace commence.

My Lord, Paris, January 25, 1856. 
M. DE BOURQUENEY’S telegraphic despatch, announcing the arrival 
at Vienna of the messenger from St. Petersburgh, is somewhat fuller than that 
which passed through Paris from Sir Hamilton Seymour. Prince Gortchakoff 
communicated two despatches to Count Buol, the one signifying the pure and 
simple acceptance by Russia of the Austrian ultimatum, the other proposing 
the course which should be followed in order to open negotiations, It consists 
in a signature of a Protocal at Vienna, stating the adherence of the belligerent 
Powers to the terms of the ultimatum, engaging each interested Power +o name 
two Plenipotentiaries to meet within three weeks at Paris, to sign preliminaries 
of peace. The preliminaries to be followed by an armistice and the operling of 
peneral negotiations.

My Lord, Foreign Office, January 26, 1856. 

IN the despatch of Count Walewski to M. de Persigny, of which a copy 16 
inclosed in my despatch No. 144 of this day, his Excellency states that it has 
been proposed that a Protocol should be signed at Vienna, having for its object 
to fix the place and the time for the meeting of Plenipotentiaries ; these Plenipo- 
tentiaries to mect in three weeks from the date of the signature of the Protocol, 
when they will proceed to the signature of preliminaries, to the arrangement of 
an armistice, and to the opening of the general negotiation. 

Count Walewski adds that the Government of the Emperor is prepared to 
accede to this proposal; but his Excellency, in the first instance, is desirous of 
ascertaining the opinion of Her Majesty’s Government upon the subject. 

Your Excellency will accordingly inform Count Walewski that Her 
Majesty's Government see no objection to this mode of procecting ; but they 
consider it indispensable that the terms of the l’rotocol should be agreed upon 
by the two Governments before any authority for its signature is sent to Vienna. 

Tam, &c.

No. 242. 


Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 28.) 
(No. 52. Private and Confidential.) 

My Lord, Vienna, January 22, 1856. 
__ THE manner in which the news of the Russian acceptance of the propp- 

sitions of the Austrian Cabinet lins been received by various parties at Vienna, 
would (if accurately recorded) form a curious page of contemporary history. 

By the Austrian Cabinet it bas been hailed as an ample compensation for 
short but very intense anxiety; those persons who had been the least backward 
in condemning Count Buol’s rash policy (for so it was deemed) being as full of 
exultation as the rest at a result which, in the universal opinion, liberates 
Austria from all further demands upon her exertions. 

The feeling is not less universal among the public, and was unequivocally 
expressed upon the Emperor's first appearance at the theatre after the news had 
arrived of the timely acceptance by aba, His Imperial Majesty was received 
* About Colonel Turr. 


184 


upon that occasion with an enthusiasm which could hardly have been exceeded 
had he been returning from a glorious campaign. 

Of the Russian satellites, for such in fact are the Representatives of some 
of the German Courts, it is not well to speak; their position having become 
embarrassing, or, to use the more appropriate epithet, ridiculous, Heathens in 
their political worship, they have been filled with dismay at the abasement of 
their idol, and are in danger of falling into political unbelief. Their language 
had been that the last counter-propositions of Russia were the extreme effort of 

magnanimity exerted in the cause of peace; that more could not be asked, still 
less expected: that to require more argued an ignorance of public feeling in 
Russia, which was notoriously such that even supposing the Emperor Alexander 
was so bent upon peace as to be ready to make further sacrifices for its attain- 
ment, he would not be able to give effect to his wishes in opposition to the 
excited feelings of his country. 

This very foolish sort of language was held by some of my German 
colleagues at the very moment that Russia’s answer (telegraphed, to erinard 
against accidents, both by Count Nesselrode and Count V, Esterhazy) had 
actually reached the Foreign Office. 

On the preceding day, | had undertaken the unprofitable task of 
endeavouring to counteract the opinions which one of the diplomatists above 
alluded to was expressing, and | did so by remarking—first, that as a matter of 
fact L believed the public feeling in Russia to be the very reverse of what had 
heen described; that I had reason to believe that peace, at almost any price, 
was the paramount wish of the country; and secondly, that I had seen enough 
of Russia to have ascertained that what was called public opinion was a very 
convenient instrument, a thing to be put forward as a powerful obstacle when 
the Sovereign objected to any particular course, but which was utterly 
disregurded if it stood in the way of the Sovereign's good pleasure. 

It was manifest that my opinions were held to be both prejudiced and 
absurd, and so they may have continued to be thought till the following day, 
the lth instant, 

As for the Prussian Mission, their objections to the pertinacious demand of 
an unconditional acceptance was as strong as could be that of an orthodox 
Hussian. 

This continued up to the arrival of Count Nesselrode’s telegraphic despatch, 
when a great change became observable. From that moment, as appeared from 
the language of these gentlemen, it was the friendly advice of the King of 
Prussia which alone determined the Emperor Alexander upon an unconditional 
surrender, 

| should, however, be wanting in candour were I to undervalue the efforts 
of His Prussian Majesty; as far as it is in my power to ascertain the truth, 
these efforts were more strenuous than he had led his allies to expect, and were 
carried to the extent of his powers, and, as I believe, beyond the extent of Ins 
instructions, by the Prussian Envoy at St. Petersburgh, 

It remains for me to speak of the Rusaian Mission at Vienna, Their 
position is become very embarrassing, and as for Prince Gortchakoff, it is not 
easy to understand how he ean well remain at his present post after that very 
indisereet and excited language which he held during the late crisis. 

Had he contined his remarks to the policy of the Austrian Government, 
all might be aseribed to diplomatic zeal and ardour; but as he talked freely of 
the disgrace which Russia would incur were she to adopt the Austrian propo- 
sitions, it would be anomalous that he should remain the exponent of a policy 
which he has condemned by anticipation, 

It is true that Prince Gortchukoff acquainted Count Buol some days ago 
that he was about to be named Minister of Foreign Affairs, but there are some 
persons who consider the announcement a little premature, who imagine that 
the Prince may have mistaken # contingent summons to St. Petersburgh for a 
romise of a portfolio, and the impending portfolio for the particular one which 
is so long been held by Count Nesselrode. 

Were the Russian Emperor intent upon continuing the war, he might be 
supposed likely to call to his counsels aman recommended by his name, his 
violence, and his orthodoxy; all these cease, however, to be recommendations, 
if, worn out by an unequal struggle, Russia is really intent upon bringing it to 
i peaceful conclusion, unless, indeed, it be judged politic that a strictly Russian 
name should be affixed to a Treaty not very honourable to Russia, 


185 


Some there are, who, in their assumed acuteness, are apt to overlook the 
truth when lying palpably before them, and these are disposed to imagine that 
the Russian Mission were all along prepared for the final decision of their Govern- 
ment, Such, I am convinced, is not the case, No Russian, certainly no 
Russian employé, places himself by anticipation in contradiction to the fiat of 
his Government. While it may then be said that the whole of the Russian 
Mission had formed a false estimate of the views of their master, none was more 
taken by surprise than General Stackelberg, who, having left St. Petersburgh 
some days before an unconditional acceptance had been resolved upon, eould 
hardly be brought to credit the intelligence which, upon his arrival here, he: 
found to have just reached Prince Gortchakoff by telegraph. 

‘As my despatch is a confidential one, | may take the opportunity of 
recording the conversation which passed between Prince Gortchakolf and Count 
Buol on the 15th instant, and which was altogether the more striking from 
the Prince having been previously at the pains of declaring very openly that he 
felt obliged to break off all communication with a Minister who had acted such 
a part as Count Buol. In pursuance of this resulution, he called upon him 
twice on the morning of the 15th instant, and not finding him at home, returned 
at 9 o'clock at night, when again he met with the same answer. He took his 
place, accordingly, in the ante-room, waited patiently till Count Buol returned, 
and then followed him into his study, where, alter stating that he was likely to 
be Count Nesseirode’s successor, he spoke with his habitual indiseretion of the 
“ politique de vengeance ” which it was not improbable Russia might be expected 
to pursue, 

To this Count Buol replied coldly and sarcastically, that for his part he 
was not a believer in that sort of policy, which might indeed be acted upon at 
certain moments, but could never be systematically carried out. “No,” Count 
Buol said, ‘ Russia will not be long vindictive. If you are fortunate enough to 
obtain a peace, you will have wounds to heal, roads to repair, banks and manu- 
factories to establish, and in these domestic occupations your energies may be 
long very usefully employed.” 

These details, trivial as some of them may appear, will enable your 
Lordship to judge correctly of the relations which exist between the Russian 
Misgion and the Austrian Government. Knowing that Austria is accustomed 
to lean upon some ally, and seeing that the Russian alliance will not be available 
for some time, your Lordship will at once foresee to what quarter she is likely 
to look for support. 

I will take this opportunity for apprizing your Lordship of the determining 
cuuse (according to Count Buol’s opinion) of the acceptance by Russia of the 
terms which have been lately offered her. 

“The acceptance,” said Count Buol, “as I learn in the strictest confidence, 
is owing, not to Count Esterhazy’s efforts, not to the representations of the 
King of Prussia, but simply to the belief which Russia entertains of Bngland 
being resolved upon waihe the war with vigour, and the expectation that 
aeceptance may be followed by dissensions among the allied Powers.” 

It is safer to Speak of past than of coming events ; to record than to predict. 
I venture, however, to remark to your Lordship that Austria, after a strong and 
very unusual effort, will in all probability be seen to exert all her diplomacy 
towards the peaceful enjoyment. of the advantages which she has secured for 
herself; that she will endeavour to efface the recollection of the forward part 
which she played during twenty-one days, and that whilst her demeanour 
towards France will be that of confiding friendship, her bearing towards Russia 
and Prussia will be that of apologetic conciliation.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Hart of Clarendon.—( Received January 28.) 


(No. 53.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 22, 1856. 

IN pursuance of the orders contained in your Lordship's telegraphic 
despatch of the 18th instant, I waited upon Count Buol on the 20th, for the 
purpose of inducing him to acquaint Prince Gortchakott with the precise 
demands which the two belligerent Powers would have to make upon Russia 
under the fifth Article of the ulfimatum. | 

A conversation which I had previously held upon the subject with his 
Excellency, had fully prepared me for the reception which the proposal I had to 
make would meet with, | 

As I had expected, I found Count Buol’s objections to the plan proposed 
hy your Lordship insuperable, | 

"© Austria,” he said, “had undertaken to provide preliminaries of peace, 

but was not disposed to charge herself with the execution of commissions, or 
with the drawing up of Articles of Peace. She had fulhlled her part of an 
engagement with scrupulous exactness, She had aright to demand that the 
obligations implicitly or explicitly taken by others should be observed with the 
same good faith, He hada nght to expect that preliminaries should be signed, 
and an armistice agreed upon, without loss of time, and without observations. 
When the moment for the negotiation of this Treaty artived, there would be the 
opportunity for bringing forward the demands of England and France, and these 
demands would be honeatly and cordially supported by Austria, Any previous 
attempt at making them known to Russia, would only endanger the approaching 
negotiation, and would give Russia the opportunity of recalling her late 
acceptance of the Austrian proposals.” | 

Count Buol was convinced that the danger he alluded to was not an 
imaginary one. ‘The Emperor Alexander had made an immense effort in meeting 
the Austrian proposals as he had done; if so bitter a cup as that now proposed 
for him were at once to be held to his lips, he might retuse to drain it off; if 
His Imperial Majesty were enabled to state to his people that the sacrifices which 
he had resigned himself to make for their sakes had not produced the immediate 
relief which had been held out, any fresh appeal which he might make to their 
sympathy and support would come with redoubled fore. le 

Although Count Buol conceived himself able to support his views by the 
strongest arguments, he did not wish to argue upon the subject; he wished only 
to point to an agreement or understanding upon which he had acted with perfect 
good faith, and which he expected should be observed by others in the same 
spirit. 
3 [t had been said that it was the wish of the English Government that 
Russia should be apprized distinctly of the conditions of peace, but what was 
now seen? The demand for the non-fortification of the Aland Islands was 
indeed clear and distinct, but nothing could be more vague than the intention of 
taking into consideration the state of a vast extent of territory. Again Count 
Buol would remark that Austria had not been dealt with as she had every night 
to expect. Her relations towards Russia became most painful if she were unable 
to ensure the execution of engagements which she had taken for others. Never 
engaging her own word lightly, Austria had a right to expect that her allies 
should be equally scrupulous in keeping faith with her. 

| pointed to the various occasions upon which Her Majesty's Government 
had insisted upon the precise nature of our demands being, as good faith 
required, made known to Russia, but Count Buol would not admit that the 


expression of a strong wish could be construed to mean insistance upon a sine 


gud non condition. 

My object, as 1 then told Count Buol, was not to employ strong words, but 
to seek by all possible means to bring the views of our two Governments into 
aecordance; that above all | was cager not to compromise the fair chances of 
peace by allowing differences of views to appear which might be made use of by 
the Russians for the purpose of creating dissensions in the camp. 


ls7 


I would here remark to your Lordship, that as my great object is always to 
take care that our line should be conformable, as far as possible, to that of our 
French ally, I called upon Baron Bourqueney before visiting the Foreign Office, 
and inquired of him whether he were ready to join with me in requesting Count 
Buol to put himself in communication with Prince Gortchakoff respecting the 
demands to be made under the fifth Article, 

| found Baron Bourqueney, as he ever is, most ready to act hand in hand 
with me, and he undertook, without hesitation, to join his representations to 
mine. 

His efforts proved, however, as ineffectual as mine had been; they were 
met. by objections of the same nature as had been offered to my proposal, and 
he left Count Buol, after a conversation which lasted two hours, as resolute as 
ever upon not departing from the line traced out in the memorandum.

Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 28.) 


(No. 63.) 
My Lord, Vienna, January 23, 1856 

THE situation of affairs here may be deseribed in a few words. 

The Austrian Government claim pertinaciously the exact payment of what 
they consider their bond, 

They maintain that they stood pledged to England and France to break off 
their relations with Russia if she declined the propositions which Count Esterhazy 
conveyed to St. Petersburgh, the belligerent Powers being on their side pledged 
to Austria to sign preliminaries without delay or conditions, in the event of the 
propositions being acceded to by Russia. Upon this ground the Austrian 
Cabinet have taken up their position, and from that position no argument or 
entreaty will induce them to move. Count Buol’s opinions upon the point agree 
entirely with those of his Imperial master, and no change in them is, | am 
convinced, to be looked for. 

It is a question, not so much of policy, as of dignity and of respect for a 
written engagement, 

{fT had entertained any previous doubts upon the subject, they would have 
been removed by a conversation which I held last night with Count Buol, of 
which a précis has been sent to your Lordship in a telezraphic despatch. 

Count Buol said that no consideration could induce hin’ te swerve from 
what he had already stated to me, 

‘That we were in that crisis at which either a safe or a very dangerous 
course was about to be entered wpon; that the negotiation would begin and 
proceed smoothly, or would Jead to very serious complications. 

If, he said. the Western Powers sign the preliminaries without condition or 
demur, Austria will have redeemed her pledge to Russia, and she is then as 
willing us she is able to act vigorously aud cordially with her allies. In the 
contrary supposition she is held up to Europe as faithless to her word, and her 
position becomes one “ not only of embarrassment but of ridicule!" "To that 
she cannot submits at any price or risk her dignity must be upheld.” 

“Sign the preliminaries,” he said, “and all goes on as you desire; your 
demands are brought forward in the course of the negotiations; they meet with 
our cordial support, and we are sure at least of obtaining, not an engagement is 
to the non-fortification of the Aland Islands, but a cession of the islands 
themselves. We will carry this, if necessary, at the price of sacrificing our own 
interests.” ) 

These latter words were pronounced with great earnestness, and with a 
siznificance of manner which leads me to feel confident that Count Buol has 
obtained some knowledge of the late French plan, and that he intended to 
convey to me that he should consider the cession of a part of the newly acquired 
territory in Bessarabia as a price which ought to be paid for promoting the 
objects of the allies in the Baltic, . 

In urging Her Majesty's Government, as I have felt it my duty to do, to take 
into full consideration the feelings of the Austrian Cabinet, I will only entreat of 
your Lordship to believe that I am not influenced by any Austrian leaning 


189 


of pregaions: my feelings, as well as my prejudices, are indeed exclusively 
anglish, 

; I feel only that Austria has some grounds for understanding that we are 
pledged to act as she calls upon us to do, and that her assistance is requisite for 
ultimately carrying out the objects upon which Her Majesty's Government are 
so deeply intent. 

It is held by some persons that the whole affair might be settled without 
Austrian concurrence, and this is the more probable as Russia might not be 
found reluctant to requite her Imperial ally for what she considers an act of 
ingratitude, or perhaps of defection. | 

It may, however, I think be safely assumed that any settlement of the 
so-called Eastern question, to which Austria is not a willing party, would be a 
very insecure arrangement ; I believe, in a word, either that Austria will be one 
of those Powers which will be pledged to resist the encroachments of Russia, or 
that particular Power which, when opportunity offers, will be ready to join with 
Russia in despoiling a weak neighbour. I will not conclude my despatch without 
remarking to your Lordship that [ have long known Count Buol, and know him 
tohe a man who not only means what he says, but who weighs his words with 
great exactness. Like most of the public men of this country he is a formalist, 
and desirous of keeping close, or bemg supposed to keep close, to the text of an 
engagement. His language, however, convinces me that he might have 
expressed himself even more strongly than he did, and that not only he has 
taken care to let it be known to Russia that we have demands to make upon the 
Aland Islands, but that he has ascertained that the demands will not be 
obstinately resisted : were this not the case he would not have ventured to state 
with confidence that there would be less difficulty in obtaining a cession of these 
islands than an engagement for their non-fortification; what he contemplates 
can be nothing else than the exchange of a portion of the ceded territory of 
Bessarabia against the islands. 

I beg to apologize to vour Lordship for the great freedom which | use in 
expressing my opinions; the heavy responsibility, however, which T incur by so 
doing will, at least, satisfy you how convinced | must he of their correctness, 

l have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 2632, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 28.) 


(No. 46. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 26, 1856. 


WITH reference to my telegraphic despatch of the 22nd instant, on the 
subject of the communication which had been made to the Prussian Government 
by Count Georges Esterhazy, expressing the sense entertained by the Austrian 
Sovernment of the services rendered by Baron Werther at St, Petersburgh in 
obtaining the final acceptance of the ultimatum by Russia, I have endeavoured 
to learn whether any further observation has been made to the Austrian Minister 
respecting this affair, but nothing has transpired. Baron Manteuffel has given 
no answer, and Count Esterhazy believes that nothing more will be done in the 
matter until the wishes of Her Majesty’s Government and that of France are 
known. 

I have already informed your Lordship that the Prussian Government 

would much prefer to come into the Conferences at the invitation of England 
and France than of Austria; but I presume, from what Count Esterhazy has 
said to me, that if it is thought advisable that Prussia should assist at the 
Conferences, the wish will be intimated in a collective invitation from the three 
Powers. 
That the King of Prussia should be anxiously waiting for an invitation to 
the Conferences, there can be no doubt, and that such a step would be gratifying 
to His Majesty, the Court, and people, is beyond a doubt; but the obtaining 
the adhesion of Prussia to a Treaty for the pacification of Europe, and perhaps 
her guarantee to the future delimitation of the Russian Empire, would be dearly 
bought by mass of difficulties that would be raised by her in. discussing 
different matters connected with the Eastern question. 

In the first place, who are the Representatives that Prussia would probably 
select to attend the Conferences? Public opinion says that Count Alvensleben 
and M, de Bismarck would probably be chosen. ‘The former is a man of sense, 
talent, and experience, but who, instead of throwing light into dark and intricate 
matters, would probably only embroil them more, His predilections are 
Austrian. M. de Bismarck is thoroughly Russian; and, therefore, between 
these two, if the King’s choice should fall on them, or either of them, T see no 
gain for the Western Powers, but public advocates of our enemy’s cause. 

No other person has been mentioned as likely to be selected for the Con- 
ferences, and in the diplomatic service of Prussia I know of none who would 
have a chance of selection, in whose impartiality we could place the least 
reliance. Such, in fact, is the present dilemma of this Government, that though 
Baron Manteuffel would wish to see Prussia occupying her proper position in 
Europe, he would be almost as well satisfied to avoid the responsibility of the 
Conferences, for he feels that Prussia will not be admitted without engagements, 
and that the King is not likely to submit to anything that will bind bim down 
to act with the Western Powers if the Conferences should have no result. 

But to form any calculation of what the King may ultimately do is vain; 
one thing is certain, that he would prove a clog in every negotiation that may be 


193 


undertaken, and, though anxious for peace, would not be likely to support us 
against Russia to the extent to which it may be found necessary to go, In order 
to arrive at a lasting peace. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

(No. 109. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 28, 1856. 

A QUESTION will arise in the course of the negotiation with Russia as 
to the renewal of the ancient Treaties between Turkey and Russia. 

Those Treaties, however, contain a variety of stipulations which it may have 
been necessary to insert at the time of their conclusion, in consequence of the 
alteration of territorial limits and in the general character of relations between 
the two countries agreed to in the successive negotiations, but which it would 
seem superfluous now specifically to reproduce, and it may be doubted whether 
at the present time it would not be better, as regards the political relations 
between the two countries, that they should be regulated by an entirely new 
arrangement, which might be effected by inserting in the new Treaty, without 
any reference to the former Treaties, what are thenceforth to be the territorial 
limits between the two countries, 

The commercial relations of the two countries may, however, require more 
detailed and specific stipulations. : 

I wish, therefore, that your Excellency should consider this matter, and 
report to me with as little delay as possible your opinion as to the manner in 
which the ancient Treaties with Turkey and Russia should be dealt with in the 
approaching conferences,

Inclosure in No, 262, 


Memorandum. 


LEMPIRE et la souveraineté de la dynastie Ottomane duns leur juste 
extension se rattachent de nos jours au grand systéme Européen, et les 
Puissances amies et alliées de la Porte ont constamment 4 coeur d'éloigner tout 
danger qui pourrait les atteindre. Le désir de ces mémes Cours de fournir 4 Sa 
Majesté le Sultan les occasions, pour ne pas dire les moyens, dasseoir son 
indépendance sur des bases solides et permanentes n’admet pas de question. 

___ Le progrés de la guerre fait prévoir que selon toute probabilité les opéra- 
tions combinées auront, tht ou tard, pour résultat une pacification conforme aux 
veeux de I'Europe et aux besoins de la Turquie. Mais ce qui peut aitler 
d'avance lachévement d'une si belle ceuvre n’en est pas moins digne d’attention, 
Il est urgent, au contraire, de fixer dés a present les principes eb de concerter, 
wutant que possible, les mesures nécessaires pour en obtenir tout Veffet au 
hénétice de VEmpire, objet de tant de soins et de sacrifices. Garantir le 
territoire Ottoman contre les dangers d'un envahissement, et abandonner en 
méme tems aux vices intérieurs qui le font dépérir & vue d'oeil, que serait], 31
