MY late communications to your Lordship can have left no doubt in the 
minds of Her Majesty’s Government as to the state of feeling of the French 
nation—at least as fur as I can ascertain it—in regard to the alliance with 
England, I can only repeat that it is far more Russian than English; and if | 
were to attempt to define it more closely, I should say that it was essentially 
Austrian. 

It is not my intention in this despatch to trace the causes which have led ta 
this state of things; but there is one point to which I desire to eall your Lord- 
ship's attention, because I believe that in no other country in the world could 
such an anomaly exist. | allude to this, that while the Emperor has—it is 
impossible to doubt it—taken the English alliance as the basis of his policy, and 
maintained and defended it against all attacks, the language of the | miperial 
Government, and of the members of His Majesty’s Court, has been such ais must 
have made those who are unacquainted with His Majesty's real sentiments 
helieve them to be the reverse of friendly towards Great Britain. 

It has been for some time upon my mind to speak to His Majesty upon this 
matter whenever an opportunity offered itself for so doing. A favourable ocea- 
sion presented itself on Sunday last. His Majesty had expressed to me the 
pleasure and satisfaction which he had experienced on learning from M, de 
Persigny that Her Majesty's Government had accepted his last propositions ; 
and | replied that Her Majesty’s Government had accepted them out of deference 
to His Majesty alone. It was, in fact, a sacrifice which they had made to the 
maintenance of the alliance: But sacrifices suchas these, I continued, would 
not avail to maintain the alliance unless they were duly appreciated ; and I could 
not but fear that, if the sentiments which now pervaded the French nation were 
allowed their sway unchecked, not all the good intentions of His Imperial Majesty, 
responded to as they cordially were by the British nation, would prevent the 
alliance from crumbling under our feet. 

His Majesty said that he thought 1 greatly exaggerated the state of public 
feeling; that no doubt in Paris there was a great desire for peace ; and that some 
irritation had been expressed against: the warlike propensities which were alleged 
to prevuil in England; but that | made the mistake of supposing that the salons 
of Paris represented the French nation. Such was not the case, France was 
quite prepared to continue the war, if necessary. As a proof that such was the 
case, His Maiesty said that he had the most satisfactory accounts of the 
sentiments with which the new conscripts joined their colours. 

I asked His Majesty's permission to reply with perfect freedom ; and having 
been graciously invited to do so, I said that | would not venture to dispute the 
more authentic information which must reach His Majesty from the interior, 
though I confessed that the reports which I had heard did not tally with those 
just stated by His Majesty; but what I wished to convey to His Majesty was 
this—that, with the exception of himself, | could not name a Frenchman who 
was a cordial supporter of the [English alliance, I did not exempt from this 
sweeping declaration even His Majesty's own Ministers ; and I aske admitting 
that this unfriendly feeling towards England was at present conlined to Paris— 
how long it would be before it s yread through the provinces, if thase who were 
in duty bound to support His Majesty's policy, made no secret of their repug- 
nance to it. 

His Majesty asked me whether my statement was capable of proof. 

o 


208 


I replied that it might be difficult to bring proofs of the truth of what I 
asserted; but that it was matter of such notoriety that I was perfectly ready to 
assume the responsibility of my words. But your Majesty admits, I said, that 
the feeling of irritation against England, to which I have alluded, exists to 4 
strong degree in Paris. It 18 said that England is determined on prosecuting 
the war for her own purposes. Does not your Majesty’s Government know that 
this accusation is unfounded? Are they not convinced that we are as ready fis 
they are to make an honourable peace? But have they collectively or indivi- 


dually, though sure of this, and being the representatives of your Majesty, done 


one single thing or made the slightest effort to counteract the dissemination ofa 
contrary opinion, which, ifallowed to gain ground, must sow the seeds of distrust 
towards Great Britain throughout the length and breadth of the Empire, Why 
did they not come forward and answer for the honour of those whom they called 
their allies ? ; ; 

The Emperor, without replying to these observations, said that unfortunately 
the opinion that Her Majesty's Government were determined on continuing the 
war prevailed throughout the Continent. ; 

« Look,” exclaimed His Majesty, taking up a paper from his table, “here 1s 
the last telegraphic despatch received from M. de Bourqueney, and here he tells 
us that the conviction of the Emperor of Austria is that the British Government 
‘< determined on continuing the war, and that Count Buol is also beginning to 
feel uneasy.” 

“Sire,” I replied, * your Majesty could not have furnished me with better 
means for illustrating that which, in my relative situation to your Majesty, it was 
difficult and delicate to convey to you. In my hamble opinion, Count Walewski 
should pot have had that despatch five minutes in his possession before another 
was employing the telegraphic wires between Paris and Vienna, to desire M. de 
Bourqueney to see Count Buol without loss of time, and to tell him that: the 
Imperial Government answered for the honourable intentions ol the British 
Cabinet as they did for their own; and your Majesty has here a eample of what 
daily takes place in Paris. Your Ministers hear convictions such as those 
partaken by the Emperor of Austria expressed without attempting to contradict 
them. ( could have added my persuasion that they as often originate them.) 
What wonder then, that there should be so much irritation when no attempt Is 
made by those who know the truth to divert the current of public opinion ie 

His Majesty again seemed desirous of avoiding this particular line of argu- 
ment, but he entered at some length into the general question which has been 
under discussion, p 

His observations, while implying the necessity of the present mode ot 
treating the particular conditions, yet admitted that Her Majesty's Government 
were right in the main, He said among other things that there were untor- 
tunately no statesmen in France, meaning by that that there were no men who 
could take a broad political view, and consequently follow a determined policy, 
which he attributed to the unsettled state in which France lad been for so many 
years. He expressed, however, great confidence in his own influence over the 
French nation, and concluded much as he had begun by assuring me that I had 
taken too exaggerated a view of the consequences to be apprehended from the 
difficulties of the present moment. 

Whether this is the case or not, time can alone determine, but 1 do not 
regret having spoken to the Emperor, for 1 repeat that the greatest enemies of 
England are His Majesty's own Ministers. 

If T had aaaies for my own conviction additional proof of that which I so 
confidently assert, the Emperor would have furnished it himself, for in his 
endeavoura to convince me that my apprehensions were exaggerated he said that 
he himself had been the object of attack from his Ministers, and that one af 
them had gone so far as to ask him, how he dared, with his name and with his 
knowledge of the feelings of the French nation, make himself subservient to the 
interests of England. 

I cannot refrain from giving the Emperor’s reply as His Majesty stated it 
tome. “My answer was very simple,” said His Majesty; ~ I told my interro- 
gator that there was no question of subserviency, but that England was right, 
and France was wrong, and that I could not therefore act otherwise than | 
had done,”  ‘T have, &e. A

1 HAVE to inform you that Her Majesty’s Government, while giving you 
full credit for your motives, and making due allowance for local influences and 
exaggerated apprehensions which appear to exist at Vienna, yet cannot concur 
in the reasons stated in your despatch No. 44 of the 16th instant, which 
induced you to suspend the communication to Count Buol of my despatch 
No. 16 of the 8th instant. You would have been justified in doing so, and 
would have taken upon yourself proper responsibility, if that despateh had 
contained any matter calculated to cause surprise to the Austrian Government, 
or if between the time when it was written and the date at which it was received, 
any circumstances had occurred which would have made its communication 
inexpedient ; but the despatch contained nothing but the report of a conversation 
between Count Colloredo and myself upon the subject of an inquiry which he 
had been directed to make, and which you must have been aware had been duly 
reported by Count Colloredo to his Government. Count Buol, however, 
hearing nothing upon the subject from you, and knowing, probably, that you 
were withholding a despatch upon it, might not unnaturally have inferred that you 
concurred in opinion with him, rather than intheviewsof Her M ajesty'’s Government. 

You say it is not to be doubted that a portion of the Cabinet, possibly the 
Emperor himself, would be glad of a motive or an excuse for undoing what has 
lately been done, and such excuse or motive would be afforded by the decla- 
ration that Her Majesty’s Government decline all recognition of the memorandum 
of the 4th of November. 

Her Majesty’s Government, however, have not declined all recognition of 
the memorandum, as you will find on reference to my despatch No. 16 of the 
8th instant, and if your convictions are well founded, and the Austrian Govern- 
ment is even now so unsteady in its policy and so fearful of the consequences 
of its own acts as to meditate a reconciliation with Russia, simply because Her 
Majesty's Government continues to insist upon certain conditions of peace, and 
thinks it would be an act of good faith to make those conditions known to 
Russia, it is clear that no reliance ean be placed on Austrian support during

WITH reference to your despatch No. 48 of the 16th instant, 1 have to 
state that, although Count Buol may have expressed regret at receiving frum 
vou the copy of my despatch No. 16 of the 8th instant, he can have felt no 
surprise at its contents, as that despatch did nothing more than record the 
answer I had given to Count Colloredo, who been instructed to inquire whether 
Her Majesty's Government adopted the memorandum of November 14th, which 
had been agreed to by Count Buol and M. de Bourqueney. Count Colloredo 
reported our conversation to Count Buol, who remar ed upon it in a despatch 
dated the 9th instant, of which Count Colloreda has given me a copy + and 
Count Buol was therefore perfectly well informed of the contents of my 
despatch, and had even expressed his opinion upon them several days before 
you gave him a copy of it, 

Count Buol says that he considered that Austria was pledged to Her 
Majesty’s Government, and that he held the pledge of Her Majesty’s Govyern- 
ment, in return; and his Excelleney inquires whether or not Her Majesty's 
Government had insisted upon certain alterations being made in the ultimatum, 
and whether, by their acceptance, the ultimatum had not become bond fide an 
English as well as an Austrian document! 

Upon this 1 have to observe, that Count Buol appears to confound two. 
things which are totally distinct, viz., the memorandum and the ultimatum ; 
and he must be aware that they are distinct, because it was not until after the 
ultimatum had been sent to St. Petersburgh that he instructed Count Colloredo 
to inquire whether Her Majesty's Government agreed to the memorandum. 
But, with respect to the ultimatum, Count Buol is quite right in saying that the 
two Governments are pledged to each other; and, consequently, Her Majesty's 
Government have not disputed, and will not recede from, any of the conditions 
contained in that ultimatum, Moreover, they insisted upon certain alterations 
being made in it, in order that it might become an English as well asan Austrian 
document, and that they might take their share of responsibility of its bein 
sent to St. Petersburgh, instead of that responsibility, as was originally proposed, 
being borne exclusively by Austria. | 

Her Majesty's Government, however, although pledged to Austria not to 
accept less from Russia than the terms of the ultimatum, assuredly never 
pledged themselves not to demand more; but, on the contrary, they at once 
declared upon what further conditions they should insist. The Aland Islands ; 
the Consuls in Russian ports of the Black Sea; and the right to consider the 
state of the countries east of the Black Sea; were announced as indispensable 
conditions. Austria adopted the one respecting the Consuls, but declined to 
‘nsert the other two in her ultimatum, She had a right so to decline, and it 
was admitted by Her Majesty's Government; but Austria had uo right to 
consider that the other two were regarded by Her Majesty’s Government as less 
xine wid non conditions than that about Consuls; and, as she adopted the onc, 
Her Majesty's Government had a fair nent ta expeet that at leagt she would have

No, 285. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 


(No. 40. t | 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 29, 1856, 
~ COUNT BERNSTORIF called upon me last week, and with great earnest- 

ness expressed his hope that Prussia might be admitted to the Conferences for 
the restoration of peace, which Bey shortly be epee to take place. : 

In favour of this he urged that Prussia had been mainly instrumental in 
inducing Russia to accept the Austriin ultimatum ; and he added further that 
the prudence might well be questioned of excluding Prussia, one of the Great 
Powers of Europe, from taking part in the settlement of questions which were 
essentially of an European character. oa: 

| reminded Count Bernstorff of the various occasions OF which, in the course 
of the last two years, T had lamented the imprudence which Prussia Somes 
by excluding herself from the consideration of European questions, and | assure 
lim that now, when there was some prospect of peace, it was a5 much a matter 
of regret to Her Majesty’s Government that Prussia should have abdicated her 
position as a great European Power as it had been during the course of the war ; 
but as such had been her policy, | was ata loss to understand upon what sy i 
nable ground Prussia could rest claim to take part in the negotiations for 
De Conn Bernstorft had expressed his belief that Prussinn intervention at 
st, Petersburgh had led to the acceptation of the Austrian ultimatum, and it might 


2p 


have been so, but we had no knowledge of it. Count Bernstorff had admitted 
that he had not seen the instructions sent to Baron Werther, and was unac- 
quainted with the tenour of them, or whether the Prussian Minister had been 
informed that the terms of the ultimatum were approved by his Government, 
and that he was on that account to support them; but we did know that the 
Prussian Minister at Vienna had been ordered to support the Russian modifica- 
tions of the ultimatum, which were equivalent to its rejection. 

I then recalled to the recollection of Count Bernstorff, that the Prussian 
Government, through its Diplomatic Agents, by its circular to the German Courts, 
and its speeches in the Chambers, had missed no opportunity of proclaiming that 
the war in which the Western Powers were engaged involved no German interests, 
and that until German interests were affected, Germany was bound to stand 
aloof. Moreover, whenever Austria, whose interests were endangered by the 
aggressive policy of Russia, had been disposed to take a more active part in the 
contest, her intentions had always been paralyzed by the opposition of the 
German Courts and the Dict at the instigation of Prussia. In fact, throughout 
the war, Prussia, under the garb ofneutrality, had rendered important services to 
Rnssia, fur she had supported Russian interests tm German; she had supplied 
Russia with munitions of war; and it was through her ports that Russian trade 
had been carried on; but, if it were true that the advice of Prussia had led to the 
acceptance of the ultimatum, there could be little doubt that that advice given at 
any time during the last two years, might equally have led to peace, and Prussia 
therefore could hardly eseape from responsibility for the duration of the war. 
Prussia, moreover, I said, gloried in her policy, and congratulated herself upon 
having husbanded her strength while the belligerents were exhausting their 
resourees, and she had no right therefore to expect that when all danger was over 
she should be permitted to put cif her exclusive German character and to assume 
the position and claim the privileges of a great European Power, Nevertheless, 
| added, it was probable that the allies might not carry the principle of exclusion 
beyond its necessary limits, and that Prussia would be invited ta aceede to any 
General Treaty that BE be signed; but Count Bernstoff said he did not see 
how Prussia could accede to a Treaty if she had not been a party to the previous 
negotiations. 

On the following day Count Bernstorff again called on me to say that he 
understood a difficulty had arisen with respect to the Aland Islands, and he 
wished to suggest that Prussia might be admitted to the conferences if she 
obtained from Russia an engagement that no fortification should be erected on 
those islands. 

[ told Count Bernstorff that as the non-fortification of those islands was a 
condition sine gud non of peace it was a question to be settled between the 


belligerents, und it neither required nor admitted the intervention of another 
Power.

The Earl of Clarendon to Sir Hamilton Seymour. 
(No. 60.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, January 30, 1856- 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to mea despatch from Count Nesselrode 
to Prince Gortchakolf dated the q{th instant, stating that in consequence of the 
communication which Prince Gortchakoff had heen directed to make at Vienna, 
Count Esterhazy had been instructed to read to Count Nesselrode a confidential 
despatch relating to the fifth clause of the Austrian ultimatum. Count Nessel- 
rode informs Prince Gortchakoff that this despatch contained positive assurances 
as to the meaning of the fifth clause, and that it explicitly indicated that the 
belligerent Powers would not make use of the latitude reserved to them by that 
clause to demand territorial cessions or indemnities of war, but would avail them- 
selves of it only within such limits as would cause no obstacle to the conclusion 
of peace. 

Count Esterhazy was instructed, Count Nesselrode states, by Count 
Buol to communicate these assurances to the Russian Government in order to 
‘aduee them not to insist upon the elimination of Article 5; and the Austrian 
Minister also read to him a telegraphic despatch from Count Buol, in whieli 
his Exeelleney remarked upon the little difference which existed between the 
original terms of the Austrian ultimatum and the Russian variations, and especially 
pointed out, with reference to the filth paragraph of the first clause, that in fact 
the Austrian no less than the Russian version reserved for the definitive nego- 
tiation the final understanding upon the new boundary-line. 

The Russian Cabinet, Count Nesselrode says, took note of the assurances 
and explanations thus communicated to them by the Austrian Minister for 
Foreign Affairs. 

Count Nesselrode then goes on to observe that the object of the Hussian 
Cabinet has always been to proceed. to formal negotiations, in order to put an 
end to the calamities of war: but nevertheless before making sacrifices 50 
important as those implied by the Austrian proposals, the Russian Cabinet 
desired at least to be certain that these sacnifices would lead to peace. The 
assurances now given by the Austrian Government appearing to offer a lavour- 
able chance, the Russian Cabinet would, on its eide, do everything to remove 
the difficulties which prevented the opening of negotiations, and it had _ therefore 
determined to accept the five Austrian propositions as a project of preliminaries, 
and immediately to open the way for negotiations of peace. 

This acceptance had been announced to Count Esterhazy in a note dated 
the jth instant, which Prince Gortchakoff had at the same time been instructed 
to communicate to Count Buol. 

A copy of this note was read to me by Count Colloredo, and is to this 
effect :-—The Russian Government accept the five propositions contained in the 
document annexed to Count Buol’s despatch of the 16th of December, to serve 
as a project of preliminaries, and to open the way immediately to definitive 
negotiations for peace. 

Count Nesselrode concluded his despateh to Prince Gortchakoff by observing 
that no doubt Count Buol will admit that the Russian Cabinet, in adhering 
without reserve to the project of preliminaries, has carried its desire for peace 
far beyond what was required by the necessities of the situation, and will there- 
fore consider it equitable that the principle of a just compensation should he 
rene as the basis in questions which may be presented for negotiation under 

ticle 4. 

By this means, also, Count Nesselrode thinks that the work of peace will be 
accelerated, and he adds that the Russian Cabinet will contribute to this work 
both in this manner and also by hastening the agreement as to the course to be 
followed for the signature of preliminaries, and the entering upon the definitive 
negotiations. Prince Gortchaloff is instructed to read and give a copy of this 
despatch to Count Buol.

No. 294. 


The Borl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 173.) 
My Lord, Foveiqn Office, January 30, 1856. 

I HAVE to state to your Excellency that Her Majesty's Government are 
of opinion that, with regard to the armistice, there are strong reasons why it 
should be only an armistice by land and should not extend to the sea. The 
Russians have no naval force in existence with which the naval forces of the 
allies could by possibility come into conflict between this time and the 3st of 
March. But during that interval the Russian forces in the Black Sea might 
(derive great advantage from the establishment of free communications by water, 
that is to say by the cessution of all blockades and of all interruption to the 
navigation of Russian and neutral vessels by the ships of war of England and 
Frnee. The right of blockade is, however, a belligerent right, and ils exercise 
during an armistice by sea might be questioned by neutrals. 

Moreover, the Baltic might, or some Russian ports in it might, become 
open before the expiration of the armistice, and it would be very unwise not to 
have the power of resuming the blockades in the Baltic at the earliest 
practicable inoment, 

Her Majesty's Government are desirous that these considerations should be 
stated to the French Government, as reasons why the armistice ought not only 
to be limited to a short period of time for its duration, but should also be 
confined to the land forces of the belligerents. England and France might give 
an assurance verbally to the Russians that it is not our intention during the 
continuance of the land armistice to employ their ships of war in making any 
attack upon any of the Russian seaports or towns on their ceast, 

Your Excellency will accordingly direct the immediate attention of the 
French Government to this subject. 

Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord Paris, January 31, 1856. 

COUNT WALEWSKI stated to me this afternoon that he had received 
a telegraphic despatch from M. de Thouvenel dated yesterday, in which that 
Ambassador informed him that the Porte had made very large and unexpected 
concessions in the religions questions connected with the fourth point, but that 
the ‘Turkish Ministers resisted the demand made upon them to sbolish the 
punishment of apostates from the Mussuliman religion. 

M. de Thouvenel appeared to think that the persistance of Lord Stratford 
to obtain a declaration from the Sultan in the sense alluded to above would 
imperil the concessions already made by the Porte, and he asks Count Walewski 
to obtain instructions from Her Majesty's Government to Lord Stratford, 
directing him to withdraw, or, at all events, to modify his demands. Count 
Walewski added that he was going to send a copy of M. de Thouvenel’s 
despatch to M. de Persigny, with a request to your Lordship to transmit to Lord 
Stratford the instructions suggested by M. de Thouvenel. 

T asked Count Walewski whether he had reflected that the Christian 
Powers would probably never have so favourable an opportunity of setting aside 
this barbarous Turkish law, and whether it would not be better to persist in, 
rather than desist from, our attempts to have it abolished. 

His Excellency replied that it would be hard to force the Porte to repeal 
laws which were permitted to exist in Christian countries. For instance, in 
Italy and, he believed, in Sweden there were penal statutes against heretics. 

| observed that 1 apprehended that Her Majesty's Government would find 
it necessary, in order to satisfy Parliament and the country, to obtain an engage- 
ment from the Sultan that punishment for apostaey should be abolished. 
Whether this engagement could be obtained by some sort of Convention between 
the Sultan and his allies, which need not be published in ‘Turkey, but which 
would satisfy public opinion in Europe, and secure the object to be attained, 
was, perhaps, a question which the two Governments might consider. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.,

No, 305. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 1.) 


(No. 60.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 16, 1856. 

‘THE whole of this morning has been devoted by M. Thouvenel, Baron 
Prokesch, and myself to the question, the twofold question, of privileges and 
reforms. We met by agreement at the French Embassy. ‘The memorandum, 
which [had drawn up and transmitted to your Lordship with my despatch 
No, 51 of the 14th instant, was read over and approved by my colleagues, with 
the reserve, in which I partook, of eventual amendments. I observed with 
pleasure, and drew a favourable inference from, the spontaneous accordance of 
our epiniane 

n talking over some of the points, language such as [ should have held 
myself, was used by the Austrian as well as by the French Representative. At 
their suggestion, | introduced a clause for extending to foreigners the privilege 
of holding land in this country. 1 had contemplated the addition of this very 
essential auxiliary to an effective system of reform, but reserved the expression 
of it fora later and more promising occasion. Baron Prokesch stated that in 
conversing with the Grand Vizier, he had found that Minister well disposed 
on the subject, 1 cannot say that any such intimation has ever reached me from 
a Turkish quarter; and on the subject of holding land, | believe that in 
England we still lie open to the charge of a strong remnant of exclusiveness. 

From the French Embassy we went to the Grand Vizier's house in Constan- 
tinople. Prince Callimachi was there with the two Turkish Ministers, Our 
proceedings were necessarily limited to an open perusal of the Turkish enumera- 
tion of privileges, which had been previously communicated by the Grand Vizier, 
and to-a free exchange of remarks and explanations relative to certain passages. 
A translation of this paper is inclosed herewith. It was understood to be a 
mere basis for discussion. It must be allowed to exhibit in its full extent a 
greater umount of liberality towards the Sultan's Christian subjects than 1s 
enerally supposed. ‘Two things are particularly striking, namely, the depree 
of power attributed to the patriarchs and other dignitaries of the Christian 
churches, particularly of the Greek, over their respective dependents, and the 
little provision inade for protecting the latter from any abusive exercise of 
authority. Upon the whole, it may be affirmed with confidence that when the 
ancient and modern immunities are taken together, reality of application and 
practical enforcement are more palpably wanted than any considerable number 
of additional measures; and it must be added in fairness that the best work of 
amendment will be imperfect so long as the Greek and other Christian commu- 
nities are not brought decidedly and practically within the pale of reform. 

It was suggested, | think with propriety, that a Commission composed so 
as to command a sufficient degree of respect and confidence, should be charged 
with the duty of inquirmg and reporting for that purpose. 

It was agreed that another meeting should be held on the 19th instant, 
and as the three Representatives intend to consult together beforehand, with the 
view of going into Conference with opinions completely identical, | venture to 
BDF that essential progress will be made in our joint task before the end of the 
week,

Inclogure in No, 305. 


Memorandum as to Privileges granted ab antiquo fo the Christian Subjects of the 
Porte with reference to Sprritual Affairs. 


(Translation. } 

WHEN the Greek Patriarchate falls vacant, the Archbishops whose sees 
are in the neighbourhood of the capital, being those of Heraclea, Cygicus, 
Nicomedia, and Chalcedon, together with the Synod at Constantinople, proceed 
to elect a prelate in accordance with their religious rites and their opinion, after 
which they address a report announcing their choice to the Porte, who confirms 
the person chosen in the dignity of Patriarch. ‘The elections of the Armenian 
and (Armeno) Catholic Patriarchs are effected by the spiritual heads and notables 
of those nations and their investitures, as im the previous case, 

The Patriarchs, as long as they do not oppress their flocks or aet contrary 
to their religion, are not dismissed, or unless they voluntarily resign, but hold 
office for life. If, as said before, they are dismissed, upon the unanimous 
consent of the Synod, after an accurate investigation of the facts. 

The direction and arrangement of their religious affairs, their income and 
expenditure, and other business of the Patriarchate does not depend, according 
to their religious customs, upon the aetual Patriarchs exclusively; as these 
affairs are under the control of the Archbishops, the Patriarchate seals are 
consigned to those of the latter, ehosen among themselves for the purpose. 
In the same manner the seals of all the convents in the Empire are in the hands 
of the Synod. 

From a very ancient period the Archbishops are unable to proceed to 
Constantinople occasionally without the express sanction of the Patriarch and 
Synod. 

: The subjects of all classes must have recourse lo the Patriarchs upon 
all matters within the competency of the latter, whom they must obey in 
everything. a 

The Patriarch names and deposes, without hindrance, the Archbishops, 
Vicars, Bishops, and priests, in all the places under his jurisdiction. 

When it becomes necessary to change a Greek Archbishop, the seal of the 
Synod must be used for the purpose ; and when a Bishop or Vicar of another 
community is to be changed, a memorial, bearing the seal of the Patriarch and 
Medjlis of that nation, is to be presented, upon which the person elected will 
receive a Berat, enabling him to take possession of his post, and with it a firman 
inclosing the conditions imposed upon him by the Porte. No one can be 
named Archbishop or Vicar upon representations coming from other quarters. 

If the Pashas or Cadis denounce the misconduct of an Archbishop, Vicar, 
or Bishop, and demand his dismissal or exile, the complaints are not to he 
entertained without reference being made to the Patriarch for information ; and 
if by chance a firman should be issued in consequence of the complaints of a 
Pasha or Cadi, the necessary steps are taken, 

[fan Archbishop, Vicar, or Bishop comes to Constantinople on business, 
leaving in his place another priest to represent him, no obstacle is met with by 
him in such a proceeding. 

No interference can be offered by any one to the Patriarcha, Archbishops, 
Bishops, Vicars, and Priests yeading the Seriptures m their dwellings, lighting 
lamps and candles, hanging curtains and images, fixing stools, swinging censers, 
or holding a crozier in the exercise of their rites. ; 

No objection can be made to the members of any community whatever 
burying their dead in accordance with their rites, nor any molestation offered 
to their churches in their possession from old times, or their holy places, 
whether in Constantinople or in the Provinces. ; 

Respect is paid to the memorials bearing the patriarchal or synodal seal, 
or that of the National Assembly, Every request having reference to their rites 
is accorded, 

No one can search the churches or convents of any community without i 
firman, 

No one can hinder the repair, upon the ancient plan and under the 
recognised principles, of the churches ay convents of any community; and 

3 


these ancient churches cannot be transferred to others upon (mere) petitions 
and written representations.* 

No-claim can be raised upon the properties ofa church or convent on 
account of another person's debts, nor can they be interfered with or held as 
security ; and if by any means any one has taken them, he will be forced, by 
law, to restore them, and consigned to the quarter whence they were taken. 

All individuals of whateyer communitity who are desirous of being married 
or divorced under the rites of their nation, must do so by means of the Patriarch 
or his representative, without the interference of any one else. When the 
Patriarch wishes to punish a priest for having married a couple uncanonically, 
and without a patriarchal, episcopal, or viearial license, no interference can be 
made, When a dispute arises between two persons with reference to marriage 
or other subjects, and the Patriarch wishes to administer oaths in the church, or 
punish any one with excommunication, no opposition should be made by the Cadis 
or their deputies. Itis contrary to the Christian religion for a person to divorce 
his wife, to commit bigamy, orto marry more than three times after the death of 
his wife: and the violation of this canonical law must be punished. Entrance 
to the church must also be forbidden to those who violate the ecclesiastical law 
of marriage; and neither the Cadis, Naibs, nor other authorities can force the 
priests to bury the body of one deceased under the ban of excommunication. 

Archbishops, Bishops, Vicars, Priests, Monks, and other Christians can 
bequeath property to their Patriarchs or churches, or to the poor, consisting of 
ome article. or of one-third of their possessions. On their death, their wills 
aré in force and valid, after the rules of their religion; and, after the reception 
of evidence, the property is recovered from the heirs of the deceased by the 
agency of the law. When Archbishops, Bishops, Priests, Monks, and Nuns die 
without heirs, the Patriarch or his deputy receive the money, effects, horses, and 
all other property of the deceased, in order to hand it over tothe public chest ; 
and the Kassam, or distributor of dead men’s effects, the Mutevellis, and the 
Muhassils cannot offer any interference. With reference to those who die 
leaving heirs, neither the Patriarch nor his deputy can seize any of the property 
belonging to them, with the exception of their ecclesiastical rabes, which are to 
be deposited in the vestry. 

The Greek Metropolitans, the Armenian and Catholic Delegates, Priests, 
and Monks, who may conduct themselves in a manner contrary to the prescriptions 
of their respective sects, are punished by their Patriarchs, each according to his 
rite: their hair is shaved, themselves deprived of the priestly ofhec, and the 
churches in their charge transferred to others; the necessary priests are elected 
in the room of the clergymen thus dismissed from their charge in accordance 
with their rules, and without any impediment or obstacle {rom other quarters. 
And those priests or monks who are not attached to any church or monastery, 
but roam about from place to place and corrupt the real Greek and Armenian 
subjects of the Porte, contrary to their rales, are apprehended by means of the 
Patriarchs under a firman, and the necessary punishment is inflicted upon them 
according to law. 

No interference on the part of any one is permitted with reference to the 
property and live stock attached to the churches and monasteries, and all their 
appurtenances situate in places dependent upon the patriarchate of each Patriarch, 
as well as to other churches; but such property is held and enjoyed as practised 
from olden times. 

The money paid by the Greek, Armenian, and Catholic subjects of the Porte 
formerly as taxes to the treasury, oras voluntary contributions, the revenues and 
expenditure of the Patriarchate, and the (personal) patriarchal income, are paid now 
as before, and no hesitation or opposition isallowed. Ifthe agents of the churches 
or monasteries appropriate or use any of the treasury or patriarchal dues, their 
accounts may be examined, and themselves forced to pay compensation without 
any interference. If the Patriarch have claims, in whatever place it may occur, 
upon the episcopal delegates or clerzy out of these dues, the persons appointed 
by them to collect the said sums, having received an Imperial order for the same, 
and also a letter from the appointing Patriarch, reevive legal assistance from the 
Cadis and Naibs, and the money is realised: while the persons thus appointed 
to secure patriarchal claims, or their deputies, receive assistance in every way

when on their journeys, and attention is paid to their safety in travelling; nor 
is any opposition made to their changing their dress or carrying arms, as tmay be

No interference or contravention of ancient practice is carried on by the 
Customs authorities at the various ports and gates with reference to the con- 
yeyance of contributions made by the Christians undés the titles of “ vineyard 
produce” and ‘‘ charity,” and destined for the Fatriarch’s own consumption, 
consisting of syrup, oil, honey, &c., to their houses; and the articles particularly 
destined for the Patriarch’s delegates, and Bishops themselves, or for their 
churches, are not subject to any demand of customs or “octroi” duty at the 
various ports and gates. 

Those of the Greek, Armenian, or Catholic persuasion, who have sincerely 
and resolvedly embraced Islam are naturally, it is clear, exempt from. inter- 
ference on the point of religion; those, however, who under their own free will 
have not embraced Islam cannot be subjected to violence or compulsion from 
any quarter. 

The imprisonment of any Greek, Armenian, or Catholic priest becoming 
necessary, under legal permission, the offender is kept in custody at the 
Patriarchate, and cannot be imprisoned elsewhere. 

No interference can be made regarding the patriarchal staff or crosier, the 
horses he rides, his men, his or their dresses and robes; or regarding the 
provincial delegates’ or bishop's horses and animals; nor can the delegates and 
bishops be obliged to afford the use of their residences as “ konack” (or 
traveller's lodging). 

Should any law-suit arise between Metropolitans, Delegates, or Bishops, and 
other individuals, it is referred to the capital, and examined and decided 
according to the principles of equity, and with a reference to its special nature 
and conditions. ; 

The Patriarchs and Capu Kiayas, together with fifteen men of the suites, are 
exempted from all taxes, Government imposts, or customary levies or demands. 


Conduct of Clerical Functionaries as practised by them under the name of the 
above “ Spiritual Privileges.” 


If the Metropolitans, their Delegates, or the Bishops, levy dues at their 
pleasure from the Christian subjects, neither as regards the amount, nor the 
method of levying, do the State authorities exercise any interference. 

Each sect may open a school of any kind and in any place, nor has the 
State any interference with or knowledge for cognizance of the method of 
instruction therein followed. Ona Patriarch, Metropolitan, Delegate, or Bishop, 
cemanding the exile of an individual, whoever he may be, among the Christians 
on the grounds of his having acted contrary to the rites of his sect, Buch 
demand is complied with and executed without a trial, 

Each Patriarch prohibits the publication and perusal of books among his 
nation and punishes those who act in a contrary manner. 


Concessions recently granted in Spiritual Matters. 


The permission formerly accorded to the reparation of churches is now 
applied to their extension or renewed construction, 

In the case of a Christian subject wishing to embrace Mahometanism, 
inquiries must be made, with a view to ascertaining that no kind of compulsion 
or violence has been employed, before the Porte in the capital and belore the 
Medjlises in the provinces, in the presence of the person’s relations and connections; 
and if he has voluntarily abandoned his faith, he is to be accepted. Permission 
is net accorded to children who have not reached the age of puberty or discrimi- 
nation to change their religion. 


Ancient Condition of non-Mussulman Subjects. 


Atal times non-Mussulman subjects have held property of every descrip: 
tion similarly with the Mussulmans, and under precisely the same title-deeds. 


While the Mussulman subjects used to pay the State an “ ushur,” or tenth, 
upon the produce of the soil, the non-Mussulman subjects used to pay the State 
a‘ aumn,” or eighth. 

Mussulman subjects paying 4 per cent. upon thicir merchandises as customs 
duty, non-Mussulman subjects used to pay a duty of 5 per cent. 

Non-Mussulman subjects were exempt from military service, and in its 
place paid compensation tax, or “tizyeh;"" besides this, they paid under various 
names and titles different taxes, from which the Mussulmans were exempt, and 
rendered certain services under the names of “amja” ( ) and “ angaria ” 
(corvée). 

They had no permission to travel out of the Ottoman dominions, except 
such as were at liberty to trade with Europe. 

The whole of the public employments and ranks were universally bestowed 
upon Mussulmans, and the non-Mussulman subjects were inelig ble to all of 
them. 

Distinctions existed between the Mussulman and non-Mussulman subjects 
inthe form and colour of their dress and houses, in all transactions and in 
employment of terms. 


Concessions accorded to non-Mussulman Subjects since the Tanzimat, 


All the Sultan's subjects are in the enjoyment of equal rights, and security 
of life and property and preservation of honour and character. 

The difference in taxation which existed between the Mussulman and now- 
Mussulman subject is entirely abolished, aud the whole of the Ottoman subjects 
are now upon an equal footing as regards the payment of taxes, whether of 
eencral taxation, of tithes, of custom or other dues. 

Voreed services of the nature of “amja,”’ or corvée, are completely abolished 
for all classes of Ottoman subjects, 

All classes of Ottoman subjects are at liberty to travel wherever they may 
please, whether for commerce, for information, or for pleasure. 

Ottoman subjects ure admitted to military service, and the commutation- 
tax is abolished; it has, however, been decided that a tax be levied, called 
“ Military Aid Pound” (Tyane-i-askeriyé) as a substitute for their rendering 
personal service. 

Non-Mussulman subjects are employed in the service of the Porte accord- 
ing to their merits and capacity, and participate in the ranks conferred by the 
state. 
In the provincial assemblies of each Kyalet, Liva, and Kaza, each nation or 
sect is naturally represented by its spiritual chiefs; but in addition to them they 
have other members respectively, who all equally have a voice in civil and 
niunicipal affaivs: and in all causes tried before these assemblies the opinions 
and: decisions of the Mussulman and non-Mussulman members are upon an 
equal footing. 

In the Tidjaret Courts, and Courts of Inquiry, established in the capital and 
the provinces, the members, likewise, consist of Mussulmans and non: Mussul- 
mans, whose opinions and decisions are on a footing of perfect equality. 

Each nation may hold an assembly in its Patriarchate for the transaction of 
its own special national affairs, such as the control of hospitals, schools, and the 
like; in the provinees, likewise, each nation chooses und appoints its own chiets 
in the cities and the villages. 

In the provinces, the larger and the smaller districts (Eyalet, Liva, and 
Kaza), the general taxation is levied by the Porte, but each nation effects: its 
own nsseasinent for purposes of raising its own national taxation, and the amount 
being obtained by means of its chiefs is deposited in the national chest, All 
Ottoman subjects being equal before the law, the legal tribunals aceept the 
evidence and information of subjects of all clagses. 

All distinctions affecting non-Mussulman subjects in the matter of dress, 
residence, and other particulars, arc completely done away with, and everybody 
is at liberty to dress himself, to build his house, and to move about precisely as he 
may like, while as regards forms, titles, and the use of terms, a treatment of 
perfect equality is practised towards all subjects of the Ottoman Empire.

My Lord, Constantinople, January 19, 1856. 
IN concert with my French and Austrian colleagues, I have devoted nearly 
the whole of to-day and yesterday to the pending question of privileges and 
reforms. ‘The progress has been considerable in so far as concerns our under- 
standing with the T urkish Ministers. ‘The result of two separate meetings on 
our part was a paper founded principally ou my memorandum, and expressive of 
our joint opinion after due inquiry and discussion. This series of articles, which 
is inclosed herewith, became the subject-matter of a third interview between the 
three Representatives and the two Turkish Ministers, assisted by Prince 
Callimachi, We met, as before, at the Grand Vizier’s house. We agreed to 
discuss the paper. alter a general perusal of its contents, article by article, noting 
down at the close of each whether, and with what alterations or reserves, it could 
be accepted unanimously. | observed with pleasure that the Grand Vizier and 
‘wad Pasha were to all appearance favourably disposed to the acceptance of our 
proposals. Thejr assents, hprerats, ye yaried with different degrees of 


220 


admission; they intimated, with respect to some leading points, an apprehension 
of difficulties elsewhere, and they reserved for the whole, in distinct terms, the 
approval of their colleagues and the sanction of their Government. It is further 
to be observed, that on two or three points they drew back at first from the 
statement which had been previously given in by themselves. They seemed to 
have much to surmount with respect to the abolition of all restraints on 
conscience in religious matters, and to the admissibility of all classes under rules 
of general application to public employment. 

It was agreed that the question of administrative improvement did not 
belong to the fourth point in the same sense as that of Christian privileges 
belonged to it. But no one demed that the two questions were virtually bound 
up together as the essential elements of an effective reform in this country. The 
Grand Vizier avowed with laudable frankness that a thorough administrative 
reform was indispensable to the existence of the Empire. 

It can hardly escape your Lordship’s notice, on comparing the series of 
articles with the propositions contained in my memorandum, that although much 
of what might scem at first sight to have been lopped off, has been only con- 
densed or moulded into a better form, yet that in several instances not only 

rominent details but even important securities have been dro ped. The change 
ig attributable to a very simple cause, It was impossible to avoid some 
differences of opinion in so extensive and complicated a work, and it was felt by 
all that whatever discussions might be found unavoidable at a later period, there 
would be great advantage in placing an unanimous opinion in the outset under 
the consideration of our Turkish allies, It was evident that their acceptance of 
the plan, as now presented to them, would be an earnest of further success both 
in urging the adoption of corresponding measures, and in obtaining whatever else 
might be necessary for the completion and enforeement of a new administrative 
syste.

WITH reference to the dissatisfaction which it would seem, from your 
Excelleney's despatch No. 40 of the 14th of January, is felt by the Porte at the 
conduct of Omer Pasha, T have to instruct your Excellency to represent to the 
‘Turkish Government, on behalf of Her Majeaty’s Governtment, how unwise it 
would be for the Porte to put aside and deprive of command the only General 
in the Sultan's service who has shown himself fit to hold a great command. 
Omer Pasha may have faults, but he is a perfect General as compared with 


2a 


Selim Pasha and other Turkish officers. He looks after his troops, provides 
as well as he can for their wants, possesses their confidence, and maintains their 
discipline. There may be better Generals in the field than Omer Pasha, but he 
is, hat the other Pashas are not, a good organizer. 

Her Majesty’s Government are aware that there are cabals and intrigues at 
Constantinople against Omer Pasha, but they wish that your Excellency should

My Lord, Paris, February 2, 1856. 
IN the course of one of the last conversations with which the Emperor was 
leased to honour me, His Majesty said that with a view of entering into the 
‘onferences under a complete understanding with Her Majesty's Government on 
all the points of detail which must necessarily come under discussion, he had 
desired Count Walewski to draw up a paper embodying these points, which His 


* No, S41. 
30 


232 


Majesty proposed sending to London for the consideration of Her Majesty's 
Government. 

| yesterday inquired of Count Walewski whether this paper was ready. 
His Execllency answered me very evasively, and as if he had no intention of 
executing the Emperor's orders. He said that upon considering the matter, he 
found that there were many points on which the two Governments were hot, 
sufficiently informed to enable them to come to any decision. 

He alluded particularly to the first and fourth points, concerning which a 
great deal must depend on the result of the Conferences now carrying on at 
Constantinople. 1 observed that if this was the ease concerning those points, 
there were others of great importance respecting which it appeared to me to be 
matter of necessity that the two Governments should thoroughly understand 
cach other. I alluded particularly to the number and size of the armed vessels 
which Russia should be permitted to have for the future in the Black Sea, and 
to the stipulations to be made in regard to the provinces to the east of that Sea. 
Count Walewski showed no wish to discuss these matters, but he evinced a 
willingness to entertain a lint which I threw out, and which proceeded originally 
from the Emperor, that the Admirals should be consulted upon the number and 
the size of the ships to be allowed to Russia, and [ venture to suggest that if 
Her Majesty's Government entertained this idea, Sir Edmund Lyons should be 
‘astructed. an his return through Paris to talk the matter over with Admiral 
Hamelin. It appears to me that, under all circumstances, a written opinion 
from them would be of value in the discussions which must ensue on this 
subject, But I should not feel that | liad done my duty by Her Majesty's 
Government if I did not earnestly invite your Lordship to insist on a prelim- 
nary discussion with the French Government of all those points on whieh Her 
Majesty’s Government are determined to insist,.and on which there is no clear 
understanding between Paris and London. The object which Count Walewski 
has in view is clear, It ia to enter upon the Conferences with as few engage- 
ments towards England as possible, but the mterests of England require that this 
abject should, if possible, he defeated, 

Besides the question which I have brought more prominently forward in 
this despatch, there is one other on which Her Majesty's Government will de 
well to insist, and to demand a categorical answer from the Imperial Govern- 
ment. [allude to the evacuation of Mingrelia by Omer Pasha being considered 
as an equivalent for the evacuation of Turkish Armenia by the Russians. There 
are also the questions of the renunciation by Russia to the erection of forts on 
the eastern coasts of the Black Sea, of the extension of commercial intercourse 
with the inhabitants of those countries, and others to which your Lordship has 
at different times called my attention, but on whieh T have never been able to 
elicit the slightest expression of interest from Count Walewski. If I might 
venture to offer an opinion, it would be that your Lordship should come to 
Paris a few days before the opening of the Conferences, in order that by your 
personal weight and superior authority, you may bring about the necessary 
unity of action on the part of the wo Governments in regard to these important 
matters.

My Lord, Paris, February 2, 1856. 

COUNT WALEWSKI has been good enough to read me a confidential 
letter which he received yesterday from the French Minister at Frankfort, giving 
an account of a conversation which he (M. de Montessuy) had held with 
M. de Brunnow, and which is not without interest at the present moment. 

M. de Brunnow had not received any official notification that he was to be 
one of the Russian Plenipotentiuries to conduct the negotiations for peace, 
though he considered it likely that he should be named. In that case he 
expected that Count Orloff would pass through Frankfort, and that they would 
proceed together to Paris, M, de Brunnow expressed himself us exceedingly 
happy at the prospect of peace. He hoped only that the allies would take the 
position of the Emperor of Russia into consideration, and consent to put the 
sacrifices made by Russia into such a written form ‘‘that they would bear 
translating into Russian.” 

He said that the great object of Russia was to advance quickly with the 
negotiations, and he was of opinion that the best plan of proceeding would be to 
come toa decision at once upon all the principal points; for, those once settled, 
the solution of the others would be comparatively easy. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Vienna, January 30, 1856. 

WITH regard to Baron Seebach’s opinions, as reported in Lord Cowley’s 
confidential despatch No. 89 of the 17th instant, | am desirous of remarking to 
your Lordship that 1 arm disposed to admit their correctness, with the abatement 
which may be due as well to the difficulty of obtaining at St. Petersburgh a 
correct knowledge of the feeling of the vast Russian Empire, as to the predilec- 
tions which Baron Seebach may be supposed naturally to entertain to a country 
with which his own interests have become identified, 

With one opinion professed by M. de Seebach | am bound to concur, 
because it is in perfect accordance with that which [ submitted to your Lord- 
ship, I believe even before the war broke out. It was clear to me t at, except 
in the very important point of recruitment, the pressure of war would be felt more 
painfully & the higher than by the labouring classes of Russia; or rather, that 
ra very evil inflicted upon the one would be a benefit conferred upon the 
ater, 

It is obvious that the consumer of foreign articles and the owner of home 
produce would suffer severely from the interruption of sea-transport ; but it was 
equally so that the poor serf would profit by the decrease which this very inability 
to obtain access to foreign markets, could not fail to bring about im the price of 
agricultural produce of all kinds. 

Many persons have spoken of the inconvenience which must be felt by the 
labouring classes of Russia from the inereased price of such articles as tea, suger, 
and coffee, not reflecting that these, although in general use among the poor of 
our own country, are utterly unknown to the serf, whose food is the blackest 
bread and the coarsest oatmeal. 

By such a man, unless he himself or a member of his family is carried off as 
a soldier, the evils of war are but little felt, 

I have, &e-

(No, 197.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 4, 1856. 


| HAVE received your Excellencv’s despatch No. 17% af the 30th. of 
January, respecting the claim put forward by the Sardinian Minister at Constan- 
tinople to be admitted to take part in the preliminary discussions now going on 
‘nthe Turkish capital, with the view of coming to an understanding with the 
Porte on the first and fourth points, previously to the general discussion on those 
points by the Plenipotentiaries about to assemble at Paris. 

The French Government, it appears, have lost no time in aequainting their 
Representatives at Constantinople and at Turin thet this claim on the part of the 
Sardinian Minister could not he admitted; and your Excellency will state to 
‘ount Walewski that Her Majesty's Government will, as matters stand, not 
abject to adopt the same course, though they would have preferred, if the 
French Government had entertained «4 diferent opinion, to concur with if In a 
recognition of the Sardinian claim. 

It may indeed be said that the discussions at Constantinople are not nego 
tiations fur peace, but friendly and confidential communications between the 
Representatives of England, France, Austria, and the Porte, with a view to induce 
the Porte to make, of its own aecord and by its own authority, internal arrange- 
ments which would have the effect of superseding negotiations on one OF Mere of 
the four points. 

On the other hand, however, although Sardinia has certainly no ground of 
right on which to found a pretension to be ranked among the great Powers of 
Europe, yet it cannot be doubted that itis very desirable for England and France 
that Sardinia should be upheld as much as possible in the general estimation of 
Furope, and that the greatest care should be taken to avoid wounding her 
susceptibilities, by insisting too vigorously on the exact observunee at the 
limitations assigned to the part she 1s to take in the negotiations for peace, 

‘The popular feeling in Sardinia is understood at present to be one of doubt 
whether Sardinia has done wisely in entering into alliance with the Western 
Powers, instead of husbunding her resources for any contingencies in the Italian 
Peninsula which might hold out to Sardinia a prospect of direct reward for any 
cooperation she might afford to other Powers; but the Western Powers have 
certainly reaped substantial advantages from theiralliance with Sardinia, not only 
in consequence of the military forees which she has placed at their disposal, but 
also from the moral effect in Kurope of the first adherence of a-secondary Power 
‘athe great cause for which they were contending, 

Whenever the period, whether remote or neal at hand, for an improvement 
in the social condition of the Ttalian Peninsula shall arrive, it will be of the 
utmost importance that the position of Sardinia should be well-defined and that 


* No. 335. 


241 


she should present an example to the other States of the Peninsula of a well- 
ordered constitutional Government; and everything that tends in the mean- 
while to encourage in the Sardinian people feelings of self-respect will be so 
mae 5 the way of preparation for the establishment of a better order of things 
in Ltaly, 

Actuated by these considerations Her Majesty's Government, on learning 
from your Excellency’s despatch No. 179 at the 3lst ultimo, that the Govern- 
ment of the Emperor did not olject to the signature of a Sardinian Plenipotentiary 
being affixed to the Protocol which was yesterday signed at Vienna, have instructed 
Sir Hamilton Seymour, iW the Sardinian Chargé d’ Affaires should apply to 
sien the Protocol, to inform Count Buol and the other Munsters that Her 
Majesty's Government concurred in the propriety of bis doing so; for it appeared 
to Her Majesty’s Government that Sardinia might think it hard that she who 
has been fighting by the side of the Western Powers, and has placed all her 
means at their disposal, should be treated with less deference, consideration and 
confidence than a Power which has been standing aloof, and should not be 
allowed to put her hand to an act by which the belligerent Powers bind them- 
selves to negotiate for the restoration of peace.

AT a ball which was given last night by the Prince of Prussia, the King 
spoke to me in 8 depressed and embittered tone on the subject of a conversation 
which Count Bernstorf! bad lately held with your Lordship respecting the 
approaching Peace Conferences. ; ; bs 

His Prussian Majesty said that, without instructions, Count Bernstorff’ had 
chosen to originate the question of the admission of Prussia to the Conferences, 
and that he feared his Minister had spoken in an unbecoming manner to your 
Lordship; that Count Bernstorff had a violent temper, prools of which he had 
himself witnessed ; that at times he had difficulty in controlling it; but that on 
the present occasion his conduct was highly blameable, and that he had given 
just cause for his displeasure, as he had taken a step unwarranted by His 
Majesty's orders and wishes in initiating the question of his admission to the 
Conferences, lor that although he might desire to assist at the Conferences, it was 
beneath his honour and dignity to do anything which could bear the appearance 
of asking for an invitation to them. 

The King appeared greatly irritated at the proceedings of his Minister in 
London ; His Majesty, nevertheless, closed his remarks by saying that he wished 
me to think no more on the subject, 

Your Lordship’s despatch No. 40 of the 20th ultimo only arrived this 
morning, and Twas consequently unable to make any other reply to the King 
than that His Majesty’s words were the first that had reached me. 

Baron Manteuffel, to whom I have since related the substance of the King’s 
remarks, told me that His Majesty had been very angry with Count Bernstortt, 
but that he had succeeded in softening the terms of the reprimand which he had 
been ordered to address to him by telegraph. 

__ have also requested his Excellency to inform Eis Majesty that in the 
despatch which your Lordship had addressed to me, giving an nceount of the 
conversation which you had held with the Prussian Minister, nothing whatever 
appeared to have been said by him in an nnbecoming tone, and that any ANXICty 
that was entertained by His Majesty on the subject might be at once “eheved: 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

tion the question of admitting Prussia to the approaching Peace Conferences. 

[called last night on Baron Manteutiel, and on alluding to the above- 
mentioned conversation, [ said that ‘e had been extremely painful to your 
Lordship to make the remarks—which of course were already known to his 
Exeelleney—to Count Bernstorff, the representative of a country with which the 
British Government must always desire to entertain friendly, nay, intimate 
relations: but that Prussia, by the policy which she considered it her interest to 
pursue, had separated herself tram all participation in the discussion of the great 
question of the day; and that ay her German interests appeared to be of greater 
value to her than her European ones, she had voluntarily excluded herself from 
all participation in the Conferences, and that your Lordship had deemed it a 
duty to record in your answer to Count Bernstorif the occurrences of the last year, 
in proof that the position which Prussia now occupies was entirely one of her 
own secking, and the natural result of the policy she had thought proper to 
pursue, 1 endeavoured then to discover from Baron Manteutfel whether any 
change was likely to occur in the King’s policy on the Eastern question, and 
whether there was any chance of His Majesty taking engagements to support 
the five points. His Excellency said, that the King had already given evidence 
af his desire to arrive at an honourable settlement of the questions about to be 
diseussed ut Paris, but that His Majesty would certainly not bind himself to 
support anything so vague as the proposals that might be brought forward in 
explanation of the fifih point ‘ithe ultimatum ; that the question of an alteration 
of the Russian Asiatic frontier might grow out of it, as well as questions of war 
indemnities, and others of equal importance ; und that it would be too much to 
expect Prussia to. bind herself to anything so undefined. [ replied, that as to 
war indemnities, | had never heard that the question had been agitated, except 
by the newspapers, but that if peace was not made this year, and that we had 
another successful campaign, of course our demands would go on Increasing 
hut said England was about to enter in good faith into negotiations for peace, 
and that as Prussia scemed as little ‘nelined us ever to make engagements as to 
her future policy, there would be nothing left for us but to propose the Treaty 
at Peace for her adhesion when we had concluded it. To this Baron Manteutlel 
replied, that Prussia would not adhere to any ‘Treaty in the negotiation of which 
she had not participated, and that therefore if she was excluded from the 
Conferences, her adhesion hereafter would be declined, I rejoined, that the 
cireumstances attending the negotiation of the Treaty of the Dardanelles would 
certainly be in his recollection, to the terms of which another great Power, 
France, had at the time refused to agree, but that the year following its signa- 
ture she found it inconvenient to he excluded, and was readmitted into the 
European Council; that perhaps this might become the ease with Prussia, aud 
if we happily succeeded in concluding peace in 1856, it might happen that in 
1857 Prussia would desire to reassume her place with the great Powers.

My Lord, Berlin, February 2, 1856. 

BARON DE BEUST, the Minister for Foreign Affairs of the King of 
Saxony, came here from Dresden a few days ago, and remains till Monday next. 
His Excellency called on me yesterday ; and after some allusion to the approach- 
ing Conferences for peace, and to the difficult position in which Prussit found 
herself with respect to them, 1 said that we deeply regretted that Prussia had 
lately abstained from joining us in our discussions of the matters relating to the 
Fastern question, and that she appeared desirous to avoid taking any engages 
ments that would define her future policy. 

Baron Beust save me to understand that the chief object of his visit was to 
endeavour to smooth the difficulties which had arisen’ between Austria and 
Prussia, and bring about a common understanding as to the direction to be 
given to the German Diet in the matter of the five points which was about to be 
communicated by Austria, 

He assured me that he hoped to have made a favourable impression here, 
and that Germany would appear more united than she had been. He then 
threw out some hints as to the admission of Germany to the Peace Conferences, 
observing that it would be an advantage for the Western Powers to assure them- 
selves of the sympathies of Germany; and it was evident that, if such a decision 
was taken, Baron Beust looked forward to becoming himself the Representative 
on the occasion, 

He spoke reasonably on the encral question; he seemed to consider that 
Russia was sincere in her wish for peace, and to believe that she had already 
suifered severely from the war; but I cannot divest myself of the impression 
that one of the objects of this visit of Baron de Beust ig to concert measures to 
guard Germany from all unnecessary implication in the war, and to prevent 
Austria from attempting to screen herself behind the Confederation, , 

In the meantime I hear that the Austrian propositions: to maintain the five 
points at the Diet meet with more favour here than they did at first, and that 
there are hopes that Germany may agree to them, 

T shall hops in a few days to be able to inform your Lordship of the results, 
ifany, which Baron de Beust's visit to Berlin may have nroduced 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Count Buol’s approval, and this morning M, de Hiibner bad renewed the appli-

the justice of her demand upon the fiet that Prussia having been a party to the 
‘Treaty of 1841, which would be modified by the arrangements now proposed, had 
a vight to be consulted. Moreover, the questions under discussion were 
Kurapean questions which concerned Prussia as much as any of the Great 
Powers. Austria, without asserting the rights of Prussia as positively as her 
northern neighbour, gave it to be understood that there would be danger in 
excluding Prussia from any Buropean arrangements, It would, Count Buol 
conceived, throw her into the arms of Russia, and perpetuate the schism 
which existed in Germany. Prussia, moreover, had expressed her willingness 
to sign the preliminaries as Inid down in the Austrian ultimatum. 

tasked Count Walewski what answer he had given to M, de Hibner.

mence, but that he could give no official answer without previous consultation 
with Her Majesty's Government. ‘To another of my questions, whether his 
Excelleney’s personal opinion had been modified by this fresh uppeal on the part 
of Austria, Count Walewski replied that under no circumstances did he 
think that Prussia should be invited to participate in the Conferences, which 
was evidently her present pretension, but that he was not inclined to make a 
declaration of exelusion which would bind the French and English Governments 
beyond the present moment, if Prussia herself made advances. He should be 
pind, he added, to know the opinion af Her Majesty’s Government after Count 
“‘olloredo, who, he supposed, would make a similar communication to that

those for M. de Brunnow to F rankfort. ‘Che general orders to prevent the 
passage of all Russian subjects into France, with the exception of the Plenipo- 
tentiuries’? suite, had been received on the frontiers, and would be maintained 
unless the negotiations terminated favourably. 

The Plenipotentiaries, on their arrival im Paris, are to be received by the 
Emperor at a private audience, and Count Walewski will inform them what 
visits they are to make. They will lodge at the hotel of the Russian Mission. 

I asked Count Walewski when he expected them to arrive. He said that 
Count Orloff would not reach Paris until the last moment, but that M. de 
Brunnow would probably be here much sooner. [ took the liberty of remarking 
to his Excellency that to allow M. de Brunnow to remain in Paris several days 
before the opening of the Conferences would be much remarked upon, antl 
certainly ought to he avoided, An early arrival would be so indecorous on his 
part, that if must be attributed to political motives, and | could not too earnestly 
recommend his being confidentially advised not to come to Paris before his 
colleague. Count Walewski at first appeared to think that it would be very 
‘ndelicate in him to interfere, but upon my telling him that 1 would not answer 
forthe remarks of the press if matters went wrong during the negotiations, 
and this most extraordinary proceeding had been permitted, he said that he 
would write to M. de Montessuy, to prevent M. de Brunnow’s undertaking the 
journey as soon as he had intended,

The Eurl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 

(No. 209.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 7, 1856. 

WITH reference to your Excellency’s despatch No. 204 of the Sth instant, 
| have to state to you that Count Colloredo has made to me a communication 
similar to that which, as you reported in that despatch, has been addressed by 
Baron Hiibner to Count Walewski. Count Colloredo dwelt at some length 
upon the importance of producing union in Germany, and the danger of 
differences in the Dict being created by Prussia with respect to the terms of 
peace, if the latter Power were not permitted to take part in the negotiations 

1 admitted to Count Colloredo that it was quite natural for Austria to 
desire unanimity of opinion in the Diet, upon any acts in which she was 
concerned; but the true object of the approaching Conferences at Paris appeared 
to have been altogether lost sight of. and I must therefore beg to remind him 
that negotiations were ubout to. be entered into by belligerent Powers, to put an 
and to the war in which they were engaged, and for that purpose the union or 
disunion, the approval or disapproval, of Germany, was of no importance, and 
could not influence the proceedings of the Conference. 1 added, that throughout 
the war, and the costly sacrifices it entailed, the Western Powers had met with 
nothing but ill-will from Prussia and the German States, whose sympathies for 
Russia had never been disguised ; and it was too much to expect that England 
and France should now invite Prussia to take part in negotiations for peace, in 
order that at their expense a temporary agreement of opinion should be created 
in Germany, where, a8 Count Colloredo well knew, the rivalry of Austria and 
Prussia, and the disturbing influence of Russia, forbad the hope of permanent 
union, Her Majesty's Government, I said, had no wish to undervalue the power 
of Prussia, nor to act harshly towards her, but it seemed to them, upon an 
impartial review of the policy of Prussia for the last two years, that to satisfy 
her ambition by admitting her now to take part in the consideration of questions 
fam which she has hitherto exeluded herself, would constitute a mischievous 
precedent and justly expose England and France to the charge of being indif- 
ferent to political dishonesty. 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received February 8.) 


(No. 64.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 6, 1856, 

IN my despatch No. 58 of the 2nd instant, I reported the impressions 
aie 1 had then received as to the object of Baron de Beust’s visit to this 

Solin, 

His Excellency returned to Dresden on Monday, and I cannot say that he 
has entirely effected a reconciliation of the differences which existed between 
the Austrian and Prussian Cabinets respecting the communication of the five 
points to the German Diet. When Barca de Buest left Berlin, it was 
understood to have been agreed that the Austrian proposal to the Diet was 
to be answered by the expression of readiness, on the part of that body, to 
accede to it upon the understanding, that if Germany adopted the five points 
she was to be invited to participate in the Conferences. 

The Prussian Government did not at the time ruse any objection to this 
conditional arrangement suggested by Baron de Beust, but on its being 
communicated to Vienna, Count Buol immediately told Colonel Manteuttel 
that it could not be taken into consideration, and it may therefore he presumed 
that the question will not be seriously pushed, though, to judge from the 
language of the Representatives of the small German Courts, they are unanimous 
in thinking the moment arrived for forcing on the question of the admission of 
the Diet to the position of one of the Great Powers, to emancipate her from her 
German sphere, and thus obtain her recognition as an active; instead of passive, 
implement in the general political negotiations of Europe. 

The opinion of Austria onthe point has already been given, and there 1s no 
doubt, if Prussia is not to be herself represented at the approaching Conferences, 
that she will never consent to her interests being delegated to any other Power, 
or to have them mixed up with those of Germany ; Russia, | hear also, has no 
desire to have Germany admitted to the Conferences, though she will endeavour 
not to give offence in enunciating: an opinion on the matter, and as | presume 
there can be no doubt as to the opinion of Her Majesty's Government and that 
of the Emperor of the French on the subject, this part of Baron de Buest’s 
proposal will fall to the ground, One result, however, of his visit is evident—the 
tone of communication between Austria and Prussia is improving, and there is a 
partial restoration of confidence between the two Governments.
