No, 364, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clorendon.—(Received February 8.) 


(No. 66, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 6, 1856. 
THE subject which absorbs public attention at the present moment 1s, 
whether Prussia is or is not to be represented at the approaching Conferences at 
Paris. The opinion of the Russian party is, that it may be regrettable far 
Prussiu, us a Great Power, not to be there, ut that it would be equally so if she 
bound herself by any engagements that would interfere with her freedom of 
action hereafter, as their desire naturally 1s that in no case should Prussia ever 
be culled upon to take part against Russia; and I have good reason to know 
that Baron Budberg gives them no encouragement, to seck for admission to the 


Conferences, as he is perfectly contented with things as they are, and that he 
has now brought forward a fresh argument—that the Emperor Alexander, in 
accepting the five points, has raised a clamour amongst the old Russian party ; 
and that if Prussia were now to join the Western Powers, his position would 


258 


become one of extreme danger from internal commotion, and that he would be 
perhaps forced to continue the war. 

The Liberal party regret the humiliating position of their country, and 
seeing it reduced by the policy of the present Government to a mere German 
State, they, however, do not desire to see the King take engagements, at the 
suggestion of Austria, which would bind Prussia to the position of a second-rate 
Power in Germany. Then, again, there are many of both parties who, putting 
aside the question of the dignity of their country, are clad to see it free from 
any immediate danger; and they trust to the King's political ingenuity to 
seoure Prussia from being involved in serious difficultics hereafter. 

The language of the Austrian Minister, ‘1 his late communication to this 
Government, has been to induce a common attitude at the Diet; and he has 
latterly declared the anxiety of his Government that Prussia shall be represented 
at the Conferences. ‘The language of the French Minister has been of friendly 
admonition, stating that if Prussia pursued her present impulses, she could not 
he admitted: but he has not concealed from Baron Manteuffel that the unfa- 
vourable disposition of his Government towards Prussia has been increased by 
arguments from England. We are therefore held up as the determined oppo- 
nents of the pretensions of the King of Prussin to be invited to take part in the 
Conferences; and your Lordship can well imagine that the partizans of Russia 
are not idle in promoting the anti-English feeling which, unfortunately, exists to 
a considerable extent. 

The Marquis de Moustier sets out for Paris to-morrow, on a short leave of 
absence for family affairs. He saw Baron Manteufiel last night; and on asking 
if his Exeelleney could not charge him with a favourable word for Paris—some 
urguinent which would enable Count Walewski to shake the present disposition 
of England towards Prussia—he was told in answer that the opinions of the 
Prussian Government have not undergone any modification, but that Prussia, in 
order to avoid giving a “spectacle” to Europe, will not appear in a different 
line from Austria at the Diet. 

or the moment, the opinion of this Government appears to be that they 
will enter into no binding engagements as to the future; that they will not seek 
an invitation to the Conferences, to which, as a great Power, they consider they 
have a right of access; and that, further, no European arrangement can be 
completed without their participation, 

The question now, rises in how far it might be for the interests of Europe to 
admit Prussia to these Conferences, and whether her presence would be advan- 
tugcous or not, 

Tt must not be expected that she can at once change the part she has been 
playing in the interests of Russia, fox one of tendency towards the policy of the 
Western Powers} but with her great desire for the reestablishment of peace on a 
ecod and solid foundation, might not Prussia be found useful in assisting us in 
obtaining from Russia concessions, if she felt that withholding them would entail 
n continuance of hostilities f 

The terror of war is such that she might be better disposed than we imagine 
to act with us in the Conferences ; though at the same time it is not likely that 
she would ever take a decided part. 

That Austria should wish for Prossia in the Conferences is natural. If she 
can obtain her adhesion to the five points, she will find her a ready ally to 
support her to, the extent of her own objects, and also to prevent the Western 
Powers from pressing on the Conference more than she wishes them to obtain 
with regard to the Additional Articles, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

peace obtained in common, We shall not hesitate to declare ourselves ready to 
sign with them the preliminaries : we shall thus best prove that we are determined 
to accept this document in future, although we did not cooperate in its details 
at the Commencement, as a point of departure for our political conduct, and wall 
certainly strive with all our strength in order not to sce the bases of harmony 
already gained again postponed and destroyed. ‘To make a further special 
communication to the Cabinets of London and Paris on the subject, since they 
have not even now made known to us officially their consent to the preliminaries 
accepted by Russia, would not only not be in accordance with the position 
which we have maintained hitherto, which wished to avoid the appearance of 
pushing into negotiations withheld from our knowledge; but, on the CONEY 
prove a troublesome mistrust of our intentions asa German and European Power, 
which is foreign to the King and His Majesty’s Government. 

We regard with the liveliest interest the proposal before us, respecting the 
communication by Austria to the Diet, and hope, with the Austrian Mimater at 
this Court, that it will be of a nature to prove the unity of the Germame 
Confederation, in its judgment of the great political question of the moment, and 
of the duties aceruing to it therelrom. | | 

You will bring this despatch to Count Buol’s knowledge, with the repeated 
assurance of our bounden gratitude for the Austrian communication of the 20th 
instant.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 11.)

My Lord, Berlin, February 9, 1856. 

| CALLED on Baron Manteuffel last night, with the view of softening, if 
| was not unable to remove, the impression which exists generally here, that the 
exelneien of Prussian from the approaching Conferences rests mainly with 

ingland., 

: I said to his Excelleney that I had been surprised to find that this opinion had 
erown almost into afixed idea at Berlin, and that though we should never shrink 
from a just responsibility, this was carrying the matter rather too far ; that we had 
‘avited Prussia, and had hoped that she would not have refused to adopt and 
appropriate the five points, which would have given a colour to her policy ; anil 
that having refused to do so, the affair remained unsettled, and that France was 
perfectly agreed with us on the subject. 

Baron Manteuflel replied that the Marquis de Moustier had certainly always 
spoken to him in this sense, and had said that the two Governments were of one 
and the same opinion, but there had been a shade of difference in the mode of 
treating the matter, and that England had held much more decided language 
than France. 

This, I said to his Excellency, might perhaps be explained by the different 
preparations being overlooked, at a time when nearly all the nations of Europe 
mode of transacting business in the two countries. In England there was gene- 
rally more bluntness of manner; our opinions were expressed plainly and 
clearly, and we had a_ straightforward way of acting, which resulted from the 
nature of our institutions. We sought less of concealment than ather people. 
We had nothing to hide, and were in the habit of going straight to our point, 
and not by a circuitous route; a recommendable system, im my opinion, but 
which I was sorry to say was rarely appreciated, 

I then endeavoured to learn from his Excellency what would be the result 
of the Austrian communication at Frankfort. 

He enid that the Committee would consider their report; but not a word 
dropped from him which indicated his ultimate intentions, and the probability is 
that he does not know them. 

I then asked if the King was resolved to keep aloof from the Conferences. 

His Excellency answered that His Majesty would not buy his entrance 
into them, 

Then. I said, the position that would probably be occupied by the Prussian 
Government at the head of the smaller States, who were all clamouring to. be 
represented at Paris, was exactly that which would be most agreeable to Russia. 

Prussia would keep out of all responsibility, and, if peace should not result from 
the Conferences, would be ready to play the same friendly part to Russia that 
she had done throughout the war, In fact, | said, you almost constitute yourself 
the ally of Russia. 

This, Baron Manteuffel denied; but he threw out some unintelligible hints 
that our policy might drive her in a direction that might not be agreeable to us, 
and that she would probably find allies that understood her better than we did, 


265 


This morning the French Chargé d’ Affaires called on me, and informed me 
that he had just seen Baron Manteuffel, whom he found firm on the question of 
refusing to enter into any species of engagement ; and his Excellency, it appears. 
finished his conversation wtih M. Rothan with words to the-following effect, 
which he doubtless said in order that they might be repeated to me as a 
supplement to our conversation of last might; “that he hoped peace would 
resuit from the Paris Conferences, that he looked forward hereafler to a close 
alliance being established between France and Russia, and that when the time 
came Prussia might be inclined to join it.” | 

This was evidently meant to flatter the French Chargé d'Affaires, who, 
however, attached as little value to the words as they deserved, and to be 
repeated to me as a menace of what would occur to the relations of England and 
Prussia if we persisted in our present policy.

No. 375. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon, —(Recewed February 11.) 


(No. 75.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 9, 1856. 

THE greatest confusion and contradiction appears in all the instructions 
that emanate from the Cabinet of Berlin at this moment, the jealousies of the 
different states have been roused, and Germany presents a spectacle to Europe 
of weakness and internal division impossible to describe. Bavaria has declared, 
as | understand from good authority, that she is willing to adopt only the four 
first points of the Austrian ultimatum, and will not agree to Baron Beust’s idea 
of a general representative of the Confederation at the Paris Conferences, because, 
as the third great Power of Germany, she claims to be represented by her own 
Minister. 

Hanover is ready to adopt and maintain, as Saxony is said to be, the 
principle of the five points at the Dict, but only on the condition that Germany 
is represented at the Conferences, ‘This latter point seems a settled project 
aa the smaller States, and as Prussia is not admitted at the Conferences, she 
naturally, to the dissatisfaction of Austria, will place herself at the head of them, 
and if their differences amongst themselves can be removed they may form a 
compact body, and be able yet to render important services to Russia. 

The immediate consequence of Baron de Beust’s mission, Lam sorry to 
observe, has been, for the moment, greatly to increase the influence of Russia in 
Germany, and I must not omit to mention to your Lordship, that he stated to 
one of my colleagues during his stay here, that he had reason to believe that 
France would not object to a representative of the Diet at the Paris Conferences. 
I cannot learn what he considered to be the feeling on the subject at London 
and St. Petersburgh, but one would suppose that, out of gratitude to Germany, 
Russia would be less opposed to the idea now than she was in 1848, when she 
refiised to have an Envoy from the Diet sent to St, Petersburgh ; still, | under: 
stand that Russia would object to the entrance of a German representative on 
principle. 

The visit of the Saxon Minister for Foreign Affairs may have originated in 
a desire to pave the way for more unity between the States of the Confederation, 
and to obtain the adoption by them of the five points ; but the results, as for as 
they at present appear, have been to widen the breach between Austria and 
Prussia, to promote the interests of Russia, and the union between Prussia and 
and her followers. 

Austria stands apparently, at the present moment, alone at Frankfort. She 
wants the aid of Prussia to carry her object in the Dict, and Count Buol has 
again expressed to the Austrian Envoy at this Court, this very day, his great 
and unabated desire to see Prussia at the Paris Conferences, He apparently 
hopes that, if the motion before the Diet is carried, the door muy yet be opened 


oe 


266 


for her admittance ; and he ‘s the more desirous for this, as he is under no 
delusion as to the goodwill of Germany being opposed to Austria, who could not 
expect to be empowered to act at Paris for the interests of Germany. 
T have, &e-. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Inclosure 2 in No, 876. 
Note addressed to the Porte by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


SEVERAL years have passed awity since the execution of a young 
Armenian at Constantinople, who had renounced the Mahometan faith and 
returned to that of Christ, followed shortly afterwards by another similar 
infliction at Broussa, excited the indignation of Europe, and induced the Govern- 
ments of England and France to unite in preventing the repetition of 20 ereat i 
scandal, ‘The Sultan and his Ministers were not deaf to their persevering 
remonstrances. ‘The promise given personally by His Imperial Majesty to the 
Rritish, and also to the French ‘Ambassador, in addition to the official engage- 
ments of the Porte, had every appearance of sufficing to seeure the Christian 
aubjects of the Empire from religious persecution, and, in particular, to abolish 
the barbarous practice of putting seceders to death. 

it cannot, however, be conceded that in practice these diplomatic agret- 
ments between the Porte and its allies, though crowned with the Sultan’s 
promise, have not been attended with results so steady or effectual as the French 
and British Governments were entitled to expect. In two known instances, 
individuals have lately sutfered death by the band of the executioner on account 
of religious considerations. In other cases, imprisonment, ill-treatment, and 
foreed removal to a distance have been employed, either to obtain an unwilling 


1 af 


“aa Pigta PL 
Teen TT Ca 


bs TL VAF... 
Ee om Bie es IS net 


268 


recantation, or to appease the malice of a fanatical populace. Whole families of 
Catholic converts were on one occasion driven from their homes and sent across 
the sea into Asia, under circumstances revolting to humanity, and operating on 
their lives with futal effect, Protestants, though recognized by Imperial firmans, 
and recommended to the local authorities, have been exposed to unmerited 
vexations, while Turkish functionaries, far from protecting them against the 
violence of their Christian persecutors, have themselves but too often connived 
at the work of persecution. 

Surely the time is come when these remnants of an ignorant age should be 
completely and permanently effaced, when the Porte’s enlightened declarations 
should be carried into full effect. Acts which, to speak plainly, are absurdities 
“1 the view of reason, and horrors in that of humanity, can no longer with 
prudence defy the common sense and good fecling of nations united by the 
closest ties. “True policy condemns, and civilization rejects them. A legislative 
system which retains the anomaly is dangerous to those who uphold it. A 
riation, incapable of throwing off the taint, forfeits at length the sympathy of 
others, and finally becomes the victim of its insulated weakness. 

Deeply convinced of these important truths, and anxious to reseue the 
Ottoman Empire from evils generated by neglect of them, a friendly Govern- 
ment, in concert with a powerful and generous ally, appeals once more to that 
wisdom and magnanimity which on critical occasions have rarely been wanting 
to the counsels of the Porte. 

England and France, as every one knows, are making gigantic efforts, and 
submitting to enormous sacrifices, in support of the Sultan’s Empire. ‘Though 
many glorious successes have marked the progress of their arms, they have still 
a wide field of exertion before them, and Providence alone can determine the 
final issue. 

Such are the circumstances under which the Undersigned is instructed by 
his Government to press this subject most earnestly on the attention of the 
Ottoman Porte. He is ordered to observe that the Great European Powers can 
never consent to perpetuate, by the triumphs of their fleets and armies, the 
enforcement in Turkey of a law which is not only a standing insult to them, but 
4 source of crucl persecution to their fellow-Christians. They are entitled to 
demand, and the British Government distinctly demands, that the Mahometan 
who turns Christian shall be as free from every kind of punishment on that 
aecount as the Christian who embraces the Mahometan fnith. It stands to 
reason that, in all such cases, the human conscience being left free, the temporal 
arm must abstain from interfering to coerce its spiritual convictions. 

The Undersigned entertains a firm hope that the Sultan’s Ministers, 
enlightened by experience, and duly attentive to the exigencies of time and 
circumstance, will not only do justice to the motives of this demand, but recog- 
nize the necessity of redressing a grievance which stands in such painful 
contrast with the services rendered to Turkey by Christian Powers. 

It rests with the Porte to determine in what manner this just and indis- 
pensable reform may be most satisfactorily completed, The Undersigned cannot 
for a moment doubé that the Turkish Government, in doing away with the last 
remnaut of sanguinary fanuticism, and clearing its antecedent pledges from every 
shade of uncertainty, will maintain an inviolable protection over all its subjects, 
of whatever creed, who, following the dictates of conscience in religious matters, 
may exercise its rights without secking to disturb the peace of ageless: 

Hitherto the British Government has treated with similar liberality the 
millions of Mussulman population brought under its rule in India, and it would 
deeply lament the necessity of adopting a less generous policy towards them. 

The Porte, unwilling to incur so deep a responsibility, will, doubtless, bear 
in mind that society may be secured against sedition working under religious 
forms, and that religion itself may be secured from reproach. by special enact- 
ments applied with judgment and moderation to cases of open turbulence and 
undisguised blasphemy. Her present and first obligation is to meet the demands 
of her ally with gratitude equal to the ciroumstances which inspire that senti- 
ment, and with wisdom adapted to the political prospects of her Empire, and to 
the welfare of those who profess the Mussulman creed beyond as well as within 
its limits. 

The Undersigned, &c. 

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, Constantinople, Jaminry 28, 1856. 

I CALLED upon the Grand Vizier a few days ago to thank him for the 
willingness he had shown to comply with my wishes respecting the temporary 
disposal of Abbé Hamilton on his arrival here. ‘The visit afforded me an oppor- 
tunity of going once more over two or three points of the question of privileges 
and reforms which I thought susceptible of improvement under the general 
principles jointly recommended by the three HKepresentatives, and formally 
accepted by the Turkish Ministers, 

It is unnecessary to trouble your Lordship with the particulars of our 
conversation. The appointment of some one, among the intended Representatives 
of the Christian communities in the Supreme Council, to correspond with their 
fellow-Christians in the Provinces; the nomination of Deputies from the same 
communities to take part in the management of their affairs in the capital ; the 
aclection of a Christian adviser to be attached to each provincial Governor, 
and a complete recognition of the rights of conscience in religious matters, are 
the leading matters on which I dwelt. 

It was not my fortune to make much apparent impression on Aali Pashu. 
His Highness abounded in objections to each of my suggestions. He did not, 
however, recede from his general declarations in fuvour of reform, or positively 
shut the door against any extension of the accepted principles. Feeling, never- 
theless, the inexpediency—not to say uselessness—of going into a prolonged 
discussion, | intimated an intention to send in the official note which T had 
long prepared on the subject of religious persecutions, and took my leave after 
exchanging a few sentences on less important matters. ;

Sultan either to abrogate the Muzsulman law, or to make any public declaration 
equivalent to its abolition in that respect. The Ministers assure me that they 
are sincerely willing to mech our wishes to the utmost of their power, but they 
entreat our forbearance, and urge that time and the progress of opinion will not 
fail to. consummate the work of humanity. Observing that my Christan 
colleagues were not prepar ‘to go the whole length with me, and ape by 
M. Thouvenel of his Inst unfavourable instruction from Count Walewski, I found 
myself under the necessity of either modifying my demand, or delaying 
indefinitely the completion of the fourth point, I preferred the former course, 
as being the least inconvenient, and likely im the end to be attended with the 
smallest sacrifice, 1 therefore accepted the Porte’s version of the clause relating 
to religious liberty, slightly amended, with the reserve of obtaining @ separate 
anawer to my official note on that subject, which should incorporate the version 
previously adopted and amended by the three Representives. Both these 
versions are inclosed herewith for your Lordship’s information, the former 
marked A, the latter B. iN CS, 

With respect to the possession of land by foreigners, the Porte is unwilling 
to make so great a concession Without some security against the interference of 
foreign protection in virtue of the Capitulations. Objections on this ground 
could only be met with friendly assurances and earnest exhortations, The 
Sultan's Ministers were reminde that on the question of land, us on that of 
religion, the establishment of a cordial sympathy between Turkey and Christen- 
dom was the main object in view, and that they would best consult their 
Sovereign's glory and the welfare of the Empire by declaring the principle at 
once with becoming frankness, and leaving such guards and securities as might 
be required for a friendly and honourable arrangement hereafter between the 
respective Powers, 

" Our conference broke up at a late hour, with a mutual understanding that 
the Grand Vizier and Fuad } ha would support the propositions, a3 mo ified, 
in discussion with their colleagues, and that a final decision should be taken 
and deciared with the least practicable delay.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarencdon.—(Received February 12.) 
(No, 229.) 


My Lord, Paris, February 9, 1856. 

2 I SPOKE this afternoon to Count Walewski, as instructed by your Lord- 
ship’s despatch No, 215 of yesterday's date, respecting M. de Beust’s proposition 
for the admission of the Germanic Confederation to take part in the negotiations 
for peace; and 1 expressed the hope that this proposition would meet with no 
encouragement from the French Government, 

Count Walewski’s reply was more evasive than positive. He said that, as 
the proposition had found no support any where, it was useless pronouncing an 
opinion upon it. 

I was not surprised at the answer; for in some of the conversations which 
T have lately had the honour to hold with the Emperor, I have found His Majesty 
more or less imbued with an idea that it would be possible, by admitting the 
smaller States of Germany to take part in the Conferences, to raise up a third 
Power in Germany, which, supported by France and England, would be able to 
hold Austria and Prussia in check. 1 have observed to His Majesty, in the first 
place, that M. de Beust’s proposition, as I understood it, was, that the Confede- 
ration should be admitted to take part in the Conferences. But the Confederation 
included both Austria and Prussia; and the scheme, therefore, if it succeeded, 
would net bring about, as the Emperor supposed, a schism among the German 
Powers, but, on the contrary, a greater ap ironimation. | 

But, in the second place, I said that { had lived long enough in Germany to 
be assured of what would happen, were this idea of the third party to be sincerely 
entertained. Austria and Prussia would forget their rivalry, for the moment, 
for the purpose of conjointly crushing a rising Power which might beeome 
formidable to them: and it would eventually be found that, instead of diminish- 
ing the influence of these two, the allies had aided to consolidate it, unless, 
noes: they were prepared to go to war to support the cause of the secondary 

_ Thirdly, I observed that, as yet, the secondary States had done nothing to 
entitle the Western Powers to hope that, even if they obtained greater power 
that power would be exerted against Russia, ; 

The policy of the smaller German Powers, I added, never varied. They 
would never allow one of the greater German Powers to obtain such an 
ascendancy over the other as would endanger their own security ; and unless 
France was desirous of strengthening Germany, she had better leave the States 
to their interminable jealousies and discords. 

The Emperor appeared to listen with much interest and attention to what | 
told him, and, at all events, to be convineed that the scheme of raising a third 
Power in Germany was not likely to succeed at present. 

I have, &c, 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 12.) 


(No, 280,) 


My Lord, | Paris, February 9, 1856. 

WITHOUT in any way quoting Lord Bloomfield, | have, as divected by 
your Lordship's despatch No. 212 of yesterday's date, informed Count Walewski 
of the language held by the French Minister at Berlin, with regard to admitting 
Prussia to the Peace Conferences. 

T had previously, on more than one occasion, spoken to Count Walewski 
respecting the rumours which had reached me, in regard to the language of the 
French Diplomatic Agents in Germany, and the manner in which they attributed 
to English councils the refusal to admit Prussin to the said Conferences. 


274 


Count Walewski said that he had this morning had a long conversation 
with M. de Moustier, and that that Minister had, in the most unqualified 
manner, denied ever having given the Prussian Government the slightest reason 
to suppose that any difference of opinion existed between the two Governments 
in regard to this matter. On my mentioning what M. de Moustier was reported 
to have said, on taking leave of Baron Mantenffel before leaving Berlin, Count 
Walewski said that M. de Moustier had represented his own language in a very 
different light. He had merely said to M. de Manteuffel that Prussia wished to 
enter into the Conferences, and yet would not furnish him with a single 
argument of which he could make use at Paris. | 

As a proof of his own <entiments, Count Walewski added that he had 
yesterday received letters from two of the French Ministers in Germany (he 
would not name them, he said) who neserted that a general opinion prevailed 
that France was well disposed towards Prussia and England the contrary, an 
that he had not lost a moment in replying that there was no difference of 
opinion between the French and English Governments.

The Earl of Clarendon to Mr. Howard. 
(No. 1.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, February 12, 1856. 


HER Majesty's Government approve the language held by Lord Cowley to 

Count Walewski, as reported in his Excellency’s despateh No. 204 of the 5th 
instant, on communicating to Count Walewski the substance of what passed at 
my interview with Count Colloredo on the subject of the admission of Prussia to 
take a part in the Conferences to be held at Paris for the reestablishment of 
peace, 
The arguments used by the Governments of Austria and Prussia that the 
latter Power ought to be admitted nto the Couferences, because the proposed 
Treaty will modify the Treaty of 1841, has no force; for the only modification of 
the Treaty of 1841 which is pro sosed to be made, consists in the admission of 
two small vessels, of each of the ontracting Parties not having territories on the 
Black Sea, to lie off the mouths of the Danube, to watch the freedom of 
navigation of that river. The great principle of the Treaty of 1841, namely, the 
shutting of the Straits to ships of war of all nations while the Porte is at peace, 
is maintained. 

The Treaty of 1841 allowed of exceptions for light vessels with despatches, 
or in the service of Embassies and Missions at Constantinople, and the same 
principle includes light vessels for the mouths of the Danube.

(Signed) CLARENDON.

Les questions i régler par la Commission dont nous avons parlé regardent ; 

l. Liétat social du pays. 

2, L'organisation de Vassemblée ou Divan. 

4. L'administration, les tribunaux, et les finances. 

4, Les rapports de l'Eglise avee |’Etat. 

Il est important que sur tous ces points, la legislation du pays soit mise en 
lharmonie avec sa nouvelle condition politique. 

1, L'état social des Principautés réclame impeérieusement de sérieuses 
réformes. Ces réformes doivent avoir pour objet de faire disparaitre le principe 
en vertu duquel la noblesse est attachée aux fonctions publiques, véritable source 
de la corruption que l'on reproche aux deux Provinces; de supprimer la franchise 
dont jouissent les propriétés nobles en matiére d’impdts, au détriment des revenus 
publics; enfin, de constituer la propriété des paysans, aujourd'hui encore 
organisée sur la base de la sujétion et grevée de telles obligations arbitrairement 
établies, qu’aucun progrés matériel n'est possible s'il n'y est d'abord rémédié, 

2. Létat social du pays ayant une base plus équitable, il sera plus facile de 
déterminer les principes de la loi destinée & former Vassemblée ou le Divan. 
Cette loi devra tenir compte des intéréts de la grande et de la petite propricté, 
de ceux de l'industrie, des Geoles et de léglise. 

4. L'administration devra (tre organisée de manitre a faire prévaloir sur 
tous les points laction du Pouvoir Central, en laissant cependant aux Municipa- 
lités et Ades Conseils de District qui remplaceraient les Assemblées actuelles de 
Département, une juste part dans les affaires locales et départementales. 

Liorganisation tes tribunaux sera révisée, et l'on s’attachera, dans les 
réformes que pourra exiger l'état de la magistrature, 4 lui assurer plus de moralité 
et dindépendance. 

Quant au systéme financier, il aura 4 subir des modifications profondes, par 
suite méme de l'assimilation de toutes les terres relativement 4 Vimpét; la capita- 
tion pourra étre supprimdée et transformée ; les monopoles établis au profit des 
crands propriétaires seront abolis, Les biens des monastéres nationaux seront 
taxés comme les propriétés laiques; il y aura lieu d’examiner si ceux des 
monastéres dédiés, et dont les revenus considérables passent aux couvents du 
Mont Athos et de la Palestine, ne doivent pas étre réunis aux domaines de 
l’Etat; selon le voeu du pays. 

4. Les rapports de PEclise avec \'Etat pourront également étre lobjet de 
Vattention de la Commission. 

Dans toutes les mesures qui concerneront |"Eglse Moldo-Valaque il y aura 
lieu de prendre en considdration sa tendauce & le soustraire  V'action directe du 

Jatriarchat Gree de Constantinople. En confiant au Prince l'élection du 
Métropolitain, qui appartient aujourd'hui, ainsi que celle des Evéques, aux grands 
Boyards, on supprimera une source d’intrigues, ct dans le cas ot I'Mglise Imirait

Quant a la Servic, sa position vis-4-vis de la Porte et de l'Europe ne réclame 
point les mémes modifications que celle des deux autres Principautés. Les” 
Plénipotentiaires n’auront done qu’A déclarer que les rapports actuels de cette

que comporte son administration intérieure sera confié & la Commission des 
Représentants des Puissances et de la Porte, dans le sein de laquelle les deux 
membres Moldo-Valaques seront remplacés par un députe Serbe, La tache

et du Prince, dé maniére d faire ceaser les conflits qui sont devenus perinanents

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Brigadier-General Mansfield. 


Dear Sir, British Embassy, January 27, 1856. 


YOUR last communications with the Seraskier, compared Witu my own, 
and a review of the various points which firmed the subject matter of your 
conversation this evening, taken in connection with recent advices rom Brze- 
room, increase my anxiety to press forward every preparatory measure pearing 
on the prospects of another campaign, and at all accessible to the influence o 
this Embassy. 

Whatever may be the result of the late diplomatic oecurrences at Vienna 
and St. Petersburgh, it stands to reason that no relaxation can, with common 
prudence, be allowed to take place in our endeavours to prepare for the eee: 
ance of the war. Such, | am persuaded, is the feeling in England, and Iam 
gratified to observe that the Turkish Ministers are not backward im making @ 
similar profession, But more than profession is wanting. — Time is on the wing, 
and our Mussulman allies have need of every stimulant to overcome their natural 
reluctance to take time by the forelock. 

lt is therefore my carnest wish, fully, I know, partaken by yourself, that 
you should repeat and keep up on my behalf your personal communications 
with Fuad Pasha and the Seraskier, not omitting the Grand Vizier when neces- 
sary. 
! The points of most urgent interest are those which have been pressed 
repeatedly on their attention :— ie . 

Be The provisioning of Erzeroom and its increasing army. or 

2. The preparing and forwarding, as weather and circumstances admit, the 
additional poles of all kinds, including ene and ammunition, required 
either for defence or future operations in the field, 

3. The recall, without further delay, of Selim Pasha, and the departure of 
a trustworthy General to supply lis place. 

4. The are of further measures for restoring order among the troops 
at Erzeroom, ae 

j 5. ‘The return of ‘Tahir Pasha to that place, and a diminution of the number 
of useless Pashas already there. © ee nN ‘ 

It may be presumed that the Porte is waiting for a definitive answer from 
Omer Pasha; but whatever the Generalissimo’s decision may hes to taking 
the command at Erzeroom, no time should be lost in making a provisional 
arrangement, and correcting those recognised abuses which retard the progress 
of improvement. 

‘ou are aware that Ismail Pasha still retains the nominal appointment 
of Commander-in-chief on the side of Mrzeroom, and that the preference is 
justified by his general reputation. He ought, I eonceive, to be sent to the 
scene of hig intended command without further delay, or, if he cannot go, it is 
evident that the most efficient General at the Porte’s disposal should’ be sent in 
his stead, | 

The Contingent is another object of deep interest with reference to the 
eventualities of an approaching campaign. [t 1s long since L gave instructions 
to apply for ground on which to establish ita dept, and the question of its 
recruitment has been for a still longer period before the Porte ant the Seraskier. 
Difficulties of real force exist,no doubt, in this respect; but I trust that they 
will be made to yield to the necessities of the case. t he first experiment ol 
Christian conseription might be made in favour of the Contingent; and ordinary 
casuulties may, | presume, be provided for by supplying it with recruits from the 
annual amount of conscripts for the Nizam. ; : 

I take this occasion to record your own suggestion as to the expediency ot

I have thought of what you said about a medal for Kars. ‘The army and 
garrison of that unfortunate place are worthy of every distinction; but it is 
worth considering whether a medal could be struck with prone for the 
defence of a fortress taken by the enemy; and whether the Sebastopol medal 
could be extended to those who were not concerned in the reduetion of that 
fortress. If anything were to be done, it should rather refer to the splendid 
repulse which the Russians underwent on the 29th of September. 

I approve entirely of your suggestion that Major Cathcart should be 
employed in examining the positions and communications, including that by 
the Choorooksoo, from Batoom to Artvin, and thenee in the direction of 
Erzeroom. As the interpreter selected to accompany him turns out to be unfit

undertaken with the least practicable delay. 

[ am under an impression that we must wait to hear from General Shirley 
before anything further can be done with respeet to offences committed by 
Irregular Cavalry in Her Majesty's pay. 

I should like to obtain some clearer information as to the result, efficiency, 
and position of the Egyptian troops sent on from Trebizond.

Inclosure 2 in No 393, 
Brigadier-General Manajield to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Pera, January 29, 1856. 

I HAVE the honour to inform your Excellency that I yesterday paid u 
long visit to Fuad Pasha, and urged the several subjects referred to in your 
Exeellency’s instructions, dated January 27. 1 found his Excellency disposed 
to take the part of Selim Pasha, while he declared, however, that his final 
removal was a thing decided on; but as yet without an answerfrom Omer Pasha, 
and no communication having been received from Dervish Pasha, the Govern- 
ment had not been able to nominate his successor. 

Dervish Pasha had received orders to inquire whether Omer Pasha’s amy 
was required hy the allies for an invasion of Georgia, or if it could be directed 
altowether to the defence of Erzeroom. 

If the former should be the intention, it would be useless to move the army, 
&e., for the purpose of bringing it back hereafter. 

Such plausible excuses can hardly be accepted as sufficient for the satis- 
faction of your Excellency, and | impressed on Fuad Pasha, by every argument 
in my power, that something definite regarding Selim Pasha is required by your 
Excellency, for communication to Her Majesty’s Government, 

His Excellency said he would certainly bring the subject before the Council 
at its first meeting. 

I then desired that the attention of the Government should be turned 
seriously to the road between Trebizond and Erzeroom. 

His Excellency admitted all that was said in its disfavour; that 50,000 
packages of all sorts of military stores were now waiting at Trebizond, &e., &e. ; 
that its repairs formed part of their plans; but I could not discover that any 
positive directions had been given, or that his Excellency is more impressed with 
the absolute necessity of improving the communications than his less enlightened 
countrymen. 

For what passed relative to Tahir Pasha, 1 would beg to refer your 
Excellency to my memorandum on Mr. Brant's despatches, 

On the important question of the enlistment of Christians to serve in the 
ranks of the army, I found his Execllency absolutely recoil from any favourable 
answer. 

Admitting, as he cannot avoid, the wants of the Turkish population ; fully 
alive to the circumstances through which the Christians at present evade both

No, 398. 


Sir Hamilton Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 17.) 
(No. 120. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, February 10, 1656, 

IT has been with some satisfaction that | have learned that the unfriendly 
feelings of the Court of St. Petersburgh towards that of Vienna have been 
manifested by the Emperor of Russia having allowed several weeks to pass 
before he noticed Count Esterhazy’s demand for an audience. 

The Portuguese Minister, who arrived at St. Petersburgh twenty days later 
than the Austrian Envoy, was received some days sooner than his colleague, 
whose reception took place, I believe, only on the 6th instant. 

This sort of slight, which is deeply felt by a Court which weighs every 
diplomatic movement and form as scrupulously as that of Vienna, is, no doubt, 
the prelude to many others of the same description; and the effect of such 
demonstrations can hardly fail of being that of keeping up estrangement, and of 
disposing Austria to feel that the countenance a goodwill of England is the 
more necessary to her, 

[say England, and not the Western Powers, because as regards the inti- 
macy between France and Austria, it is already at least as close as can he 
suitable for general interests. 

The whole attitude of Austria shows her to have grown into an espalier 
Power, which feels the necessity of looking in one direction or another for 
support. 1 do what lies in my power to convince Count Buol and any of the 
other Ministers with whom I have the opportunity of conversing, that the 
strength of Russia, always over-estimated, has been so impaired that peace is 
absolutely essential to her; and that it depends solely upon the unity and con- 
fident bearing of the allies whether that peace shall be near at hand, and of 
a nature to provide for years to come against any danger which may approach 
Europe from the north: and I lose no occasion for showing that, aiter the 
exertions made by France and England, the demands made under the fifth 
Article should be considered even by Russia as evidences of their extreme mode- 
ration. It is possible that they would have been so regarded if Russia had been 
led to expect that a heavy pecuniary indemnity, as well as a territorial cession, 
was to be wrung from her, 

However this py be, ] make no secret of its being my conviction that 
should Russia now allow peace to slip through her hands she will have to 
purchase it later on more severe terms than those now within her reach, 

L have been assured in strict confidence that my professed opinions are 
borne out by those expressed in intimacy by the Minister of Wurtemberz, who, 
although representing a Court completely devoted to Russian interests, has been 
heard to admit the necessity felt by Russia for concluding the war, 

My colleague of Stuttgardt, if his words have been correctly reported to me, 
stated that he believed Russia to be better prepared to make fresh financial 
efforts than she was commonly held to be ; that he believed that she was capable 
even of taking the field again in a creditable manner; but that there was too 
much reason to fear that a third campaign would leave her in such a state of 
prostration as would disqualify her from concluding any but a very disastrous 

G. 
ee I understand likewise that the Wurtemberg Minister is one of those persons 
who has reason to believe that the supply of saltpetre is running shite in 
Russia, Here then is a fresh reason, were any requisite, for adhering to the 
intention of Her Majesty's Government of not suspending blockades during the 
progress of negotiation, 

LT will not conclude my despatch without remarking, as [ have alluded to 
Stuttzardt, that I have some reason for suspecting that that capital is again 
made the channel for private communications between the Winter Patace and the 
Tuileries. 1 can offer no proof of what I feel obliged to hint at, but T have 
grounds for supposing that persons who have already been eniployed in this 
service have lately been made use of for carrying any friendly messages from 
St. Petersburgh to Paris. T have, Se. 

(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No. 401. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetred February 17.) 
(No. 83.) 


My Lord, Berlin, Februery 16, 1856. 

YOUR Lordship will doubtless have already been informed by Her 
Majesty’s Minister at Frankfort, of the result of the late Austrian commu- 

nication to the Dict, and of the obstacles raised by M. de Bismark, the Prussian 
Minister, to a satisfactory reply being prepared by the Commission. | under- 
stand that the sense of the resolution 1s as follows: 

_ The Confederation thanks Austria for her efforts in the work of peace; 
declares that she will adhere to the four points, and maintain them; and that 
she will associate herself to the fifth point when she has examined its details. 

Two days ago intelligence was received here from Frankfort, that M. de 
Bismark had declined agreeing to the resolution, as proposed, without fresh 
instructions from Berlin, ‘This was evidently done for the purpose of gaining 
time, and seeing whether it would not be possible to create further embarrass- 
ments, for lam assured that the Representatives of the smaller States were 
agreed, and that even M. de Bismark was in possession of the necessary 
instructions to subscribe to the proposition. 

On the arrival of his report here, more precise orders were transmitted to 
Frankfort, and unless some fresh difficulties are created by the Prussian 
Minister this week, an insignificant resolution will have passed. 

In this proeceding your Lordship will find a further proof, if any is wanting, 
of the spirit of bitter opposition with which this Representative of Prussia is always 
animated, and his readiness to arrest the progress of any measure which may 
have a tendency to compromise the relations of Germany with Russia, 

M. de Bismark on this, as on other occasions, acts frequently without, and 
sometimes contrary to his instructions; his chject is to create and maintain 
disunion in Germany, and to place Prussia and the smaller States on one side, 
and Austria on the other, whilst his unceasing desire is to isolate the latter 
country. 

What has just occurred at Frankfort may be considered another Prussian 
triumph, and will probably be hailed with a certain degree of satisfaction at 
St. Petersburgh, because it will furnish Austria with a ready excuse for holding back 
from the Western Powers at the approaching Conferences. She still clings to 
the desire that Prussia should be admitted to these Conferences, and Count Buol 
gave this assurance to Count Georges Esterhazy, the Austrian Minister at this 


Court, who went to see his Excellency on his passage three days ago through 
Dresden. 


I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

The Karl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 
(No. 195.) 
My Lord, 


Foreign Office, February 18, 1856. 

WITH reference to the question of religious persecutions in Turkey, and 
the efforts which your Excellency, a5 stated in your despatch No, 100 af the 
asth of January, very properly continues to make to effect the abolition of the 
punishment of death as applied to apostates from Islamism, I have to state to 
your Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government are of opinion that it might be 
strongly represented to the Porte that, as the Turkish Empire is by treaty 
stipulations to be declared part and parcel of the European system, it is quite 
impossible for the Powers of Europe ta acquiesce in the continuance in Turkey 
of a law and @ practice which is a standing insult to every other nation in Burope. 
if Turkey is to gain the great and important advantage of being deemed part of 
the European family of nations, she must by necessity adapt her laws and 
practices so as 10 make them compatible with her association with the 
community of States into which she desires to be admitted. 


Tam, sc. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 20.) 
(No, 158.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, February 11, 1866. 

I AM unable to write as fully to your Lordship to-day as I had wished, 
being obliged to attend at a conference appointed to take place this morning at 
the Grand Vizier's house, previous to his Highness’ departure for Paris to-morrow. 

[ have, however, the honour to inclose, for your Lordship’s information, 
copy of a paper containing certain Articles agreed upon yesterday by M. Thouvenel, 
Baron Prokesch, and myself, with respect to the first point. ‘This paper was 
communicated yesterday to the Turkish Ministers, and we shall, I hope, be able 
to obtain their acceptance of it to-day, though probably not without some 
modifications. . 


[reserve all necessary remarks and explanations for the next opportunity, 
which I hope will occur to-morrow, 


The firman respecting the rights and privileges of the non-Mussulman 
subjects of the Porte, will be forwarded to your Lordship by the next opportu- 
nity. It has received the Sultan's sanction, and there is every reason to expect 
that it will be promulgated with due solemnity in two or three days. It is a 
mere translation of the Articles neces upon, with an addition suggested by me, 
as to the encouragement of agriculture and trade, and the employment of foreign 
capital and industry. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 415. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—{Recewed at Paris, February 24.) 
(No, 90. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Borlin, February 20, 1856. 

WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatches Nos. 59 and 65 of the 
12th instant, inclosing copies of despatches from Her Majesty's Ambassador at 
Paris, respecting the language which I reported M. de Moustier to have held to 
Baron Manteuffel a fortnight ago, and which had given rise to a conversation 
between Lord Cowley and Count Walewski, resulting in the declaration by the 
latter that there was no difference of opinion between the French and English 
Governments on the question of the admission of P ussia to the Conferences, | 
have now the honour to inform your Lordship that I have conversed on this 
affair with M. de Moustier, since his return from Paris. His language pourtrayed 
the strongest desire that a complete understanding should exist between our 
two Governments at the approaching Conferences; and on my alluding to the 
question of the admission of Prussia, he informed me that Count Walewski had 
told him, when taking leave, that he was most anxious for your Lordship’s 
arrival at Paris, in order to discuss the whole bearing of the question with you, 
and see whether something might not be done to facilitate an arrangement with 
Prussia; but that he looked upon the matter as one of minor importance, and 
on which no trifling difference of opinion that might exist would have the least 
influence on the cordial understanding which it was so essential to maintain 
between the two Governments on the great points which were soon to he 
discussed at Paris. 

M. de Moustier added that he should probably hear something on_ this 
matter by his next messenger, but this messenger, who has just arrived, has 
brought nothing, 

Your Lordship will perceive from the foregoing, that although the French 
Government refused to acknowledge the existence of any difference of opinion 
with Her Majesty's Government, there is still a strong tendency to listen to the 
counsels of Austria, and the arguments which Count Bual has been lately 
pressing on the consideration of the Cabinet of the Tuilleries. This was 
evident from the conduct and language of the Marquis de Moustir before his 
journey to Paris; and to judge from what he haz confidentially said to me since 
his return, 1 am but strengthened in the opinion that the French Government is 
much more favourable to the admission of Prussia to the Conferences than that 
of Her Majesty. At the same time I cannot speak too highly of the personal 
desire of my French colleague to act with ine, but itis not to be denied that his 
impression as to the opinions of Count Walewski on this matter are far less 
decided than those which I have received from your Lordship’s despatches. 

I shall naturally be most: careful to avoid anything like the appearance of 
the existence of a difference of opinion between our Governments on this or any 
other point connected with the Fastern question, for nothing would at this 
moment be hailed with so much satisfaction by our enemies as a marked difference 


in the appreciation by England and lrance of any of the important occurrences 
of the day. 


Lhave, ke. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No. 416, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 24.) 
(No. 92.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 20, 1856. 


__ LHAVE had the honour to receive your Lordship’s despatch No, 66 of the 
12th instant, in reply to one which I had addressed to you respecting the state 


of feeling in Germany with regard to the claim of the smaller States to take part 
in the negotiations for peace, 


: 
C 
0 
c 
e 
F 

f 


S06 


The language which I held here on this subject before the arrival of your 
Lordship's despatch has been, that as Germany had all along declined taking any 
active part in the war, and had pursued a policy which only caused embarrass- 
ment to the Western Pawers, | could not see what argument she could possibly 
put forward in support of the claim to pee at the Paris Conferences, 
where no Powers would be represented but belligerents, and Austria, whose 
policy at all events bespoke an approach towards ours, and who: had exposed 
herself to the risks of war if Russia had rejected the five pots. 

Prussia’s pretension to assist at the Conferences is not bused on her desire 
to become the protector of Gerinin ‘nterests; but on her being one of the Great. 
Powers, and on her right as such to be represented at the approaching revision of 
Treaties to which she is a party, and more especially of that of 1541 respecting the 
Dardanelles. She pretends also that her bemg # party ton future Treaty would 
render it a greater security for Europe. | 

‘The claim of the smaller States to be represented at the Paris Conferences 
appears to have had only au ephemeral existence ; 1b was produced by Baron de 
Beust, and ceased almost with his dey arture from Berlin, except in the minds of 
a few of the * exalted,” who are always planning to make Germany more active, 
and give her the rights of a great Power. 

The only argument which the smaller States can possibly bring. forward im 
support of the idea of a special Representative ol the Diet 15 to be found in the 
490th Article of the Final Act of Vienna, 1620, wherein it is stated ‘* hit when 
there uriscs & question of a negotiation for peace, or an armistice, the Diet will 
appoimt a special Committee to consider the question, the Diet will name at the 
aame time Plenipotentianes to conduct the negotiation, &c. 5 but this argument 
‘< not tenable fora moment, as the smaller States seem to forget that they have 
not been bellizerents, and that Germany, not having been involved in war, can 
have no claim to be represented at Paris. ‘There have. 1 believe, been only two 
oceasions on which the Diet has heen represented abroad; the one was at the 
London Conferences on the Hollando-Belgian question, and for the express 
purpose of discussing an exchange of territory, and the annexation of Luxembourg 
fo the Confederation. ‘The second was when a special Envoy of the Dict was 
sent to London during the Revolution of 1848. ‘The subject, however, has now 
lost all immediate interest, the hopelessness of the attempt meeting with success 
has been demonstrated, and the question will now be allowed to rest and wait for 
better days, : 

LT have, &¢. 
(Signed) BLOOMVIELD. 


No. 47. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clorendon.—(Receired al Paris, February 24. 


(No. 96.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 22, 1856. 
NOTHING has transpired respecting any communications which may have 
been made by Count Orloff to the King of Prussia or his Government, during 
the two days which he passed a Berlin, He is described to me as having been 
generally reserved as to the mission with which he is charged, and by no means 
expansive towards this Governinent in expressions of goodwill or acknowledg- 
ments for the services which they have rendered to Russia during the war. 
Baron Manteutffel, whom 1 haye seen this evening, told me that Count Orloff 
would have much preferred wot to. have been employed on this service; that he 
declined the first proposal ou the subject which had been made to him by 
Count Nesselrode, but that le was unable to refuse the Emperor. In reply to 
my inquiry as to the opinions which Count Orloff had Canad as to the 
approaching negotiations, and as to any diffeulties which he foresaw as likely to 
impede them, Garon Manteutlel suid that he had not alluded to any that were 
likely to be serious, except in the question of the rectification ot the Asiatic 
frontier, and that he had declared that Russia would refuse any cession ot 
territory in that quarter ; that he had conversed with him about Kars, and that 


307 


he seemed to attach great value and importance to that district, but did not 
say what were the intentions of Russia respecting It. 

His Excellency said, that shortly before Count Orloif left St. Petersburgh, 
the Emperor had received a letter from Schamyl, containing assurances that he 
would continue to remain quiet, and not to molest the Imperial troops, and 
thanks for the kindness which had been shown to his son, ah your Lordship 
‘s aware. was educated in one of the cadet corps at St. Petersburgh, On the 
whole, Baron Manteuffel did not seem to me to be much gratified by what he 
had heard from Count Orloff, or to be impressed with the idea that Russia 
would be found as well-disposed to meet all the demands of the allies as he 
could have wished. I asked if he was aware whether Russia would make 
difficulties about the Aland Islands. He said that he heheved not, neither about 
the question of Consuls in the ports of the Black Sea; and that he had no 
reason to suppose that there would be any serious ones raised, except, as he had 
already told me, on the question of the Asiatic frontier. 

Baron Manteuffel spoke in nearly the same tone to the Marquis de Moustier 
last night, and that Minister has already sent off a report on the subject to 
Count Walewski. His Excellency appears to have said further to my French 
colleague, that Count Orloff wished Prussia to remain in her present attitude; 
and had observed that if peace did not result from the Paris Conferences, Russia 
could, without difficulty, go on for three years longer with the war, that her 
porersineney was not depreciated ; and that, although the commerce of St, Peters- 

urgh was sadly crippled, that of the interior was flourishing ; that Russia was

No. 418. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 24.) 
(No. 160.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 11, 1856. 

EVERY practicable exertion has been made by me and my colleagues to 
bring the preparatory arrangement of the first and fourth points, as they ane 
called, of the impending negotiation to a close before the departure of Aali Pasha 
for Paris. We have succeeded with respect to the latter, and I entertain a 
sanguine hope of being able to complete the former also in time, though we have 
now only twenty-four hours at our disposal for the purpose. Our difficulties 
have been greatly inereased by the want of instructions bearing on the particulars, 
or even on the principles, to which it is desirable that our proceedings should be 
adapted in providing for the future condition of Wallachia and Moldavia. 
The field is wide, and offers many difficult and entangled questions for 
consideration, 7 

Your Lordship is aware that there are, chiefly, two principles, either of 
which presents a clear point to set out from, though in different directions One 
is that of a material, the other of a moral, barrier against foreign encroachment. 
Could a strong frontier line be obtained against Russia, such, for instance, as the 
course of the Dniester, with its long-established fortresses, 1t might be well 
worth while to unite the two Provinces under a single Government; to give to 
its Administration a vigorous and decisive character; to place a foreign Prince 
at its head: and to entrust him with the command of sufficient forces for the 
defence of the frontier. More than one Power might object to so determined an 
arrangement, but the real European interest attached to it would probably 
overrule the objections, as well at Constantinople as elsewhere. 

The idea of a moral barrier, without exeluding the employment of military 
means for defence, addresses itself more particularly to the social and adninis- 
trative condition of the Principalitics, and to the wellare of the inhabitants at 
large as resulting from that condition. In the supposed case the institutions of 
the country should be such as to content all classes of the population, and their 
contentment would naturally operate xs a bond of union, confidence and goodwill 
between the Porte and her yrateful epene ne 

4 


308 


_ If I may be allowed, in the absence of instructions, to express @ personal 
opinion, I confess that the adoption of the former principle would have been 
preferable in my judgment but, under the circumstances, it would have been 
‘useless for me to take my stand on that ground, and the only result of such an 
experiment would have been the failure of our endeavours to send a basis of 
arrangement to Paris before the commencement of the negotiations. 

I felt myself, therefore, compelled to abandon the course which I should 
have preferred, and to jon simply with my colleagues and the Sultan's Ministers 
in patting forward such principles and institutional forms for each Principality 
as might hereafter secure the welfare of its inhabitants, and bind them both more 
closely to the Sultan's Empire. 

The result of our discussions, as between the three Representatives, has 
been already transmitted to your Lordship. It remains for us to obtain the 
assent of the Turkish Ministers, and to combine our ideas with theirs on the 
subject of Servia. 

Your Lordship will observe that the proposition relating to Moldavia and 
Wallachia sets aside the Organic Statutes, and grounds the future institutions 
of the two countries on a modified confirmation of their ancient privileges. It 
has the salutary effect of substituting the Sultan’s charter for Russian dictation, 
and of being on that account more acceptable to the Principalitics. In the 
remaining Articles we have endeavoured to combine @ proper dependence of the 
Principalities on the Porte, with securities for the maintenance of their privileges, 
for the administration of justice, for the abolition of abuses, for placing all 
classes of the population on an equal footing, and, finally, for investing the 
Prince with a suitable amount of authority, 

With respect to the defences of the country, and a Legislature founded on 
national representation, I had not the good fortune to take the same view 08 my 
colleagues of France and Austria, On the former pomt it was my wish to 
define the Sultan’s right of sending an arny ‘nto the Principalities for the 
defence of the frontier, or erecting fortresses on their territory, in such manner 
as to guard, in their ‘nterest, agaist abuse without crippling the action of the 
Sovereign in cases of real necessity. On the second, I was desirous of obtaining 
a Representative body, capable of exercising t wholesome control over the 
Executive without opening too much room for popular excitement. 

Inclosed herewith are the conflicting paragraphs, which appeared respec- 
tively in my draft of the propositions, and im that presented by M, Thouvenel, 
and supported by Baron Prokesch, A mutual wish to agree, and want of time 
for prolcnged discussion, induced us to adopt the version as it now stands in the 
series of numbered articles. 

On the whole, my Lord, I trust that, although my position was in almost 
every case of disagreement that of a minority, our work, however imperfect, will 
be found sufficient for the main object immediately in view. 

L have, &e. 
(Signed) SPRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe ta the Earl of Clorendon.—(Received at Parts, 
February 24.) 
(So. 169. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 12, 1856, 

1 CALLED on Aali Pasha at his house this morning, before he proceeded 
to embark for Marseilles in the French steam-frigate placed at his disposal by 
M. 'Thouvenel. He had just returned from taking the Sultan’s last commands, 
Our conversation was naturally brief. I tried to discover in what spirit he was 
likely to act in any case of difference between England and Franee respecting 
the terms of peace, 1 infer from his language, which was, however, guarded, 
that he is inclined to view any eventual demand maintained by England as 
favourable to the Porte’s interests, and he requested me to state that your 
Lordship will find him disposed to be useful. | encouraged this sentiment, by 
assuring him that he would be treated, 1 felt certain, with confidence by the 
British nezotiators. His personal cast of thought is for peace, and I am well 
convinced that in this respect he enjoys the Sultan's sympathy ; but I have 
heard nothing to warrant a belief that he ts for peace at any price. The spirit 
of his administration ig at the same time French, and I consider him a main 
clement of M. Thouvenel’s one-sided influence, and also the chief instrument of 
Reshid Pasha’s exclusion from power. In cases where no difference of opinion 
exists between England and France, the Porte’s Representative is very unlikely 
to have instructions empowering him to resist. In reply to my inquiry whether 
any points connected with the Principalities would be subjected to fresh discus: 
sions by him at Varis, he gave me to understand that no such instruction existed. 

We talked over some other matters of separate interest, which will be 
reported to your Lordship elsewhere. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received at Parts, 
February 240 | 
(No. 170.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 12, 1856. 

| HAVE received from Fuad Pasha the note which he had promised in 
reply to my representations and demands on the subject of religious opinions, 
and the eapUty of renegades, Inclosed herewith is an English translation of it, 
made by Mr. Smythe, who assures me that its correctness may be perfectly relied on. 
Your Lordship will perceive that the Porte acknowledges and confirms its former 
declaration respecting renegades, and extends it expressly to all, including 
Mussulmans, though not mentioned by name. It is an official note signed by 
the Secretary of State, and given expressly with the Sultan’s sanction. ‘Taken 
‘1 connection with the Article recommended by the three Representatives, 
adopted by the Porte, and inserted in the Sultan’s firman, invested with a hatti- 
sherif, it may be viewed as covering the whole of your Lordship's requisition. 
[f this impression of mine should not be confirmed by Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, the door is open for a return to the question; but if no one is to be 
molested on account of the religion he professes, and no one to be punished as 
au renceade, whatever form of faith he denies, I do not see what room there ean 
jossibly be for any practical persecutions in future within the limits of the 

ultan’s Empire. 

The law of the Koran is not abolished, it is true, respecting renegades, 
and the Sultan's Ministers affirm that such a stretch of authority would exceed 
even His Majesty’s legal power. But, however that may be, the practical 
application of it is renounced by means of a public document, and Her Majesty's 


a26 


Government would at any time be justified in complaining of a breach of engage - 


ment if the Porte were to authorize or to permit any exeeption to its own official 


declaration.

Fuad Pasha to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
( 'ranslation.) February 12, 1856. 


THE. official communications made formerly and recently by your Excel- 
lency, both in writing and verbally, upon the subject of religious mutcers, have 
heen taken into minute consideration, The important and friendly services 
which the Porte has at all times, and more particularly of late, experienced on 
the part of her illustrious allies the English and other Governments, are appre- 
ciated in the highest degree by His Majesty the Sultan; and the feelings of 
gratitude inspired by them will remain for ever impressed upon the heart of the 
Ottoman nation. In addition to the sincere desire entertained by the Porte to 
meet, as far as 1s possible, the friendly representations of her allies by satis- 
factory measures, she is also well acquainted with the spirit of the age; and she 
hastens accordingly, with the Imperial sanction, to communicate the decision 
adopted regarding the above point, In consequence, the assurances formerly 
wiven to the British and French Governments with reference to the question of 
renegades are at present renewed and confirmed afresh, while an additional 
assurance is declared and made known that the terms of the decision at that 
time adopted will be held to comprise absolutely all renegades. It is sincerel 
hoped that this decision, which 1s a new and practical proof of the Porte's 
refraining on all oceasions from senselessly thwarting or opposing measures of a 


practicable nature, will meet with the satisfaction of your illustrious allies, 
(Signed) MEHEMET FUAD.

Inclosure in No. 440. 


Memorandum, 


THE question at issue between Russia and Turkey relative to the Tchoo- 
rooksoo frontier depends for its solution upon the settlement of the ancient 
frontier of Gouriel, from the Black Sea to Imeritia, which is adopted as the 
definite boundary between the two countries by the Treaty of Adrianople. ‘The 
actual territory in dispute may be defined as the triangle formed by the little 
Rivers Cholok and Chirapunia, and the mountain range containing their head 
waters. ‘The Russian claim rests upon the alleged authority of ancient Khans 
or Chiefs of Gouriel over the territory in question, as supported by evidence, 
oral and documentary. Evidence of a similar nature, consisting of berats, title- 
deeds of landed property, &e., is equally brought forward by the people of Tchoo- 
rooksoo on their side; but neither party admits the validity of the other's 
statements. In the year 1835 the district was provisionally made over to the 
people of Gouriel, to be possessed and occupied by them until the final settle- 
ment of the question, by Abdullah Pasha, the then Governor of ‘Trebizond, and 
this fact in itself denotes previous possession on the part of the Turks,

practised by the Turkish officials shall be put an end to, and that all the requisite 
arrangements for the organization of the troops, and for the defence of the 
place, shall be made without delay. I have accordingly to instruct your Excel- 
lency to make a communication to the above effect to the Porte, and to obtain 
its eee in the proposed arrangement, — 

At present there is no British officer at Ezeroom of sufficient rank for sa

Her Majesty’s Government are endeavouring by all means to effect, shall be sufhi- 
ciently strong to admit of his undertaking the duty, he would be unquestionably 
selected for ite But should that unfortunately not be the case, Her Majesty s 
Government will be prepared to name another officer of suitable rank whenever

Inclosure 1 in No. 438, 
Lord Stratford de Nedeliffe to Consul-General Colquhoun, 


Sir, Constantinople, February 16, 1856, 
THE intention of emancipating the Gypsies in Wallachia, as announced in 
your despatch No, | of this year, does credit to the Local Government, and it is 
satisfactory to know that the example set by the authorities of Jassy has operated 
with so fiir a promise at Bucharest. 

The measure will, no doubt, be incomplete unless a just indemnity be 
granted to those who are called upon to give up their Gypstes. But there is 
something so unjust and odious in the pretension of any man to hold his fellow 
creature in servitude against his will, that I sincerely hope the measure will be 
carried through, notwithstanding such possible difficulties as may stand in the 
way of assigning a full compensation to those proprietors who would have to 
resign their Gypsies. 

[ have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 443. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Karl of Clarendon.—(Received at Parts, 
February 28.) 


(Telegraphic.) Constantinople, February 27, 1856. 

THE new Imperial firman, great as are the prospects which it opens, will 
require much steady attention and vigilance to curry it into effect and insure its 
full results. I have acquainted you that its engagements, though indispensable 
for the regeneration of this Empire, cannot be left with any degree of confidence 
to the Turkish Government, Responsibility towards Europe must stimulate 
their sense of duty in that respect. 

The fourth point cannot therefore with or prudence be omitted 
from treatment. The right of superintendence which Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment refused to Russia, may be given without inconsistency to Europe, if care 
be taken that no single Power acquire a pretext [for] interference or on light 
grounds. The fear of joint interference from all can hardly fail to give weight 
to the representations of those who fought for the Turkish Empire and conquered 
its hest securities.

Inclosure 2 in No. 445, 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to Mr, Pisant. 


Sir, Pera, Felouary 19, 1856. 

[ AM vlad to learn from you that you remarked to Fuad Pasha, after the 
solemnity of yesterday, the defective character of the Sultun’s hatti-sherif, 
notwithstanding my previous exhortations and his assurances. | am glad also 
to learn that you lost no time in reminding him of several pending questions, 
which had been reserved till after the promulgation of the firman. 1 have now 
to instruct you on both subjects. You will inform the Secretary of State that I 
was much disappointed by the ordinary character of the hatt, which, as [under- 
stood from him, was to be more comprehensive, and calculated to show a deeper 
interest than usual in the enforcement of the firman. | have no pretention to 
prescribe the forms of what 1s an internal act of the Government, but I regret, 
on so important and vital an occasion, that anything capable of giving full 
weight and effect to the Sultan's most gracious intentions should have been. 
omitted or abridged; the more so as 1 had reason to believe that lis Excellency 
entered into my sentiments, and felt the importance of investing the Sultan's 
charter with all that might impress respect upon the people and confidence on 
foreign nations. Whut is done, ‘; done. Lnow look to the execution of the 
measures proclaimed, and to the fulfilment of all the reforms and improvements 
so solemnly promised. It would be a great satisfaction to know in what manner 
it is proposed to carry out the firman, and for that purpose what regulations are 
to be framed, and what auxiliary steps to be taken. 

With respect to the pending questions alluded to above, 1 earnestly solicit 
attention ta the representations which you addressed to Fuad Pasha yesterday 
with much propriety. There is the Greck Convention on brigandage; the 
transfer of the Tirjaret; the improvement of the eustom-house ; the settlement 
of the harbour dues; the recruitment of the Contingent. There may be others, 
which do not occur to ine at this moment, of less Importance indeed, but calling, 
nevertheless, far carly attention. 

[have to desire that you will talk these several matters: over with the 
Pasha, so as to ascertain his present state of mind respecting them, and to enable 
me to put them inore completely in train. 

T wish also that you would sound him as to the expediency of establishing 
1 Crédit-Mobilier Bank, In the opinion of mercantile people, there are sufficient 
elements for the creation and progress of such an institution, and [ am myself 
acquainted with a respectable iad intelligent individual having command of or 
necess to the necessary umount of capital who might be induced to embark in 
the enterprise and even to conduct tt. 

Nothing further remains to be suggested at this moment. 

L have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFPE, 


P.S.—I wish you to read this ‘yatruction to Mehemed Pasha as well as to 
Fuad.
